children.name: Perciformes
Percidae
Etheostoma
children.description: Typical darters are small, colorful freshwater fish that live on the bottom of streams, rivers, and ponds throughout New England. They get their name from their quick, darting swimming style as they move from rock to rock along the streambed. These fish are excellent indicators of water quality since they need clean, well-oxygenated water to survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish that swim continuously in the water column, typical darters have reduced swim bladders and spend most of their time resting on the bottom substrate. They have large pectoral fins that help them prop themselves up on rocks and gravel.
children.funFact: Male darters become incredibly vibrant during breeding season, developing bright blues, oranges, and reds to attract females and establish territories on the streambed.

children.name: Percina
children.description: Roughbelly darters are small freshwater fish that live on the bottom of rivers and streams throughout eastern North America. They get their name from the rough, sandpaper-like scales on their bellies that help them grip rocky surfaces in fast-flowing water. These slender fish are excellent swimmers that dart quickly between rocks while searching for small insects and other prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other darters, roughbelly darters have distinctly rough scales on their undersides and tend to be more elongated in shape. They also typically have more prominent snouts and are generally larger than most other darter species.
children.funFact: The Common Logperch can grow up to 7 inches long, making it one of the largest darter species in North America - much bigger than its tiny relatives that rarely exceed 3 inches!

children.name: Perca
children.description: Perches in the genus Perca are freshwater fish known for their distinctive spiny dorsal fins and vibrant coloration. These popular game fish are excellent predators that hunt smaller fish, insects, and crustaceans in lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers throughout temperate regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True perches have two separate dorsal fins - a spiny front fin and a soft-rayed rear fin - along with distinctive dark vertical bars on their sides. They're distinguished from other perch-like fish by their deeply forked tail and the sharp spines on their gill covers.
children.funFact: Yellow perch can live over 10 years and form large schools that work together to corral prey, with some schools containing thousands of individuals moving in synchronized hunting formations.

children.name: Sander
children.description: Pikeperches are freshwater fish that combine features of both pike and perch, despite being more closely related to perch. They are predatory fish with elongated bodies, sharp teeth, and excellent vision that helps them hunt in murky waters. These fish are prized by anglers for both their fighting ability and their tasty, flaky white meat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true perch, pikeperches have a more elongated, streamlined body shape and a distinctly pointed snout filled with sharp canine teeth. Their large, glassy eyes reflect light, giving them superior night vision compared to most other freshwater fish.
children.funFact: The walleye's scientific name 'vitreus' means 'glassy,' referring to their distinctive reflective eyes that glow when light hits them - a feature that helps them see prey in low-light conditions but also helps anglers spot them in the water.

children.name: Ammocrypta
children.description: Sand Darters are small, slender freshwater fish that have evolved to live in sandy river and stream bottoms. These specialized fish are perfectly adapted for burying themselves in sand, where they hunt for small invertebrates and hide from predators. They belong to the larger darter family, which includes many colorful and diverse freshwater fish species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other darters, Sand Darters have translucent, almost see-through bodies and lack the bright colors typical of their relatives. Their elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies and reduced fins make them perfectly suited for their sand-dwelling lifestyle.
children.funFact: Sand Darters can completely bury themselves in sand in just seconds, leaving only their eyes exposed to watch for prey and predators passing overhead.

children.description: The Percidae family includes some of New England's most important freshwater fish, from the familiar yellow perch caught by anglers to tiny colorful darters that dart along stream bottoms. These fish are characterized by having two separate dorsal fins - a spiny front fin and a soft-rayed back fin - along with spiny rays in their anal fins. Most species are predators that feed on smaller fish, aquatic insects, and crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Percids can be identified by their two distinct dorsal fins and the presence of spines in both their dorsal and anal fins. Unlike many other fish families, they have rough, sandpaper-like scales called ctenoid scales.
children.funFact: Many darter species are so small and specialized that they live their entire lives in just a few square meters of stream bottom, with some species found only in specific types of rocky riffles or sandy pools.

children.name: Gasterosteidae
Gasterosteus
children.description: Threespine sticklebacks are small, distinctive fish easily recognized by the three sharp spines along their backs. These hardy little fish can live in both freshwater and saltwater environments, making them remarkably adaptable to different aquatic habitats throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other stickleback species, members of this genus have exactly three prominent dorsal spines (rather than more or fewer), and they possess bony plates along their sides that can vary in number and coverage.
children.funFact: Threespine stickleback males are devoted fathers who build elaborate nests from aquatic plants and algae, then guard their eggs and fry with impressive dedication, even fanning them with their fins to provide oxygen.

children.name: Apeltes
children.description: Apeltes is a genus containing just one species - the Fourspine Stickleback, a small freshwater and brackish water fish found in coastal New England waters. These fish are part of the stickleback family and are characterized by their distinctive spines along their back and their ability to build elaborate nests.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sticklebacks that typically have three or more spines, members of Apeltes are unique in having exactly four dorsal spines (though sometimes three), which is reflected in their common name 'Fourspine Stickleback.'
children.funFact: Male Fourspine Sticklebacks are devoted fathers who build intricate barrel-shaped nests from plant material and algae, then guard their eggs and fry for weeks after spawning.

children.name: Pungitius
children.description: Nine-spined Sticklebacks are small freshwater fish known for their distinctive row of bony plates and spines along their backs. These hardy little fish are well-adapted to cold northern waters and can survive in both freshwater and brackish environments. They're closely related to the more familiar Three-spined Stickleback but represent their own distinct group.
children.distinguishingFeatures: As their name suggests, these sticklebacks typically have 8-11 dorsal spines (usually 9-10), which is more than their three-spined cousins. They also tend to be smaller and more slender, with a more elongated snout.
children.funFact: Male Nine-spined Sticklebacks turn jet black during breeding season and build elaborate nests from aquatic vegetation, where they court females and then guard the eggs until they hatch.

children.name: Culaea
children.description: Culaea is a genus containing just one species - the Brook Stickleback, a small freshwater fish found in cool northern waters. These fish are characterized by having several sharp spines along their back and are part of the stickleback family, known for their unique breeding behaviors and armor-like plates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brook Sticklebacks can be distinguished from other sticklebacks by having 5-6 dorsal spines (rather than 3 like three-spined sticklebacks) and by lacking the bony plates along their sides that many other stickleback species possess.
children.funFact: Brook Sticklebacks are one of the few fish species that can survive being completely frozen in ice during winter - they produce antifreeze proteins that prevent ice crystals from forming in their body fluids.

children.description: Sticklebacks are small, spiny freshwater and marine fish known for their distinctive rows of sharp spines along their backs and sides. These hardy fish are found in ponds, streams, and coastal waters throughout New England, where they play important roles in aquatic food webs. Most species are quite small, typically measuring just 2-4 inches long.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sticklebacks are easily recognized by their prominent dorsal spines (usually 3-9 depending on species) and their lack of scales, instead having bony plates along their sides. Unlike most fish, they can lock their spines upright as a defense mechanism against predators.
children.funFact: Male sticklebacks are devoted fathers who build elaborate nests from plant material and guard their eggs and young, even fanning them with their fins to provide fresh oxygen.

children.name: Triglidae
Prionotus
children.description: Prionotus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as searobins, characterized by their large pectoral fins and ability to "walk" along the ocean floor. These bottom-dwelling fish use modified fin rays like legs to move across sandy and muddy seafloors while searching for food. They are distinctive coastal fish found in temperate Atlantic waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bottom fish, searobins have enlarged, wing-like pectoral fins and several free fin rays that act like sensitive fingers for walking and detecting prey in sediment.
children.funFact: Searobins can produce loud grunting and croaking sounds by vibrating muscles against their swim bladders, which is how they got their name - they sound like robins chirping underwater!

children.name: Peristedion
children.description: Peristedion is a genus of bottom-dwelling fish commonly known as armored searobins or armored gurnards. These fish are characterized by their heavily armored bodies covered in bony plates and ridges, along with large, fan-like pectoral fins that they use to 'walk' along the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other searobins, Peristedion species have extensive bony armor plating covering their heads and bodies, giving them a distinctly angular, almost box-like appearance. They also have a more pronounced snout and smaller mouths compared to their less-armored relatives.
children.funFact: Armored searobins use their modified pectoral fin rays like fingers to probe the seafloor sediment for buried prey, essentially 'feeling around' in the mud for small crustaceans and worms.

children.description: Searobins are bottom-dwelling marine fish with distinctive fan-like pectoral fins and armored heads covered in bony plates. These fascinating fish use modified fin rays as leg-like appendages to 'walk' along the seafloor while searching for food. They're known for the croaking or grunting sounds they make using their swim bladders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Searobins are easily recognized by their oversized, wing-like pectoral fins and the free fin rays that extend from these fins like fingers. Their heavily armored heads with bony ridges and spines set them apart from other bottom fish.
children.funFact: Searobins can actually taste with their walking fin rays, using them like tongues to detect buried prey in the sand and mud.

children.name: Cottidae
Cottus
children.description: Freshwater sculpins are small, bottom-dwelling fish that live in cold, clear streams and lakes throughout New England. These hardy little fish have large heads, wide mouths, and fan-like pectoral fins that help them grip the rocky bottoms where they hunt for insects and small crustaceans. They're perfectly adapted to life in fast-flowing, oxygen-rich waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other freshwater fish, sculpins lack swim bladders and have smooth, scaleless skin covered in a protective slime coating. Their oversized heads and tapering bodies give them a distinctive tadpole-like appearance.
children.funFact: Sculpins are such devoted parents that males will guard their eggs under rocks for weeks, fanning them with their fins and fighting off any intruders that threaten their nest.

children.description: Typical sculpins are small, bottom-dwelling fish with large heads and wide mouths that live in cold, clear waters. They have smooth, scaleless skin and fan-like pectoral fins that they use to prop themselves up on rocks and gravel bottoms. These hardy fish are well-adapted to life in fast-flowing streams and rocky lake shores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other fish, sculpins lack swim bladders and must rest on the bottom rather than hovering in the water column. Their oversized heads, tapering bodies, and mottled brown coloration help them blend perfectly with rocky substrates.
children.funFact: Sculpins are such devoted parents that males will guard their eggs under rocks for weeks, fanning them with their fins to keep them oxygenated and clean.

children.name: Psychrolutidae
Myoxocephalus
children.description: Shorthorn sculpins are a group of bottom-dwelling fish found in the cold waters of New England's rocky shores and deeper ocean areas. These sturdy fish have large, spiny heads with prominent eyes and wide mouths, giving them a somewhat prehistoric appearance. All members of this group are well-adapted to life on the seafloor, where they hunt for small crustaceans, worms, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sculpins, shorthorn sculpins have relatively short spines above their eyes and distinctive patterns of head spines that help identify each species. Their bodies are typically more robust and their fins are positioned for life spent resting on rocky or sandy bottoms.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating spiny appearance, shorthorn sculpins are excellent parents - the males guard their bright orange or yellow egg masses for weeks until they hatch, fanning them with their fins to keep them oxygenated.

children.description: Fathead sculpins are bottom-dwelling marine fish with large, broad heads and wide mouths that give them their distinctive appearance. These cold-water fish are well-adapted to life on the seafloor, where they hunt for small crustaceans, worms, and other invertebrates. They're typically found in northern oceans and can tolerate very cold temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sculpin families, fathead sculpins have particularly large, flattened heads relative to their body size and lack scales on most of their body. Their pectoral fins are notably large and fan-like, helping them maneuver along the bottom.
children.funFact: Some fathead sculpins can survive being frozen solid in Arctic waters and will revive when temperatures warm up, thanks to natural antifreeze proteins in their blood.

children.name: Epinephelidae
Hyporthodus
children.description: Hyporthodus is a genus of large, deep-water groupers found in tropical and subtropical oceans around the world. These are robust, heavy-bodied fish that typically live near the bottom in deeper waters, often around rocky reefs and ledges. They are skilled predators that feed on smaller fish, crustaceans, and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hyporthodus are distinguished from other grouper genera by their specific body proportions, fin ray counts, and coloration patterns. They tend to be among the larger groupers and often have more compressed bodies compared to their shallow-water relatives.
children.funFact: The Snowy Grouper can live over 40 years and doesn't reach sexual maturity until it's around 7-10 years old, making it particularly vulnerable to overfishing.

children.name: Epinephelus
children.description: Epinephelus is a genus of large, robust marine fish commonly known as groupers. These predatory fish are characterized by their broad mouths, heavy bodies, and ability to rapidly change color patterns. They are typically found in warm coastal waters and are popular among both commercial and recreational fishers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Epinephelus can be distinguished from other grouper genera by their specific fin ray counts, scale patterns, and jaw structure. They typically have 11 dorsal fin spines and lack the prominent canine teeth found in some related grouper species.
children.funFact: Many Epinephelus species are sequential hermaphrodites, starting life as females and later transforming into males as they grow larger and older.

children.name: Mycteroperca
children.description: Mycteroperca is a genus of large, robust groupers found in warm and temperate ocean waters. These fish are characterized by their heavy bodies, large mouths, and ability to change colors and patterns for camouflage and communication. They are important predators in marine ecosystems, feeding on smaller fish, crustaceans, and cephalopods.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Mycteroperca are distinguished from other groupers by their particularly large size potential, elongated body shape, and distinctive color-changing abilities that often include complex mottled patterns.
children.funFact: Many Mycteroperca groupers are protogynous hermaphrodites, meaning they start life as females and can transform into males as they age and grow larger, usually when they reach a certain size or when social conditions favor the change.

children.description: Groupers are large, heavy-bodied marine fish known for their impressive size and voracious appetites. These predatory fish have big mouths that can expand to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves, and they're often found lurking around rocky reefs and underwater structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Groupers are distinguished by their massive heads, large mouths with protruding lower jaws, and robust, stocky bodies. Unlike many other reef fish, they lack the bright colors and instead display mottled patterns of browns, grays, and greens that help them blend with rocky surroundings.
children.funFact: Many groupers are protogynous hermaphrodites, meaning they start life as females and later transform into males when they reach a certain size or age.

children.name: Liparidae
Liparis
children.description: Liparis is a genus of small, tadpole-shaped fish commonly known as snailfish. These soft-bodied marine fish have smooth, scaleless skin and are typically found in cold waters along the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snailfish have a distinctive sucker disk on their belly formed by modified pelvic fins, which they use to attach to rocks and other surfaces in strong currents.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate appearance, some snailfish species hold the record for living at the greatest depths of any fish, surviving in ocean trenches over 26,000 feet below the surface.

children.description: Snailfishes are small, soft-bodied marine fish with loose, gelatinous skin that gives them their distinctive appearance. They have large pectoral fins and a sucker disc on their belly formed by fused pelvic fins, which they use to attach to rocks and other surfaces on the ocean floor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, snailfishes have no scales and their skin feels slippery and jelly-like to the touch. Their fused pelvic fins create a circular sucker that allows them to cling to surfaces in strong currents.
children.funFact: Snailfishes hold the record for living at the greatest depths of any fish - some species have been found thriving in ocean trenches nearly 5 miles below the surface!

children.name: Scorpaenidae
Sebastes
children.description: Rockfishes are a large genus of marine fish known for their spiny fins and ability to live for exceptionally long periods. These bottom-dwelling fish are typically found in rocky areas and deep waters, where they feed on smaller fish and crustaceans. Most rockfish species give birth to live young rather than laying eggs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rockfishes are distinguished by their prominent spiny dorsal fins, large eyes, and robust bodies with thick scales. They differ from other similar fish by having venomous spines and typically reddish or orange coloration.
children.funFact: Some rockfish species can live for over 200 years, making them among the longest-lived fish in the world!

children.name: Helicolenus
children.description: Helicolenus is a genus of marine fish known as rockfish or ocean perch that live in deep waters along continental slopes. These fish are characterized by their robust bodies, large heads with prominent eyes, and venomous spines on their dorsal fins. They are slow-growing, long-lived fish that typically inhabit rocky bottoms in depths ranging from moderate to very deep waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Helicolenus are distinguished from other rockfish by their particularly large eyes adapted for deep-water vision and their distinctive coloration patterns with reddish or orange hues. They also have a more elongated body shape compared to many shallow-water rockfish species.
children.funFact: Blackbelly Rosefish can live for over 40 years and don't reach sexual maturity until they're around 10-15 years old, making them particularly vulnerable to overfishing.

children.description: Scorpionfishes are marine fish known for their spiny fins and often venomous spines that can deliver painful stings. They typically have large heads, wide mouths, and mottled coloration that helps them blend in with rocky bottoms and coral reefs. Most species are bottom-dwellers that ambush small fish and crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Scorpionfishes can be identified by their prominent venomous spines in the dorsal, anal, and pelvic fins, along with their characteristically large, bony heads. Their eyes are usually positioned high on their heads, and they often have elaborate skin flaps or projections that aid in camouflage.
children.funFact: Some scorpionfishes are masters of disguise - they can change color and have skin flaps that make them nearly indistinguishable from algae-covered rocks on the seafloor.

children.name: Pholidae
Pholis
children.description: Pholis is a genus of small, elongated marine fish commonly known as gunnels. These slender, eel-like fish are adapted for life in rocky intertidal zones where they can squeeze into tight crevices and under rocks during low tide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gunnels have extremely compressed, ribbon-like bodies with long dorsal fins that run almost the entire length of their backs, and they lack pelvic fins entirely.
children.funFact: Rock gunnels can survive out of water for hours during low tide by breathing air through their skin and gills, allowing them to hide under seaweed and in tide pools.

children.description: Gunnels are elongated, eel-like marine fish that live in shallow coastal waters along rocky shores. They have long, ribbon-shaped bodies and a continuous dorsal fin that runs along most of their back, making them well-adapted for squeezing into tight crevices between rocks and under seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, gunnels have separate pectoral fins and their long dorsal fin is supported by hard spines rather than soft rays. Their bodies are laterally compressed (flattened from side to side) rather than cylindrical like an eel's.
children.funFact: Rock gunnels can survive out of water for hours during low tide by wrapping their flexible bodies in coils under damp seaweed, breathing through their skin and gills as long as they stay moist.

children.name: Serranidae
Centropristis
children.description: Centropristis is a genus of marine fish commonly known as sea bass, found along the Atlantic coast. These are robust, bottom-dwelling fish that prefer rocky reefs, wrecks, and other hard-bottom habitats where they can hunt for crabs, fish, and other prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their stocky build, large mouth, and ability to change color patterns. They have strong spines in their dorsal fins and are protogynous hermaphrodites, meaning they can change from female to male as they age.
children.funFact: Black sea bass start life as females and transform into males when they reach about 9-13 inches long, with the largest, most dominant fish in an area typically being males.

children.description: Sea basses are a diverse family of marine fish found in warm and temperate waters around the world. They are typically predatory fish with robust bodies, large mouths, and strong jaws equipped with sharp teeth for catching smaller fish and crustaceans. Most species have spiny dorsal fins and are known for being excellent table fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sea basses can be distinguished from other fish families by their combination of spiny and soft-rayed dorsal fins, large mouths that extend past their eyes, and typically three spines on their anal fins. Many species also have the ability to rapidly change color patterns for camouflage or communication.
children.funFact: Many sea bass species are hermaphrodites that start life as females and later transform into males as they grow larger and older, a strategy that helps ensure reproductive success in their populations.

children.name: Hemitripteridae
Hemitripterus
children.description: Hemitripterus is a genus of sculpin fish found in cold northern waters. These bottom-dwelling fish are characterized by their large, flattened heads and bodies covered in spines and bony plates that give them excellent camouflage among rocks and seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively large pectoral fins and multiple rows of sharp spines along their backs and sides, making them easily recognizable among other sculpins.
children.funFact: Sea ravens can change color to match their surroundings, shifting from reddish-brown to dark green or mottled gray depending on the ocean floor beneath them.

children.description: Sea ravens are distinctive bottom-dwelling fish found in cold northern waters. They have large, flattened heads with prominent spines and ridges, giving them a somewhat fearsome appearance despite being relatively small fish that typically grow to about a foot in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sea ravens can be distinguished from other sculpins by their extremely large pectoral fins that they spread like wings, and their ability to change color dramatically to match their surroundings.
children.funFact: Sea ravens get their name from their large, wing-like pectoral fins and their habit of "flying" along the seafloor by spreading these fins wide as they glide from rock to rock.

children.name: Cyclopteridae
Cyclopterus
children.description: Cyclopterus is a genus of unusual fish known as lumpfish or lumpsuckers. These chunky, round-bodied fish are easily recognized by their distinctive appearance and their ability to cling to surfaces using a specialized sucker disc on their belly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, lumpfish have thick, gelatinous skin covered in tubercles (bumps) instead of typical scales, and possess a powerful ventral sucker disc that allows them to attach firmly to rocks and other surfaces.
children.funFact: Male lumpfish are devoted fathers who guard their eggs for up to two months, rarely leaving the nest and often changing color from blue-green to bright red during breeding season.

children.description: Lumpfishes are round, chunky marine fish with thick, scaleless skin covered in rows of bony tubercles or bumps. They have a distinctive sucker disc on their belly formed from modified pelvic fins, which they use to attach to rocks and other surfaces in cold northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish families, lumpfishes have a powerful ventral sucker disc and lack scales, instead having thick skin covered in bony bumps or tubercles arranged in rows.
children.funFact: Male lumpfish are devoted fathers who guard their bright orange or red egg masses for up to two months, rarely leaving to feed and often turning dark colors while protecting their nest.

children.name: Stichaeidae
Ulvaria
children.description: Ulvaria is a small genus of marine fish in the blenny family found in cold northern waters. These bottom-dwelling fish are characterized by their elongated bodies and ability to live in shallow coastal areas where they can tolerate exposure during low tides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Ulvaria can be distinguished from other blennies by their distinctive radiation-like pattern of lines extending from their eyes, which gives the Radiated Shanny its common name.
children.funFact: Radiated Shannies can survive out of water for several hours during low tide by breathing through their skin and gills, allowing them to live in tide pools and rocky intertidal zones.

children.description: Pricklebacks are elongated, eel-like marine fish that live in cold coastal waters. They get their name from the sharp, spiny dorsal fin that runs along most of their back, giving them a 'prickly' appearance. These bottom-dwelling fish are well-adapted to life among rocks, kelp, and tide pools.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pricklebacks can be distinguished from other eel-like fish by their continuous, spiny dorsal fin and their scaleless or small-scaled skin. Unlike true eels, they have separate pectoral fins and a more compressed body shape.
children.funFact: Many pricklebacks can survive out of water for several hours during low tide by breathing air through their skin and gill chambers, making them perfectly suited for life in the intertidal zone.

children.name: Zoarcidae
Zoarces
children.description: Zoarces is a genus of elongated, eel-like marine fish known as ocean pouts. These bottom-dwelling fish have smooth, scaleless skin and are well-adapted to cold northern waters where they live among rocks and in crevices on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ocean pouts can be distinguished from true eels by their separate dorsal, tail, and anal fins, whereas eels have these fins connected in one continuous fin around the tail.
children.funFact: Ocean pouts have natural antifreeze proteins in their blood that prevent ice crystals from forming, allowing them to survive in near-freezing Arctic and sub-Arctic waters.

children.description: Eelpouts are elongated, eel-like fish that live in cold marine waters around the world. They have long, compressed bodies with continuous fins that run along their backs and bellies, giving them a serpentine appearance. These bottom-dwelling fish are well-adapted to life in chilly waters and can be found from shallow coastal areas to the deep sea.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, eelpouts have pelvic fins located near their throats and lack the characteristic jaw structure of eels. Their long dorsal and anal fins are separate from their tail fin, and they have small, embedded scales rather than the smooth skin of many eel species.
children.funFact: Some eelpout species can survive in near-freezing Arctic waters thanks to special antifreeze proteins in their blood that prevent ice crystals from forming in their bodies.

children.name: Anarhichadidae
Anarhichas
children.description: Anarhichas is a genus of large, eel-like marine fish commonly known as wolffish. These bottom-dwelling predators are characterized by their elongated bodies, powerful jaws, and prominent canine teeth that give them their fearsome appearance. They inhabit cold northern waters and are well-adapted to life on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wolffish are distinguished from other marine fish by their distinctive dog-like canine teeth and crushing molars, which they use to feed on hard-shelled prey like sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks. Their scaleless, slimy skin and ability to produce antifreeze proteins also set them apart from most other fish species.
children.funFact: Despite their intimidating appearance, Atlantic Wolffish are actually quite docile and have been known to recognize and interact with human divers, sometimes even allowing themselves to be petted like underwater dogs.

children.description: Wolffishes are large, eel-like marine fish known for their massive heads and powerful jaws filled with prominent teeth. These bottom-dwelling predators are built for crushing hard-shelled prey like sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks in cold northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wolffishes are distinguished by their enormous canine-like front teeth and strong crushing teeth in the back of their mouths, along with their long, scaleless bodies that lack pelvic fins.
children.funFact: Despite their fearsome appearance and nickname "sea wolves," wolffishes are generally docile toward humans and some species are known to be quite curious and even playful around divers.

children.name: Cryptacanthodidae
Cryptacanthodes
children.description: Cryptacanthodes is a genus containing just one species of fish - the wrymouth. These are elongated, eel-like marine fish that live in cold northern waters and are known for their ability to burrow into sandy or muddy bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wrymouths have extremely long, ribbon-like bodies with a continuous fin running along their back and underside, plus a distinctive upward-angled mouth that gives them their common name.
children.funFact: The wrymouth can grow up to 3 feet long but spends most of its time buried in the seafloor with just its head sticking out, waiting to ambush small fish and crustaceans.

children.description: Wrymouths are unusual marine fish with elongated, eel-like bodies and distinctive twisted mouths that give them their name. These bottom-dwelling fish live in cold northern waters and spend much of their time burrowing in sandy or muddy seafloors. They belong to a small family with very few species worldwide.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Wrymouths are easily recognized by their asymmetrical, twisted mouths where the lower jaw curves to one side, and their long, ribbon-like bodies that can reach up to 3 feet in length. Unlike true eels, they have distinct dorsal and anal fins that run along most of their body.
children.funFact: The wrymouth's bizarre twisted mouth isn't just for show - it's perfectly adapted for catching small crustaceans and worms while the fish lies partially buried in the seafloor sediment.

children.name: Lumpenidae
Lumpenus
children.description: Lumpenus is a genus of elongated marine fish commonly known as snakeblennies due to their snake-like appearance and swimming motion. These bottom-dwelling fish have long, slender bodies and are found in cold northern waters where they hide among rocks and seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snakeblennies are distinguished from other blennies by their extremely elongated, eel-like bodies and their habit of weaving through the water with serpentine movements.
children.funFact: Despite their name and appearance, snakeblennies are not related to snakes or eels, but are actually members of the blenny family that evolved their elongated shape to navigate through tight spaces in rocky underwater habitats.

children.description: Eel pricklebacks are elongated, eel-like fish that live in cold marine waters. They have continuous dorsal fins that run along most of their back, giving them a ribbon-like appearance as they swim through kelp forests and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, pricklebacks have pelvic fins and their dorsal fin is made up entirely of spiny rays rather than soft rays.
children.funFact: Despite their name and eel-like appearance, pricklebacks are more closely related to sculpins and other spiny-finned fish than to true eels.

children.description: Perciformes is one of the largest and most diverse orders of fish, containing everything from the familiar yellow perch in our ponds to the spiny sculpins hiding under coastal rocks. These fish are united by having spiny rays in their fins and typically possess two separate dorsal fins or a single fin with both spiny and soft-rayed portions. Members of this group have adapted to virtually every aquatic habitat in New England, from freshwater streams to the deep ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most perciform fish have spiny fin rays (especially in the front dorsal fin), scales that are typically rough to the touch, and a swim bladder that lacks a connection to the digestive tract. Their pelvic fins are usually positioned close to or slightly behind their pectoral fins, giving them excellent maneuverability.
children.funFact: This order includes some of New England's most unusual fish, including the blobfish-related fathead sculpins that live in our deep waters, and the antifreeze-producing eelpouts that survive in near-freezing ocean temperatures.

children.name: Cypriniformes
Leuciscidae
Notropis
children.description: Eastern Shiners are small, silvery freshwater fish that belong to the minnow family and are commonly found in New England's streams, rivers, and lakes. These sleek fish typically measure 2-4 inches long and are known for their shimmering, metallic appearance that helps them blend with sunlit water. They're important members of aquatic food webs, feeding on small insects and plankton while serving as prey for larger fish, birds, and other wildlife.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Eastern Shiners can be distinguished from other minnows by their compressed, streamlined bodies and prominent lateral line that runs along their sides. Many species also have distinctive coloration patterns, such as the rosy cheeks of the Rosyface Shiner or the dark stripe of the Blacknose Shiner.
children.funFact: Emerald Shiners are so reflective that commercial fishermen once used them to make artificial fishing lures, coating hooks with their silvery scales to attract larger game fish.

children.name: Semotilus
children.description: Creek chubs are medium-sized freshwater fish that belong to the minnow family and are well-adapted to life in streams and rivers. These hardy fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies, relatively large scales, and ability to thrive in a variety of water conditions from clear mountain streams to slower-moving creeks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Creek chubs can be distinguished from other minnows by their larger size, prominent scales, and the presence of a small barbel (whisker-like projection) at the corner of their mouth. They also typically have a more robust, torpedo-shaped body compared to most other minnow species.
children.funFact: Male creek chubs become master architects during breeding season, using their mouths to move stones and build impressive dome-shaped nests that can be over 3 feet wide and contain thousands of carefully arranged pebbles.

children.name: Rhinichthys
children.description: Riffle daces are small, streamlined freshwater fish that have adapted to life in fast-flowing, rocky streams and rivers. These hardy little fish are perfectly built for navigating swift currents, with their torpedo-shaped bodies and strong fins helping them dart between rocks and through rapids.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other minnows, riffle daces have distinctively pointed, overhanging snouts that help them probe for food in rocky crevices. Their bodies are typically more cylindrical and streamlined than their pond-dwelling relatives.
children.funFact: Riffle daces are like the mountain goats of the fish world - they can actually swim upstream through surprisingly strong currents and even navigate up small waterfalls by using their powerful tail fins and the turbulence created by rocks.

children.name: Chrosomus
children.description: Redbelly daces are small, colorful freshwater fish that belong to the minnow family. These slender fish are known for their distinctive reddish coloration on their bellies and sides, which becomes especially vibrant during breeding season. They prefer cool, clear waters like streams, ponds, and shallow lake areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other daces, redbelly daces have that characteristic reddish-orange coloration on their undersides and often display two dark stripes along their sides. They also tend to be smaller and more delicate-looking than their close relatives.
children.funFact: Northern Redbelly Daces can actually hybridize with Finescale Dace where their ranges overlap, creating offspring that combine features from both parent species.

children.name: Pimephales
children.description: Bluntnose minnows are small, hardy freshwater fish known for their characteristically rounded, blunt snouts. These chunky little minnows are common in streams, ponds, and lakes throughout New England, where they play important roles as both predators of small aquatic creatures and prey for larger fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other minnows, bluntnose minnows have distinctly rounded, blunt heads rather than pointed snouts. They also tend to be more robust and deeper-bodied than their sleeker minnow relatives.
children.funFact: Male bluntnose minnows become devoted fathers during breeding season, developing breeding tubercles on their heads and aggressively guarding their nests while fanning the eggs with their fins to keep them oxygenated.

children.name: Notemigonus
children.description: Notemigonus is a genus containing just one species - the Golden Shiner, a small freshwater fish found throughout eastern North America. These fish are characterized by their compressed, silvery bodies and are important members of lake and pond ecosystems. They serve as both predators of small aquatic organisms and prey for larger fish, making them a crucial link in freshwater food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Golden Shiners are distinguished from other minnows by their deeply compressed body shape, relatively large scales, and distinctive golden-bronze coloration on their sides. They also have a complete lateral line and a small, slightly upturned mouth.
children.funFact: Golden Shiners are one of the most widely used baitfish in North America, with millions raised in commercial fish farms specifically for anglers trying to catch bass, pike, and other game fish.

children.name: Luxilus
children.description: Highscale Shiners are a group of freshwater minnows known for their silvery appearance and relatively large, prominent scales. These active schooling fish are commonly found in streams and rivers throughout eastern North America, where they play important roles in aquatic food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their notably large scales compared to other shiners, giving them their "highscale" common name. They also typically have deeper, more compressed bodies than many of their close relatives.
children.funFact: During breeding season, male Common Shiners develop bright colors and tubercles (small bumps) on their heads and fins, transforming from plain silver fish into surprisingly colorful courtship displays.

children.name: Couesius
children.description: Couesius is a small genus of freshwater fish in the minnow family, represented in New England by a single hardy species. These fish are adapted to cooler northern waters and are typically found in lakes and streams with rocky or gravelly bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lake chubs in this genus have a distinctive barbel (small whisker-like projection) at the corner of their mouth, which helps distinguish them from other similar minnows that lack this feature.
children.funFact: The Lake Chub is one of the most cold-tolerant freshwater fish in North America, thriving in waters that are too cold for most other minnow species.

children.name: Hudsonius
children.description: Hudsonius is a genus of small freshwater fish commonly known as shiners. These silvery minnows are characterized by their streamlined bodies and distinctive spotted tail fins that give them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of this genus is the prominent dark spot at the base of the tail fin, which distinguishes them from other similar-looking minnow species.
children.funFact: Spottail shiners are excellent indicators of water quality - they prefer clean, well-oxygenated waters and their presence often signals a healthy aquatic ecosystem.

children.name: Cyprinella
children.description: Satinfin Shiners are a genus of small, silvery freshwater fish in the minnow family. They are characterized by their streamlined bodies and distinctive fin patterns, with males often developing bright colors and enlarged fins during breeding season.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These shiners are distinguished from other minnows by their relatively deep, compressed bodies and the males' dramatically enlarged, colorful fins during spawning season.
children.funFact: Male Satinfin Shiners become living jewels during breeding season, developing brilliant red, orange, and blue colors while their fins grow dramatically larger to attract females and defend territory.

children.name: Scardinius
children.description: Rudds are freshwater fish in the carp and minnow family, characterized by their deep, laterally compressed bodies and bright reddish fins. They are primarily herbivorous fish that feed on aquatic plants, algae, and small invertebrates in slow-moving waters like ponds, lakes, and river backwaters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rudds can be distinguished from similar fish like roach by their upturned mouth, which is adapted for surface feeding, and their distinctive golden-bronze coloration with bright red or orange fins.
children.funFact: The Common Rudd is actually native to Europe and was introduced to New England waters, where it's sometimes called the 'American roach' despite being neither truly American nor a true roach.

children.name: Exoglossum
children.description: Cutlip Minnows are a small genus of freshwater fish found in eastern North America's clear, rocky streams and rivers. These minnows are named for their distinctive three-lobed lower lip, which gives them their characteristic 'cutlip' appearance. They are active swimmers that prefer well-oxygenated waters with gravel or rocky bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The unique three-lobed lower lip immediately sets Cutlip Minnows apart from all other minnow species. This specialized mouth structure, combined with their relatively large size compared to other minnows, makes them unmistakable.
children.funFact: The Cutlip Minnow's scientific name 'maxillingua' literally means 'big tongue,' referring to their prominent lower lip that looks somewhat like an extended tongue.

children.name: Hybognathus
children.description: Silvery Minnows are small, streamlined freshwater fish known for their distinctive silvery coloration and elongated bodies. These minnows are specialized filter feeders that primarily consume algae and organic matter by scraping it from surfaces or filtering it from the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other minnows, Silvery Minnows have a unique feeding mechanism with a specialized intestinal tract that can be up to 10 times their body length, allowing them to efficiently digest plant material and algae.
children.funFact: The Eastern Silvery Minnow's incredibly long intestine is coiled like a spring inside its small body, making it one of the most efficient plant-eating fish in North American freshwater systems.

children.name: Paranotropis
children.description: Paranotropis is a genus of small freshwater fish commonly known as shiners, which are members of the minnow family. These silvery fish are typically found in streams, rivers, and lakes throughout eastern North America. They are schooling fish that feed primarily on small insects, zooplankton, and plant matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Paranotropis shiners are distinguished from other minnow genera by their specific fin ray counts, scale patterns, and internal anatomical features. The Mimic Shiner in particular has a distinctive lateral line pattern and coloration that helps separate it from closely related species.
children.funFact: The Mimic Shiner gets its name from its remarkable ability to closely resemble other shiner species in areas where their ranges overlap, making it one of the most challenging fish for even experienced ichthyologists to identify in the field.

children.name: Margariscus
children.description: Pearl Daces are small, silvery freshwater fish found in cool, clear streams and rivers. They are members of the minnow family and are known for their distinctive pearl-like silvery coloration that gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pearl Daces can be distinguished from other minnows by their deeply forked tail, relatively large scales, and characteristic silvery-white coloration with a dark lateral stripe along their sides.
children.funFact: Pearl Daces are considered indicator species for clean, cold water environments - their presence often signals a healthy stream ecosystem with good water quality.

children.name: Miniellus
children.description: Miniellus is a small genus of freshwater minnows that are part of the larger carp and minnow family. These small, slender fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies and preference for sandy or gravelly stream bottoms where they feed on small invertebrates and organic matter.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Miniellus are distinguished from other minnows by their relatively small size, translucent appearance, and specialized feeding behavior adapted for sifting through sandy substrates.
children.funFact: The genus name Miniellus literally means 'little small one,' reflecting these fish's diminutive size - they rarely exceed 3 inches in length.

children.description: True Minnows are a diverse family of small to medium-sized freshwater fish that inhabit streams, rivers, ponds, and lakes throughout New England. These fish typically have streamlined bodies, small scales, and lack teeth in their jaws, instead using specialized throat teeth called pharyngeal teeth to process food. They play crucial ecological roles as both prey for larger fish and predators of aquatic insects and small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small freshwater fish, true minnows have pharyngeal teeth in their throats rather than jaw teeth, and they possess a distinctive lateral line system for detecting water movement. Most species also have a forked tail and cycloid (smooth-edged) scales.
children.funFact: Many true minnows are incredibly important baitfish that support entire aquatic food webs - a single school of shiners can feed everything from bass and pike to herons and kingfishers!

children.name: Catostomidae
Catostomus
children.description: Common suckers are freshwater fish with distinctive downward-facing mouths that they use to vacuum up food from lake and river bottoms. These hardy fish are found throughout New England's cooler waters, where they play important roles as both predators of aquatic insects and prey for larger fish like bass and pike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sucker species, common suckers have relatively thick lips and can tolerate a wider range of water temperatures and conditions. Their mouths are positioned on the underside of their heads, perfectly adapted for bottom-feeding.
children.funFact: White suckers can live over 15 years and undertake impressive spawning migrations, sometimes traveling dozens of miles upstream to reproduce in shallow, rocky areas each spring.

children.name: Moxostoma
children.description: Redhorse suckers are medium to large freshwater fish found in New England's rivers and streams. They get their name from their reddish fins and their sucker-like mouths, which they use to vacuum up food from the bottom of waterways. These fish are bottom-feeders that play an important role in keeping aquatic ecosystems healthy by cleaning up debris and small organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Redhorse suckers can be identified by their distinctive red or orange-colored fins, especially the tail fin, and their downward-facing sucker mouths. Unlike other sucker fish, they have relatively large scales and streamlined bodies adapted for life in flowing water.
children.funFact: Redhorse suckers are excellent jumpers and can leap up waterfalls and over small dams during their spring spawning migrations, sometimes jumping several feet out of the water!

children.name: Erimyzon
children.description: Chubsuckers are small to medium-sized freshwater fish with thick, fleshy lips adapted for bottom feeding. They have elongated, somewhat compressed bodies and are typically found in slow-moving streams, ponds, and swamps throughout eastern North America. These fish are specialized sucker-feeders that play an important role in aquatic ecosystems by processing organic matter from stream and pond bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Chubsuckers are distinguished from other suckers by their more streamlined body shape and smaller adult size, typically reaching only 6-10 inches in length. Their thick, protruding lips and downward-facing mouth are less pronounced than those of larger sucker species.
children.funFact: Despite their name suggesting they're chubby, chubsuckers are actually quite slender compared to other members of the sucker family, and they can survive in waters with lower oxygen levels than many other fish species.

children.name: Carpiodes
children.description: Carpsuckers are freshwater fish that belong to the sucker family, characterized by their downward-facing mouths adapted for feeding along the bottom of rivers and lakes. They have elongated, somewhat compressed bodies and are filter feeders that strain small organisms and organic matter from mud and sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other suckers, carpsuckers have a more streamlined body shape and their dorsal fin has a distinctly long base with many rays, giving them a somewhat carp-like appearance despite being unrelated to true carps.
children.funFact: The quillback carpsucker gets its name from the sharp, quill-like first rays of its dorsal fin that stand prominently upright.

children.description: Suckers are a family of freshwater fish known for their distinctive downward-facing mouths that they use to feed along the bottom of rivers, lakes, and streams. These fish have thick, fleshy lips that help them vacuum up algae, small invertebrates, and organic matter from rocks and sediment. Most suckers are medium-sized fish with somewhat cylindrical bodies and are important members of freshwater ecosystems throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Suckers can be easily identified by their ventral (bottom-facing) mouths with protruding, sucker-like lips, which sets them apart from other freshwater fish families. Unlike many other bottom-feeders, suckers lack barbels (whisker-like structures) around their mouths.
children.funFact: Despite their somewhat unflattering name, suckers play a crucial ecological role as 'vacuum cleaners' of freshwater systems, helping to keep river and lake bottoms clean by consuming algae and detritus.

children.name: Cyprinidae
Cyprinus
children.description: Typical carps are large, robust freshwater fish known for their barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) near their mouths and their ability to thrive in various water conditions. These hardy fish are excellent bottom feeders, using their barbels to detect food in muddy substrates. They're among the most adaptable freshwater fish species in the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other carp family members, typical carps have four distinct barbels around their mouth and can grow quite large, often exceeding 20 pounds. They also have a distinctive row of large scales along their sides and a deeply forked tail fin.
children.funFact: European carp can live over 100 years and are considered symbols of good fortune in many cultures, with some individual koi (ornamental carp) selling for hundreds of thousands of dollars!

children.name: Carassius
children.description: Crucian carps are a group of freshwater fish that includes the familiar goldfish and several closely related species. These hardy fish are native to East Asia but have been widely introduced around the world as ornamental pond fish and aquarium pets. They are known for their ability to survive in a wide range of water conditions and temperatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crucian carps can be distinguished from other carp species by their deeper, more compressed body shape and lack of barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) around their mouth. They also have a distinctive convex profile along their back.
children.funFact: Goldfish can live for decades and grow quite large in the wild - the oldest recorded goldfish lived to 43 years old, and feral goldfish can reach over a foot in length!

children.description: Cyprinids are a large family of freshwater fish that includes carps, minnows, and goldfish. These fish are characterized by having no teeth in their jaws, but instead have specialized throat teeth called pharyngeal teeth that they use to process food. They are found in freshwater habitats around the world and are important both ecologically and economically.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cyprinids can be distinguished from other freshwater fish by their lack of jaw teeth, the presence of pharyngeal teeth in their throat, and typically having cycloid (smooth, round) scales. Most species also have a single dorsal fin and lack an adipose fin.
children.funFact: The common goldfish is actually a domesticated cyprinid that was selectively bred from wild crucian carp in China over 1,000 years ago, making it one of the earliest fish to be kept as pets.

children.name: Tincidae
Tinca
children.description: Tinca is a genus of freshwater fish in the carp family, represented in New England by a single species - the tench. These are sturdy, bottom-dwelling fish with thick, slimy skin and small scales that prefer slow-moving or still waters like ponds and quiet streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tench can be distinguished from other carp family members by their very small scales, thick mucus coating, and distinctive olive-green to bronze coloration with rounded fins.
children.funFact: Tench are sometimes called 'doctor fish' because other fish species were historically believed to rub against them to heal wounds, though this behavior is likely just normal social interaction.

children.description: Tenchs are a small family of freshwater fish known for their olive-green coloration and thick, slimy skin coating. These bottom-dwelling fish have small scales, rounded fins, and a distinctive barbel at each corner of their mouth that helps them find food in murky water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tenchs can be identified by their olive-green to golden-bronze color, very thick mucus layer covering their body, and the pair of small barbels at the corners of their mouth. Unlike many other freshwater fish, they have tiny scales and a notably rounded, almost paddle-like tail fin.
children.funFact: The tench's incredibly thick, slippery mucus coating was once believed by medieval people to have healing properties for other sick fish - earning it the nickname 'doctor fish' as other fish would rub against it.

children.name: Xenocyprididae
Ctenopharyngodon
children.description: Ctenopharyngodon is a genus of large freshwater fish commonly known as grass carp. These fish are native to eastern Asia but have been introduced to many parts of the world, including New England waters, primarily for aquatic vegetation control.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Grass carp are distinguished from other carp by their elongated body shape and specialized diet of aquatic plants. They have a distinctive blunt, rounded snout and pharyngeal teeth adapted for grinding vegetation.
children.funFact: A single grass carp can eat up to 40% of its body weight in aquatic plants each day, making them living lawn mowers for ponds and lakes.

children.description: East Asian Minnows are a family of freshwater fish originally native to rivers and lakes across East Asia, including China, Russia, and Mongolia. These fish are typically medium to large-sized cyprinids (members of the carp family) that have adapted to various freshwater environments from fast-flowing rivers to still waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other minnows and carps, East Asian Minnows tend to be larger in size and often have more specialized feeding habits, with some species being primarily herbivorous plant-eaters.
children.funFact: The single New England representative of this family, the grass carp, can grow over 4 feet long and eat up to 40% of its body weight in aquatic plants daily, making it both a valued tool for controlling aquatic weeds and a concern for ecosystem balance.

children.description: Cypriniformes is a large order of freshwater fish that includes many of the most common species you'll encounter in New England's rivers, streams, and lakes. These fish are characterized by having no teeth in their jaws, instead using specialized throat teeth called pharyngeal teeth to process food. They're typically small to medium-sized fish with streamlined bodies adapted for life in flowing water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most other fish, members of this order lack jaw teeth entirely and instead grind food using pharyngeal teeth located in their throats. Most species also have a distinctive alarm substance in their skin that warns other fish of danger when released.
children.funFact: The common goldfish is actually a member of this order and can live for over 40 years, with some individuals reportedly reaching over 100 years old in the wild!

children.name: Carangiformes
Carangidae
Caranx
children.description: Kingfishes in the genus Caranx are sleek, powerful marine fish known for their speed and agility in ocean waters. These fish have streamlined, silvery bodies built for fast swimming and are popular among both commercial and recreational fishermen. They're part of the jack family and are typically found in warmer coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Caranx species are characterized by their deeply forked tails, metallic silver coloration, and prominent lateral line that often has bony plates called scutes along the rear portion. They have relatively large eyes and strong, streamlined bodies that set them apart from other jack species.
children.funFact: Atlantic Crevalle Jacks can live over 37 years and are known for their incredible bursts of speed when hunting, often creating feeding frenzies that attract seabirds diving from above.

children.name: Selene
children.description: Lookdowns and moonfishes are distinctive silvery marine fish with extremely compressed, diamond-shaped bodies that look almost flat when viewed head-on. These fish inhabit coastal waters and are known for their reflective, mirror-like scales that help them blend with the shimmering ocean surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their bodies are much more laterally compressed than other jacks and pompanos, giving them an almost disc-like appearance. They also have distinctively high, pointed dorsal fins and deeply forked tails.
children.funFact: Young lookdowns have extremely long, thread-like fin extensions that can be longer than their entire body, which they lose as they mature into adults.

children.name: Trachinotus
children.description: Pompanos are sleek, silvery marine fish known for their compressed, diamond-shaped bodies and deeply forked tails. These fast-swimming fish are prized by both recreational anglers and commercial fisheries for their excellent eating quality and fighting ability when hooked.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pompanos can be distinguished from other jacks by their very deep, laterally compressed bodies and their blunt, rounded snouts. Unlike many of their jack relatives, they lack prominent scutes (bony plates) along their lateral line.
children.funFact: Florida Pompano are so highly valued as table fish that they're sometimes called 'the world's most edible fish' and can command premium prices at seafood markets.

children.name: Seriola
children.description: Amberjacks are fast-swimming marine fish known for their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies and powerful tails. These predatory fish are popular among sport fishermen for their impressive size and strong fighting ability when hooked. They typically inhabit warmer coastal and offshore waters, though some species venture into New England waters during summer months.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Amberjacks can be distinguished from other jacks by their elongated bodies, deeply forked tails, and distinctive yellow or amber-colored stripe that runs along their sides from eye to tail.
children.funFact: Greater Amberjacks are among the largest members of the jack family and can live over 15 years, growing up to 6 feet long and weighing over 170 pounds!

children.name: Alectis
children.description: Alectis is a genus of large, fast-swimming marine fish commonly known as pompanos or threadfins. These silvery, disc-shaped fish are prized by both commercial and recreational fishermen for their fighting ability and excellent taste.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Young Alectis fish are easily recognized by their extremely long, thread-like fin rays that can extend far beyond their body length, giving them a distinctive streaming appearance in the water.
children.funFact: Juvenile African Pompano have such dramatically long trailing fins that they look completely different from adults - the long streamers eventually break off or wear down as the fish matures.

children.name: Selar
children.description: Selar is a genus of marine fish commonly known as scads, which are fast-swimming schooling fish found in tropical and subtropical waters. These fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies and are part of the jack family, making them active predators that feed on smaller fish and plankton.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Selar are distinguished by their particularly large eyes (hence "bigeye" scad) and their metallic, silvery coloration with distinctive lateral lines along their sides.
children.funFact: Bigeye scads can form massive schools containing thousands of individuals that move together like a single organism to confuse predators and improve feeding efficiency.

children.name: Trachurus
children.description: Jack mackerels are fast-swimming, schooling fish found in temperate and tropical waters around the world. They have streamlined, silvery bodies built for speed and are active predators that feed on small fish, squid, and crustaceans. These fish are important both ecologically as mid-level predators and commercially as food fish in many regions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jack mackerels are distinguished from other mackerel-like fish by their prominent lateral line that extends onto bony plates called scutes along their tail section. They also have two separate dorsal fins and a deeply forked tail that gives them their characteristic torpedo shape.
children.funFact: Jack mackerels can form massive schools containing millions of individuals that create spectacular underwater displays, sometimes appearing as shimmering silver walls when viewed by divers.

children.name: Decapterus
children.description: Decapterus is a genus of fast-swimming fish commonly known as scads or round scads. These sleek, silvery fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies and are typically found in warm ocean waters, often forming large schools.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctive finlets (small fins) behind their dorsal and anal fins, and a row of bony scales called scutes along their lateral line that give them added protection.
children.funFact: Decapterus species are incredibly fast swimmers and can reach speeds of up to 25 miles per hour when escaping predators or chasing prey.

children.description: Jacks are fast-swimming marine fish known for their sleek, streamlined bodies and powerful tails that make them excellent predators in open water. Most species have compressed, silvery bodies with a distinctive row of bony plates called scutes along their tail section. They're active hunters that often form schools and feed on smaller fish, squid, and crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Jacks can be identified by their forked tails, the characteristic bony scutes (hard scales) along the narrow part of their tail, and their typically deep, laterally compressed bodies. Many species also have a distinctive dark spot on their gill covers.
children.funFact: Some jack species like amberjacks can live over 30 years and grow to massive sizes - the greater amberjack can reach nearly 6 feet long and weigh over 180 pounds!

children.name: Pleuronectidae
Pseudopleuronectes
children.description: Pseudopleuronectes is a genus of flatfish that includes the Winter Flounder, one of New England's most recognizable bottom-dwelling fish. These fish are perfectly adapted for life on the seafloor, with both eyes positioned on one side of their flattened body and the ability to change color to match their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other flatfish genera, Pseudopleuronectes species are right-eyed flounders with a distinctive oval body shape and relatively small mouth. They also have a more northern cold-water distribution compared to many of their flatfish relatives.
children.funFact: Winter flounders start life swimming upright like normal fish, but as juveniles, one eye gradually migrates to the other side of their head as they transform into bottom-dwellers!

children.name: Hippoglossus
children.description: Hippoglossus is a genus containing the largest flatfish in the world - the mighty halibut. These impressive bottom-dwellers are characterized by their enormous size, with both eyes positioned on their right side, and their ability to live for many decades in cold northern waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other flatfish, halibut in this genus can grow to truly massive proportions, sometimes exceeding 8 feet in length and weighing hundreds of pounds. They have a more elongated, less diamond-shaped body compared to other flatfish like flounders.
children.funFact: Atlantic halibut can live over 50 years and are among the longest-lived fish in New England waters, with some individuals potentially reaching 100 years old!

children.name: Reinhardtius
children.description: Reinhardtius is a genus of flatfish that includes the Greenland Halibut, a cold-water species found in the deep waters of the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans. These fish are characterized by their distinctive asymmetrical body plan, with both eyes positioned on one side of their head, and their ability to thrive in extremely cold, deep marine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other halibut species, Reinhardtius has a more elongated body shape and smaller mouth. They are also unique among flatfish for their ability to live in much deeper, colder waters than most of their relatives.
children.funFact: Greenland Halibut can live at depths of up to 7,200 feet and in water temperatures near freezing, making them one of the most cold-adapted flatfish in the world.

children.name: Liopsetta
children.description: Liopsetta is a small genus of flatfish found in cold northern waters. These fish are characterized by their flattened body shape and their ability to live on the ocean floor, where they blend in with sandy and muddy bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flounders, members of Liopsetta have a relatively smooth body surface with small, embedded scales. They also have a more rounded body outline compared to the oval shape of most other flatfish.
children.funFact: The Smooth Flounder is one of the few flatfish species that can tolerate both saltwater and brackish water environments, sometimes venturing into estuaries and river mouths.

children.description: Righteye flounders are flatfish that have both eyes positioned on the right side of their head as adults, though they start life swimming upright like normal fish. These bottom-dwelling marine fish are perfectly adapted for life on the seafloor, with their flattened bodies allowing them to lie camouflaged against sand and mud while hunting for prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike lefteye flounders, these species have both eyes migrated to the right side of their head. They also tend to be larger and more robust than their lefteye cousins, with some species like halibut growing to massive sizes.
children.funFact: Baby flounders actually start life swimming upright with one eye on each side of their head, but as they grow, one eye gradually migrates around their head to join the other eye - a process that takes several weeks to complete!

children.name: Paralichthyidae
Paralichthys
children.description: Paralichthys is a genus of left-eyed flounders that are masters of camouflage, lying flat on sandy or muddy ocean bottoms with both eyes positioned on their left side. These flatfish are important predators and popular game fish along the Atlantic coast, known for their ability to quickly bury themselves in sediment and change color to match their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike right-eyed flounders, Paralichthys species have both eyes on the left side of their head when viewed from above. They can be distinguished from other left-eyed flounders by their large mouths with prominent teeth and their relatively elongated body shape.
children.funFact: All Paralichthys flounders start life swimming upright like normal fish, but during their larval development, one eye gradually migrates across their head to join the other on the left side as they adapt to bottom-dwelling life.

children.description: Large-tooth flounders are flatfish that have adapted to life on the ocean floor by having both eyes migrate to one side of their head during development. These masters of camouflage can change their color and pattern to match the sandy or muddy bottom where they hunt for prey. They are active predators that use their large teeth to catch fish, crabs, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flatfish families, large-tooth flounders have notably large, sharp teeth and typically have their eyes on the left side of their body. They also tend to be more active hunters compared to other flounders that primarily ambush their prey.
children.funFact: Summer flounder can change their skin color and pattern in just seconds to perfectly match their surroundings, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.name: Scophthalmidae
Scophthalmus
children.description: Scophthalmus is a genus of flatfish commonly known as turbots and windowpane flounders. These fish are characterized by their extremely flattened bodies and both eyes located on one side of their head, allowing them to lie camouflaged on the ocean floor. They are bottom-dwelling predators that feed on small fish, crustaceans, and marine worms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Scophthalmus are distinguished from other flatfish by their diamond-shaped body outline and relatively large mouth. They also have both eyes on the left side of their head, unlike some flatfish that are right-eyed.
children.funFact: The windowpane flounder gets its name because it's so thin and translucent that you can actually see through parts of its body, making it nearly invisible when lying on sandy ocean bottoms.

children.description: Turbots are a small family of flatfish that have both eyes on the left side of their body as adults, though they start life swimming upright like typical fish. These bottom-dwelling fish are well-adapted for life on sandy and muddy sea floors, where they can bury themselves and ambush prey. They're prized as food fish in many parts of the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other flatfish families, turbots have a more oval, diamond-shaped body and lack the distinct lateral line that runs along the body in most fish.
children.funFact: Baby turbots undergo an amazing transformation called metamorphosis - they start life swimming normally with eyes on both sides of their head, but as they grow, one eye actually migrates across their skull to join the other on the left side!

children.name: Sphyraenidae
Sphyraena
children.description: Barracudas are sleek, predatory fish known for their torpedo-shaped bodies and fearsome teeth. They are fast-swimming hunters that patrol coastal waters, using their speed and razor-sharp teeth to catch smaller fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barracudas can be distinguished from other predatory fish by their elongated, pike-like body shape and their prominent lower jaw that extends beyond the upper jaw, filled with large, pointed teeth.
children.funFact: Barracudas can swim at speeds up to 35 mph in short bursts, making them one of the fastest fish in the ocean.

children.description: Barracudas are sleek, predatory fish known for their torpedo-shaped bodies and fearsome teeth. These fast-swimming hunters have elongated jaws filled with sharp, fang-like teeth that help them catch smaller fish and squid. They are primarily tropical and subtropical marine fish, though some species venture into temperate waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barracudas can be identified by their long, cylindrical bodies, protruding lower jaws, and rows of razor-sharp teeth. Unlike many other predatory fish, they have two widely separated dorsal fins and a distinctive underbite.
children.funFact: Great barracudas can swim up to 35 mph in short bursts, making them one of the fastest fish in the ocean when hunting prey.

children.name: Coryphaenidae
Coryphaena
children.description: Dolphinfishes are large, fast-swimming ocean fish known for their brilliant golden-yellow coloration and distinctive high, compressed foreheads. These powerful predators cruise warm offshore waters, feeding on flying fish, squid, and other marine life. They are prized by both commercial and recreational fishermen for their fighting ability and excellent taste.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dolphinfishes are easily recognized by their dramatically flattened, tall dorsal fin that runs almost the entire length of their body and their characteristic blunt, high forehead. Their vibrant golden color and torpedo-shaped body make them unmistakable among ocean fish.
children.funFact: Despite their name, dolphinfishes are not related to dolphins at all - they're actually ray-finned fish that can swim up to 50 mph and are capable of incredible leaps out of the water when hooked!
