children.description: Dolphinfishes are fast-swimming, open-ocean fish known for their vibrant golden-yellow and blue-green colors. These powerful predators have distinctively compressed bodies and blunt, rounded heads that help them cut through the water at high speeds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Male dolphinfishes develop a prominent, steep forehead crest that gives them their characteristic profile, while females have more rounded heads.
children.funFact: Despite their name, dolphinfishes are not related to dolphins at all - they're called 'dolphin' because of their similar habit of following boats and leaping out of the water.

children.name: Achiridae
Trinectes
children.description: Trinectes is a genus of small flatfish known as soles that live in coastal waters and can tolerate both saltwater and freshwater environments. These fish have flattened bodies with both eyes on one side of their head, allowing them to lie camouflaged on sandy or muddy bottoms while hunting for small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Trinectes are distinguished from other soles by their ability to live in fresh water for extended periods, and they have a more oval body shape compared to many other flatfish species.
children.funFact: The hogchoker got its unusual name because early settlers noticed that pigs would choke when trying to eat these bony little fish whole.

children.description: American soles are flatfish that have evolved to live their entire adult lives lying on the ocean floor. Unlike their European cousins, these fish have both eyes on the right side of their head and are perfectly adapted for a bottom-dwelling lifestyle. They're masters of camouflage, able to change their coloration to match the sandy or muddy seafloor where they hunt for small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: American soles can be distinguished from other flatfish families by having their eyes on the right side of their head and lacking the pectoral fin on their blind (left) side. They also have a distinctive rounded tail fin and small mouth adapted for bottom feeding.
children.funFact: Baby American soles start life swimming upright like normal fish, but as they grow, one eye literally migrates across their head to join the other eye, and they settle onto their side to begin their bottom-dwelling lifestyle.

children.name: Xiphiidae
Xiphias
children.description: Xiphias is a genus containing just one remarkable species - the Broadbill Swordfish. These are large, fast-swimming ocean predators known for their distinctive long, flattened bill that resembles a sword and can make up nearly one-third of their total body length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other billfish, swordfish have a completely flattened, sword-like bill (rather than rounded) and lack pelvic fins as adults. They also lose their scales and teeth as they mature, setting them apart from related marlin and sailfish.
children.funFact: Swordfish can heat their eyes and brain up to 28°F warmer than the surrounding water using special tissue, giving them superior vision when hunting in cold, deep waters.

children.description: Swordfishes are large, powerful ocean predators known for their distinctive long, flat bills that resemble swords. These fast-swimming fish use their sword-like snouts to slash through schools of prey fish, stunning them before feeding. They are built for speed and deep-water hunting in the open ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other billfish, swordfishes have completely flat, sword-like bills (not rounded like marlins) and lack pelvic fins as adults. They also lose their scales and teeth as they mature, giving them a smooth, streamlined body.
children.funFact: Swordfish can heat their eyes and brain with special organs, allowing them to hunt effectively in cold, deep waters where their vision and reflexes remain sharp even when the surrounding water temperature drops significantly.

children.name: Cyclopsettidae
Etropus
children.description: Etropus is a genus of small flatfish commonly known as sand flounders. These bottom-dwelling fish have both eyes on one side of their head and are perfectly adapted for life on sandy ocean floors where they can camouflage themselves by partially burying in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sand flounders in the genus Etropus are distinguished from other flatfish by their small size, typically measuring just a few inches long, and their preference for shallow sandy habitats rather than deeper waters.
children.funFact: Like all flatfish, Etropus species start life swimming upright like regular fish, but as they mature, one eye actually migrates to the other side of their head so both eyes end up on the same side!

children.description: Sand whiffs are a small family of flatfish that live on sandy and muddy ocean bottoms. These fish have both eyes on one side of their head like other flatfish, and they're typically small and well-camouflaged against the seafloor. They feed on small invertebrates and worms they find in the sediment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sand whiffs are distinguished from other flatfish families by their relatively small size, translucent appearance, and specific fin ray counts. They also have a more elongated body shape compared to many other flatfish.
children.funFact: Sand whiffs can quickly bury themselves in sand by rapidly undulating their fins, leaving only their eyes exposed to watch for prey and predators.

children.name: Rachycentridae
Rachycentron
children.description: Rachycentron is a genus containing just one species - the cobia, a large marine fish found in warm coastal waters. These distinctive fish are known for their elongated, streamlined bodies and broad, flattened heads that give them a somewhat shark-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cobia are unique among fish in their combination of a long, torpedo-shaped body, a distinctively broad and flattened head, and their habit of swimming near the surface often mistaken for sharks.
children.funFact: Cobia are sometimes called 'shark suckers' because young cobia often swim alongside sharks and rays, though they don't actually attach to them like remoras do.

children.description: The Cobia family contains just one species of large, distinctive marine fish found in warm coastal waters. These elongated fish are powerful swimmers with a streamlined body shape and can grow quite large, often reaching several feet in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cobias have a distinctive flat, broad head with a protruding lower jaw, and their first dorsal fin consists of short, separate spines rather than a continuous fin membrane like most other fish.
children.funFact: Despite being the only member of its family, the cobia is sometimes called a 'shark sucker' because young cobias often swim alongside sharks and rays, though they don't actually attach to them like remoras do.

children.name: Echeneidae
Echeneis
children.description: Echeneis is a genus of fish commonly known as sharksuckers or remoras, characterized by their unique flattened suction disc on top of their heads. These remarkable fish use this specialized structure to attach themselves to larger marine animals like sharks, whales, and sea turtles, hitching rides through the ocean while feeding on scraps and parasites from their hosts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Echeneis apart from other remora genera is their elongated, streamlined body shape and the specific structure of their suction disc, which has fewer lamellae (ridges) than other remora species.
children.funFact: The sharksucker's suction disc is actually a modified dorsal fin that evolved into one of nature's most effective biological suction cups, creating such strong attachment that it can support the fish's entire body weight even when its host is swimming at high speeds.

children.description: Remoras are a unique family of fish best known for their extraordinary ability to attach themselves to larger marine animals like sharks, whales, and sea turtles. They have evolved a specialized suction disc on top of their heads that allows them to hitch rides on their hosts while feeding on scraps and parasites. This relationship is generally beneficial for both the remora and its host.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Remoras are instantly recognizable by the flattened, ridged suction disc on the top of their heads, which is actually a modified dorsal fin. Unlike other fish, they use this disc rather than swimming to move through the ocean, though they are capable swimmers when needed.
children.funFact: A remora's suction disc is so powerful that ancient sailors sometimes used these fish as living fishing hooks, attaching lines to them and letting them swim out to attach to larger fish that could then be hauled in.

children.name: Bothidae
Bothus
children.description: Bothus is a genus of flatfish commonly known as left-eye flounders, where both eyes migrate to the left side of their head as they mature. These marine fish are masters of camouflage, able to change their color and pattern to match the sandy or muddy ocean floor where they live. They spend most of their time lying flat on the seafloor, waiting to ambush small fish and invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike right-eye flounders, Bothus species have both eyes positioned on the left side of their head when viewed from above. They also tend to be more active swimmers than many other flatfish groups.
children.funFact: Bothus flounders can change their skin color and pattern in just seconds to perfectly match their surroundings, making them nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.description: Lefteye flounders are flatfish that have both eyes positioned on the left side of their head as adults. These fish start life swimming upright like regular fish, but undergo a remarkable transformation where one eye migrates across their head as they mature and settle to live on the ocean bottom.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike righteye flounders, these flatfish have both eyes on the left side of their head when lying on the seafloor. Their mouth is typically more symmetrical compared to other flatfish families.
children.funFact: Baby lefteye flounders begin life with one eye on each side of their head like normal fish, but during metamorphosis, the right eye actually travels across the top of the head to join the left eye - a process that takes several weeks to complete.

children.description: Carangiformes is a diverse order of marine fish that includes some of the ocean's most specialized hunters and masters of disguise. Despite their varied appearances, these fish share common skeletal and muscle features that reflect their evolutionary relationship. The group ranges from lightning-fast predators like barracudas to perfectly camouflaged bottom-dwellers like flounders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What unites these seemingly different fish are shared anatomical features in their fin structure and body organization, particularly in how their dorsal and anal fins are supported. Many species also show remarkable adaptations for either high-speed swimming or bottom-dwelling camouflage.
children.funFact: This order includes some of the most extreme body transformations in the fish world - flatfish like flounders actually start life swimming upright like normal fish, but as they mature, one eye literally migrates across their skull so both eyes end up on the same side of their flattened body!

children.name: Acanthuriformes
Sciaenidae
Menticirrhus
children.description: Kingcroakers are medium-sized coastal fish that belong to the drum family, known for their ability to produce croaking or drumming sounds using special muscles attached to their swim bladders. These bottom-dwelling fish have elongated bodies and are commonly found in sandy or muddy coastal waters where they feed on small crustaceans, worms, and mollusks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Kingcroakers can be distinguished from other drum family members by their distinctive barbel (whisker-like projection) on the chin and their more elongated, less deep body shape compared to their cousins like red drum or black drum.
children.funFact: Kingcroakers get their name from the loud croaking sounds they make, which can sometimes be heard by anglers even when the fish are still underwater!

children.name: Aplodinotus
children.description: Aplodinotus is a genus containing just one species - the Freshwater Drum, North America's only freshwater member of the drum family. These fish are characterized by their ability to produce drumming sounds using special muscles that vibrate against their swim bladder. They are bottom-dwelling fish that feed primarily on mollusks, crayfish, and other invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other drum family members that live in saltwater, Aplodinotus species are adapted exclusively for freshwater environments. They have powerful pharyngeal teeth specialized for crushing the shells of mollusks and crustaceans.
children.funFact: Freshwater drums are sometimes called 'sheephead' because their pharyngeal teeth look remarkably similar to sheep molars, perfectly adapted for crushing zebra mussel shells.

children.name: Leiostomus
children.description: Leiostomus is a genus of drum fish found along the Atlantic coast of North America. These fish are characterized by their compressed, silvery bodies and are commonly known as spot croakers due to their ability to produce croaking sounds using special muscles around their swim bladder.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily identified by the distinctive dark spot located behind their gill covers, which gives them their common name 'spot.'
children.funFact: Spot croakers can produce drumming or croaking sounds by rapidly contracting muscles against their swim bladder, which they use for communication during spawning season.

children.name: Cynoscion
children.description: Weakfishes are sleek, silvery marine fish in the drum family that get their name from their delicate mouths, where hooks can easily tear free during fishing. They have elongated bodies with pointed snouts and two separate dorsal fins, and are popular sport fish along the Atlantic coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other drums, weakfishes have prominent canine teeth and lack barbels on their chin. Their mouth tears easily when hooked, which distinguishes them from their sturdier drum family relatives.
children.funFact: Weakfish can produce drumming sounds by vibrating muscles against their swim bladder, and these sounds are thought to play a role in spawning and communication.

children.name: Micropogonias
children.description: Micropogonias is a genus of drum fish known for their ability to produce sounds using special muscles that vibrate their swim bladder. These medium-sized marine fish are bottom-dwellers that feed on small crustaceans, worms, and mollusks in coastal waters. They get their common name 'croaker' from the distinctive croaking or drumming sounds they make.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other drums by their smaller barbels (whisker-like projections) on the chin and their relatively compressed body shape. They also have a more silvery coloration with distinctive wavy lines along their sides.
children.funFact: Atlantic Croakers can produce sounds so loud that they were once used by fishermen as a natural fish finder - the croaking sounds could be heard through boat hulls, indicating where schools of fish were located!

children.description: Drums are a family of marine and freshwater fish known for their ability to produce sounds using special muscles that vibrate their swim bladder. These fish are typically bottom-dwellers with elongated bodies and are popular among both recreational and commercial fishers. Most drums have barbels or sensory organs near their mouth to help them find food in murky water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Drums can be distinguished from other fish families by their sound-producing ability and their distinctive lateral line system that extends onto their tail fin. They also typically have a rounded or pointed snout and a subterminal mouth positioned below the head.
children.funFact: The freshwater drum is the only member of this marine fish family that has successfully adapted to live in freshwater environments, making it quite unique among its ocean-dwelling relatives.

children.name: Sparidae
Stenotomus
children.description: Stenotomus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as porgies or sea breams. These fish are characterized by their deep, laterally compressed bodies and strong teeth adapted for crushing shellfish and other hard-shelled prey. They are popular both commercially and recreationally along the Atlantic coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Stenotomus have distinctively deep, oval-shaped bodies that are much taller than they are thick, giving them a disc-like appearance when viewed from the front. They possess powerful crushing teeth and typically show silvery coloration with darker backs.
children.funFact: Scup change their diet dramatically as they grow - juveniles feed primarily on small crustaceans and worms, while adults use their powerful jaws to crush mollusks, crabs, and sea urchins.

children.name: Lagodon
children.description: Lagodon is a genus of marine fish commonly known as pinfish, found along the Atlantic and Gulf coasts. These small, silvery fish are characterized by their compressed, oval-shaped bodies and are important members of coastal ecosystems. They are popular baitfish and frequently encountered by anglers in shallow coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pinfish are easily recognized by the distinctive dark spot behind their gill cover and several vertical bars along their silvery sides. They have small, sharp teeth adapted for nibbling on vegetation and small invertebrates.
children.funFact: Pinfish get their name from their habit of stealing bait from fishing hooks with quick, nibbling bites that feel like tiny pinpricks to anglers.

children.name: Archosargus
children.description: Archosargus is a genus of marine fish in the porgy family, characterized by their deep, compressed bodies and distinctive teeth. These fish are well-adapted for feeding on hard-shelled prey like barnacles, crabs, and mollusks along rocky shores and around structures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their human-like front teeth and strong molars, which are perfectly designed for crushing shells and scraping organisms off hard surfaces.
children.funFact: Sheepshead fish are such skilled thieves that they can steal bait right off a hook without getting caught, earning them a reputation as one of the most challenging fish for anglers to hook.

children.description: Seabreams and porgies are a family of marine fish known for their deep, compressed bodies and strong jaws filled with sharp teeth. These fish are excellent at crushing and grinding hard prey like shellfish, crabs, and barnacles. Most species in this family are found in warm coastal waters and are popular both as sport fish and food fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive strong, molar-like teeth in the back of their mouths that are perfect for crushing hard-shelled prey. They also typically have a single, continuous dorsal fin with both spiny and soft rays.
children.funFact: Many porgies and seabreams are hermaphroditic, meaning they can change sex during their lifetime - typically starting as females and later becoming males as they grow larger and older.

children.name: Moronidae
Morone
children.description: The Western Atlantic Temperate Basses are a group of silvery fish that thrive in the cool coastal waters of the North Atlantic. These hardy fish are known for their ability to move between saltwater and freshwater environments, making them common in estuaries, rivers, and nearshore ocean waters throughout New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other bass families, Morone species have distinctive horizontal stripes running along their silvery bodies and can tolerate a wide range of water salinity levels. They also have two separate dorsal fins, with the front fin having sharp spines.
children.funFact: Striped Bass can live over 30 years and travel incredible distances - some individuals tagged in New England waters have been found as far south as North Carolina!

children.description: Temperate basses are medium to large freshwater and saltwater fish known for their silvery bodies and strong fighting ability when caught. These popular game fish have streamlined bodies with two separate dorsal fins and are prized by anglers for both their sporting qualities and excellent taste.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the sea basses, temperate basses have completely separate spiny and soft dorsal fins rather than connected ones. They also tend to form large schools and can tolerate a wide range of salinities, allowing some species to move between fresh and salt water.
children.funFact: Striped bass can live over 30 years and undertake epic migrations, with some individuals traveling over 1,000 miles along the Atlantic coast between their spawning and feeding grounds.

children.name: Priacanthidae
Pristigenys
children.description: Pristigenys is a genus of deep-water marine fish commonly known as bigeyes, named for their characteristically large, prominent eyes. These fish are typically found in tropical and subtropical waters around the world, living in deeper offshore areas where their oversized eyes help them see in low-light conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished by their exceptionally large eyes relative to their body size, compressed oval-shaped bodies, and reddish coloration that helps them blend into the deep-water environment.
children.funFact: The enlarged eyes of Pristigenys fish can be up to one-third the length of their head, acting like biological night-vision goggles to help them hunt for small fish and crustaceans in the dim depths of the ocean.

children.name: Heteropriacanthus
children.description: Heteropriacanthus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as glasseyes or bigeyes. These deep-bodied fish are characterized by their exceptionally large eyes and bright red coloration, adaptations that help them see and hunt in deeper waters where light is limited.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other bigeye fish by their distinctive scale patterns and specific fin ray counts. They have a more compressed body shape compared to their close relatives in the family Priacanthidae.
children.funFact: The glasseye's huge eyes can make up nearly one-third of its head length, giving it excellent night vision for hunting small fish and crustaceans in the twilight zone of the ocean.

children.description: Bigeyes are deep-bodied marine fish with notably large eyes that help them see in darker waters. These fish are typically found in deeper coastal waters and have compressed, oval-shaped bodies with rough scales and bright red or pink coloration.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their exceptionally large eyes are the most obvious feature that sets them apart from other fish families. They also have a distinctive upturned mouth and very rough, spiny scales that give them a coarse texture.
children.funFact: Bigeyes are primarily nocturnal hunters that use their oversized eyes to spot small fish and crustaceans in the dim light of deeper waters.

children.name: Chaetodontidae
Chaetodon
children.description: Chaetodon is a genus of tropical marine fish commonly known as butterflyfish, characterized by their bright colors, disc-shaped bodies, and intricate patterns. These fish are popular in aquariums and are typically found around coral reefs in warm ocean waters. They have small mouths adapted for picking at coral polyps, algae, and small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Chaetodon are distinguished by their compressed, nearly circular body shape and distinctive eye bands or spots that often help confuse predators about which direction the fish is swimming.
children.funFact: Many Chaetodon butterflyfish form monogamous pair bonds and will defend their territory together, often swimming in synchronized patterns that make them look like a single, larger fish to potential threats.

children.description: Butterflyfishes are colorful marine fish known for their compressed, disk-like bodies and striking patterns of stripes, spots, and bright colors. These tropical reef fish are typically small to medium-sized and are commonly found swimming around coral reefs where they feed on coral polyps, small invertebrates, and algae. Most species form monogamous pairs and are active during the day.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Butterflyfishes can be distinguished from other reef fish by their laterally compressed, almost circular body shape and their small, brush-like teeth that are perfectly adapted for picking at coral polyps and small prey in reef crevices.
children.funFact: Many butterflyfish species have eye spots or dark bands across their faces that help confuse predators about which end is the head, giving them a better chance to escape by darting away in an unexpected direction.

children.name: Pomacanthidae
Holacanthus
children.description: Holacanthus is a genus of large, colorful marine angelfish found in tropical and subtropical waters. These fish are known for their stunning beauty, with vibrant blues, yellows, and other bright colors that make them popular in aquariums and beloved by divers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Holacanthus are distinguished from other angelfish by their large size (often over a foot long) and their distinctive color patterns that change dramatically as they mature from juvenile to adult forms.
children.funFact: Queen Angelfish can live up to 15 years and are known to be curious about divers, sometimes following them around coral reefs!

children.description: Angelfishes are colorful marine fish known for their flattened, disc-like bodies and distinctive fins. These tropical and subtropical fish are popular in aquariums and are commonly found around coral reefs and rocky areas in warm ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Angelfishes can be distinguished from similar fish by their compressed bodies, continuous dorsal fins, and often elaborate color patterns that may change dramatically as they mature from juvenile to adult forms.
children.funFact: Many angelfish species undergo dramatic color transformations as they grow, with juveniles often displaying completely different patterns and colors than adults of the same species.

children.name: Lutjanidae
Lutjanus
children.description: Common Snappers are a genus of marine fish known for their robust bodies, large mouths, and sharp canine teeth. These reef-dwelling fish are popular both as sport fish and for eating, with most species found in tropical and subtropical waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other reef fish, snappers have prominent canine teeth and can quickly snap their jaws shut to catch prey, giving them their common name.
children.funFact: Gray Snappers can live for over 20 years and are known to change color from silver to darker hues when they move from open water to reef environments.

children.description: Snappers are a family of marine fish known for their robust bodies, large mouths, and prominent canine teeth that give them their name. These predatory fish are typically found in warm coastal waters and coral reefs, where they hunt smaller fish, crustaceans, and other marine prey. Most snappers are prized both as sport fish and for their excellent eating quality.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snappers can be distinguished from other fish families by their deep, laterally compressed bodies, large heads with big eyes, and characteristic sharp canine teeth at the front of their jaws. They also have continuous dorsal fins with both spiny and soft-rayed portions.
children.funFact: Many snapper species can live for decades, with some red snappers living over 50 years and growing quite large as they age.

children.name: Gerreidae
Eucinostomus
children.description: Eucinostomus is a genus of small, silvery marine fish commonly known as mojarras. These fish are characterized by their compressed, oval-shaped bodies and highly protrusible mouths that can extend outward to feed on small invertebrates in sand and mud.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively extensible jaws that can shoot forward like a tube to capture prey, and they typically display a silvery coloration with subtle barring or spotting patterns.
children.funFact: Mojarras can extend their mouths up to 65% of their head length, creating a tube-like feeding apparatus that works like a biological vacuum cleaner to suck up small crustaceans and worms from sediment.

children.description: Mojarras are small to medium-sized marine fish with silvery, compressed bodies that live in coastal waters, estuaries, and sometimes freshwater. They have protrusible mouths that can extend outward to help them feed on small invertebrates and organic matter from sandy or muddy bottoms. These fish are important prey species for larger predators and play a key role in coastal food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mojarras are distinguished by their highly protrusible mouths that telescope outward when feeding, and their deeply forked tails. Their bodies are typically very laterally compressed (flattened from side to side) with reflective silvery scales.
children.funFact: When feeding, mojarras can extend their mouths up to 40% of their head length, creating a tube-like feeding apparatus that helps them vacuum up small prey from crevices and sediment.

children.name: Acanthuridae
Acanthurus
children.description: Acanthurus is a genus of tropical marine fish commonly known as tangs or surgeonfish. These colorful fish are characterized by their compressed, oval-shaped bodies and most notably, sharp spines near their tails that can be deployed like switchblades when threatened.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets Acanthurus apart from other surgeonfish genera is their distinctive tail spines and feeding behavior - they are primarily herbivorous grazers that use their small, bristle-like teeth to scrape algae from coral reefs and rocky surfaces.
children.funFact: The name 'surgeonfish' comes from the scalpel-sharp spines on either side of their tail base, which they can flick out like a switchblade to defend themselves from predators or rivals.

children.description: Surgeonfishes, tangs, and unicornfishes are colorful marine fish known for their blade-like spines near their tails that can be as sharp as a surgeon's scalpel. These tropical and subtropical fish are primarily herbivores, spending their days grazing on algae from rocks and coral reefs. They have compressed, oval-shaped bodies and are important members of marine ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The defining feature of this family is the presence of one or more sharp, retractable spines on each side of the tail base, which they use for defense. Many species also have distinctive bright colors and patterns, with some unicornfishes bearing horn-like projections on their foreheads.
children.funFact: The single New England representative of this tropical family is likely a stray that traveled north in the warm Gulf Stream waters, as these fish are typically found in much warmer waters around coral reefs.

children.description: Acanthuriformes is a diverse order of marine fish that includes many colorful and commercially important species found in both tropical and temperate waters. These fish are characterized by having spiny dorsal fins and are typically deep-bodied with compressed sides, making them well-adapted for life around reefs, rocky bottoms, and coastal areas. The group includes everything from the vibrant butterflyfishes of coral reefs to the prized striped bass of New England waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are unified by their spiny-rayed fins and specific skull bone arrangements, though they show remarkable diversity in body shape, size, and lifestyle. Unlike many other fish orders, this group spans from tiny tropical reef fish to large predatory species.
children.funFact: Despite their incredible diversity, DNA studies revealed that striped bass are more closely related to tropical butterflyfishes than to other bass species, completely reshaping how scientists understand fish relationships!

children.name: Scombriformes
Scombridae
Thunnus
children.description: The genus Thunnus contains the world's largest and most commercially important tuna species, including the mighty Atlantic Bluefin and the widely-fished Yellowfin. These are powerful, fast-swimming ocean predators with torpedo-shaped bodies built for speed and endurance in open waters. All members of this genus are warm-blooded fish that can regulate their body temperature, allowing them to hunt effectively in cooler waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other tunas, Thunnus species are notably larger and have longer pectoral fins that extend well past the second dorsal fin. They also possess a more advanced circulatory system that helps maintain their warm-blooded metabolism.
children.funFact: Atlantic Bluefin Tuna can reach speeds of up to 43 mph and maintain body temperatures up to 20°F warmer than the surrounding water, making them one of the few truly warm-blooded fish in the ocean.

children.name: Scomber
children.description: Scomber is a genus of fast-swimming ocean fish known as mackerels. These sleek, torpedo-shaped fish are built for speed and spend their lives in open waters, traveling in large schools as they hunt for small fish and plankton.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Scomber have distinctive wavy black lines across their metallic backs and a row of small finlets behind their dorsal and anal fins. Their deeply forked tails and streamlined bodies make them excellent swimmers in the open ocean.
children.funFact: Atlantic mackerel can swim at speeds up to 35 miles per hour and migrate hundreds of miles seasonally, following temperature changes and food sources along the coast.

children.name: Auxis
children.description: Frigate tunas are small, fast-swimming fish in the tuna family that are built for speed and endurance in open ocean waters. These compact predators have streamlined bodies and powerful tails that allow them to chase down small fish, squid, and crustaceans in the Atlantic Ocean. Both species found in New England waters are highly migratory, following warm currents and prey throughout their range.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Frigate tunas are much smaller than their larger tuna relatives, typically reaching only 12-20 inches in length. They can be distinguished from other small tunas by their distinctive wavy lines along the back and their relatively large eyes compared to their body size.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, frigate tunas can swim at speeds up to 40 miles per hour and have a body temperature that runs warmer than the surrounding water, helping them maintain peak performance in cooler seas.

children.name: Scomberomorus
children.description: Spanish mackerels are fast-swimming predatory fish with streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies built for speed in open ocean waters. They have distinctive spotted or striped patterns along their sides and razor-sharp teeth for catching smaller fish, squid, and shrimp.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other mackerels, Spanish mackerels have prominent canine teeth and lack the wavy lines found on Atlantic mackerel, instead displaying distinct spots or vertical stripes on their silvery sides.
children.funFact: King mackerel can swim up to 40 miles per hour and are known to leap completely out of the water when hooked, making them a prized catch among sport fishermen.

children.name: Sarda
children.description: Bonitos are fast-swimming, predatory fish in the tuna family that inhabit warm and temperate ocean waters. They have streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies built for speed and agility as they hunt schools of smaller fish like sardines, anchovies, and mackerel. These powerful swimmers are known for their distinctive dark wavy lines along their backs and silvery sides.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bonitos can be distinguished from their tuna relatives by their smaller size and the characteristic dark, wavy stripes that run diagonally across their backs and upper sides, rather than the straight horizontal lines found on many other tunas.
children.funFact: Atlantic bonitos can swim at speeds up to 40 miles per hour, making them one of the fastest fish in New England waters.

children.name: Euthynnus
children.description: Little Tunas are a small genus of fast-swimming oceanic fish that represent some of the smaller members of the tuna family. These powerful predators are built for speed and endurance, with streamlined bodies and strong swimming muscles that allow them to chase down smaller fish and squid in open ocean waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Little Tunas are smaller than their giant bluefin relatives and have distinctive wavy lines or vermiculations on their backs, along with scattered dark spots on their lower sides and belly.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'little,' Little Tunny can still reach speeds of up to 30 mph when hunting, making them one of the fastest fish in New England waters.

children.description: The Scombridae family includes some of the ocean's most powerful and fastest swimmers, including tunas, mackerels, and bonitos. These sleek, torpedo-shaped fish are built for speed and long-distance travel, with strong muscles and streamlined bodies that help them chase down prey in open waters. Many species are highly prized by both commercial fisheries and sport anglers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have deeply forked tails, multiple small finlets behind their dorsal and anal fins, and many species can regulate their body temperature to stay warmer than the surrounding water. Their bodies are typically metallic blue-green above and silver below, with smooth, small scales.
children.funFact: Bluefin tuna can reach speeds of up to 43 mph and maintain a body temperature up to 18°F warmer than the surrounding water, allowing them to hunt effectively in cold ocean depths.

children.name: Stromateidae
Peprilus
children.description: Peprilus is a genus of small, silvery fish known for their thin, deep bodies and smooth scales. These fish are commonly found in coastal waters along the Atlantic coast and are prized by both commercial and recreational fishers for their delicate, buttery flesh.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctively compressed, almost disc-like bodies with small mouths and weak teeth adapted for feeding on small invertebrates and plankton. Their fins are relatively small compared to their body size, and they lack the spiny dorsal fins found in many other marine fish.
children.funFact: Butterfish get their name not just from their taste, but also from their incredibly slippery skin - they're so hard to hold that they can literally slip right through your fingers!

children.description: Butterfishes are small to medium-sized marine fish with distinctive deep, compressed bodies that are much taller than they are wide. They have smooth, silvery scales and relatively small mouths, giving them a streamlined appearance as they swim in schools through coastal waters. These fish are known for their tendency to follow jellyfish and other floating objects, using them for shelter and feeding opportunities.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Butterfishes can be identified by their extremely flattened, disc-like body shape and their habit of swimming in tight formation beneath jellyfish or other drifting marine life. Their bodies are notably deeper than most other schooling fish of similar size.
children.funFact: Young butterfishes often live symbiotically with jellyfish, swimming beneath their bell-shaped bodies for protection while feeding on small organisms that the jellyfish stun with their tentacles.

children.name: Pomatomidae
Pomatomus
children.description: Pomatomus is a genus containing just one species - the bluefish, a fast-swimming predatory fish found in temperate and subtropical waters around the world. These powerful marine fish are known for their aggressive feeding behavior and sharp teeth, making them formidable hunters in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluefish are distinguished by their streamlined, torpedo-shaped body, prominent lower jaw, and razor-sharp triangular teeth. They have a distinctive blue-green coloration on their back that fades to silver on their sides.
children.funFact: Bluefish are such voracious predators that they often kill more prey than they can eat, sometimes going into feeding frenzies that leave trails of wounded fish in their wake.

children.description: Bluefishes are powerful, fast-swimming marine fish known for their aggressive feeding behavior and strong jaws filled with sharp teeth. They are open-ocean predators that often hunt in large schools, following schools of smaller fish like mackerel and herring along the coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bluefishes can be identified by their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies, deeply forked tails, and prominent lower jaw that extends slightly beyond the upper jaw. They have a distinctive dark blotch at the base of their pectoral fins.
children.funFact: Bluefishes are sometimes called the 'piranha of the sea' because they can become so frenzied while feeding that they'll continue attacking and biting even after they're full, sometimes injuring each other in the process.

children.name: Ariommatidae
Ariomma
children.description: Ariomma is a genus of deep-sea fish commonly known as silver-rags or driftfish. These fish are characterized by their silvery, compressed bodies and are typically found in open ocean waters at moderate depths. They are part of the medusafish family and are known for their association with floating debris and jellyfish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silver-rags have distinctively compressed, disc-like bodies with large eyes and small mouths. Their silvery coloration and ability to swim among jellyfish tentacles without being stung sets them apart from other deep-sea fish.
children.funFact: Young silver-rags often shelter beneath the bells of large jellyfish, using them as mobile homes while feeding on small organisms in the water column.

children.description: Ariommas are small, deep-water marine fish that belong to a unique family found in temperate and subtropical oceans. These silvery fish have elongated bodies and are typically found in offshore waters, often at considerable depths where they feed on small crustaceans and other planktonic organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ariommas can be distinguished from other deep-water fish by their distinctive compressed body shape, large eyes adapted for low-light conditions, and their unique fin arrangement with a long-based dorsal fin.
children.funFact: Despite being ocean fish, ariommas are sometimes called 'driftfish' because they often associate with floating debris or jellyfish in the open ocean, using these objects for shelter and feeding opportunities.

children.name: Centrolophidae
Hyperoglyphe
children.description: Hyperoglyphe is a genus of deep-sea fish commonly known as barrelfish, named for their barrel-shaped, robust bodies. These fish are typically found in deeper ocean waters and are known for their strong swimming abilities and schooling behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Barrelfish have distinctively deep, compressed bodies with a high back profile that gives them their characteristic barrel-like appearance. They also have relatively large eyes adapted for life in deeper, dimmer waters.
children.funFact: Barrelfish are known to follow large ships and marine mammals, taking advantage of the disturbed water to feed on small fish and plankton that get stirred up in their wake.

children.description: Medusafishes are deep-sea fish that get their name from their association with jellyfish during their juvenile stage. These oceanic fish have compressed, oval-shaped bodies and are typically found in open waters far from shore.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish families, young medusafishes often live beneath the bells of large jellyfish, using them for protection and transportation in the open ocean.
children.funFact: Juvenile medusafishes can actually swim inside the bell cavity of jellyfish without being stung, thanks to special adaptations that help them avoid the jellyfish's venomous tentacles.

children.description: Scombriformes are fast-swimming marine fish that include some of the ocean's most powerful predators and speedsters. Most members of this group have streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies built for life in open water, though some like butterfishes have developed different body shapes for following jellyfish. They range from small schooling fish to massive tunas that can weigh hundreds of pounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish are characterized by their specialized swimming adaptations, including deeply forked tails, multiple finlets behind their dorsal and anal fins, and often very narrow tail bases that reduce drag. Many species also have retractable fins that can be folded into grooves to create an even more streamlined profile.
children.funFact: Bluefin tunas are among the few warm-blooded fish, able to maintain their body temperature up to 20°F warmer than the surrounding water, which helps power their incredible speed and allows them to hunt in colder waters.

children.name: Tetraodontiformes
Monacanthidae
Aluterus
children.description: Aluterus is a genus of filefish found in Atlantic waters, including off the New England coast. These are medium to large-sized fish with flattened, oval-shaped bodies and rough, sandpaper-like skin that gives them their 'file' name. All members of this genus have a distinctive first dorsal fin spine and can change colors to blend with their surroundings.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Aluterus filefish are distinguished from other filefish by their larger size and more elongated body shape. They lack the prominent dewlap (skin flap) found in some related filefish genera.
children.funFact: These fish can lock their first dorsal spine in an upright position to wedge themselves into crevices when hiding from predators, making them nearly impossible to extract.

children.name: Stephanolepis
children.description: Stephanolepis is a genus of filefish known for their compressed, diamond-shaped bodies and rough, sandpaper-like skin. These marine fish are characterized by their ability to change color and their habit of swimming in an upright position among seagrasses and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have a distinctive first dorsal fin with a large, movable spine that can be locked upright, and their mouths are small and positioned at the tip of a slightly elongated snout.
children.funFact: Planehead filefish can rapidly change their color and pattern to match their surroundings, making them masters of camouflage in seagrass beds and rocky areas.

children.description: Filefishes are marine fish with compressed, diamond-shaped bodies and rough, sandpaper-like skin that gives them their name. They have small mouths with prominent teeth and a distinctive dorsal spine that can be locked upright when threatened. These colorful fish are closely related to triggerfish but are generally smaller and more peaceful.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their triggerfish relatives, filefishes have only a single prominent dorsal spine rather than multiple spines, and their skin has a distinctly rough, file-like texture from tiny scales called denticles.
children.funFact: Many filefishes are masters of camouflage and can change their color and pattern to match their surroundings, with some species even mimicking floating seaweed or coral branches.

children.name: Ostraciidae
Lactophrys
children.description: Lactophrys is a genus of tropical marine fish known as trunkfish or boxfish, characterized by their distinctive box-like bodies enclosed in a hard, bony shell made of fused plates. These unusual fish swim by fluttering their fins rather than using typical fish-like body movements, since their rigid armor prevents them from bending their bodies. They are typically found in warm coastal waters around coral reefs and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish, Lactophrys species have completely rigid, box-shaped bodies covered in a hard carapace of bony plates, with only their mouth, eyes, fins, and tail able to move. Their unique body armor makes them look more like swimming boxes than typical fish.
children.funFact: When threatened, trunkfish can release toxic compounds from their skin that can kill other fish in the surrounding water, including themselves if trapped in a small space!

children.name: Acanthostracion
children.description: Acanthostracion is a genus of tropical marine fish commonly known as cowfish, named for the horn-like projections that extend from their heads. These distinctive fish have box-like bodies encased in a hard, bony shell made of fused plates, with only their fins, eyes, mouth, and gill openings able to move freely.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other boxfish, cowfish in this genus have prominent horn-like spines projecting from both the front and back of their triangular heads, giving them their characteristic cow-like appearance.
children.funFact: When threatened, cowfish can release a toxic substance called ostracitoxin from their skin that can be deadly to other fish in the same tank or confined area, making them challenging aquarium residents despite their charming appearance.

children.description: Boxfishes are uniquely armored marine fish with bodies encased in a rigid, box-like shell made of fused bony plates. This distinctive carapace gives them their characteristic angular, geometric appearance and limits their movement to slow, precise swimming using their fins and tail. They're found in warmer coastal waters where they feed on small invertebrates and algae.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish with flexible, scale-covered bodies, boxfishes have inflexible, cube or triangular-shaped bodies formed by fused bony plates. Many species also have prominent spines or horns projecting from their armored shell.
children.funFact: When threatened, some boxfishes can release a toxic substance called ostracitoxin from their skin that can kill nearby fish and even poison themselves in confined spaces like aquariums!

children.name: Tetraodontidae
Sphoeroides
children.description: Sphoeroides is a genus of pufferfish found in marine waters, known for their ability to rapidly inflate their bodies like balloons when threatened. These fish have compact, rounded bodies and can dramatically increase their size by gulping water or air to deter predators. They are bottom-dwelling fish that feed on small invertebrates, crabs, and mollusks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sphoeroides puffers are distinguished from other pufferfish by their relatively smooth skin with small spines that become more prominent when inflated, and their distinctive beak-like mouth formed by fused teeth.
children.funFact: When a Sphoeroides pufferfish inflates, it can triple its normal size in just seconds, transforming from a streamlined swimmer into a spiky, nearly spherical balloon that's too large and intimidating for most predators to swallow.

children.name: Lagocephalus
children.description: Pelagic pufferfishes are smooth-skinned marine fish that live in open ocean waters rather than near the shore. They have the characteristic ability to inflate their bodies into a balloon-like shape when threatened, using water or air to make themselves appear larger to predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other pufferfish that live in coastal areas or coral reefs, Lagocephalus species are adapted for life in the open ocean with streamlined bodies and stronger swimming abilities.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'smooth' puffers, these fish still contain the deadly neurotoxin tetrodotoxin in their organs, making them just as dangerous to eat as their spiny relatives.

children.description: Pufferfishes are distinctive marine fish known for their ability to inflate their bodies into a balloon-like shape when threatened. They have tough, leathery skin instead of scales and possess strong, beak-like teeth that are fused together, which they use to crush hard-shelled prey like crabs and mollusks.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, pufferfishes have four large, fused teeth (giving them their scientific name 'Tetraodontidae' meaning 'four teeth') and can dramatically inflate their bodies by swallowing water or air.
children.funFact: Many pufferfish species contain tetrodotoxin, one of the most potent neurotoxins known to science, which makes them extremely poisonous to predators and humans - yet they're considered a delicacy called 'fugu' in Japan when prepared by specially licensed chefs.

children.name: Balistidae
Balistes
children.description: Balistes is a genus of triggerfish known for their distinctive diamond-shaped, laterally compressed bodies and tough, leathery skin. These marine fish get their name from their unique dorsal fin system, where the first spine can be 'triggered' or locked upright and only released when the second spine is pressed down.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Balistes are distinguished from other triggerfish by their relatively large size, robust build, and specific fin ray counts. They typically have a more elongated snout compared to other triggerfish genera.
children.funFact: Triggerfish in the genus Balistes can wedge themselves into coral crevices by locking their trigger spine upright, making it nearly impossible for predators to pull them out of their hiding spots.

children.name: Canthidermis
children.description: Oceanic Triggerfishes are deep-water members of the triggerfish family that spend their lives swimming in the open ocean rather than near coral reefs like their coastal relatives. These robust fish have the characteristic triggerfish body shape with a compressed, oval form and the ability to lock their first dorsal spine upright as a defense mechanism.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike reef-dwelling triggerfishes, oceanic triggerfishes have adapted to life in open water with more streamlined bodies and different feeding behaviors, often following floating debris or sargassum patches.
children.funFact: The Spotted Oceanic Triggerfish can lock its dorsal spine in an upright position, making it nearly impossible for predators to swallow them headfirst.

children.description: Triggerfishes are distinctive marine fish with compressed, diamond-shaped bodies and tough, leathery skin covered in small scales. They get their name from their unique dorsal fin mechanism - the first spine can be locked upright and only released by depressing a smaller 'trigger' spine behind it. These fish are typically found in warmer waters and are known for their bold behavior and strong teeth adapted for crushing hard prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Triggerfishes are easily recognized by their laterally compressed, oval bodies and their characteristic trigger-like dorsal fin locking mechanism. Unlike most other fish, they swim primarily by undulating their dorsal and anal fins rather than using their tail fin.
children.funFact: When threatened, triggerfishes can wedge themselves into coral crevices or rocky holes and lock their dorsal spine in place, making them nearly impossible for predators to extract.

children.name: Diodontidae
Chilomycterus
children.description: Burrfishes are small, round marine fish covered in short, sharp spines that give them a prickly appearance like a burr. They have the ability to inflate their bodies when threatened, making their spines stick out even more prominently. These bottom-dwelling fish use their strong, beak-like teeth to crush shells and feed on mollusks, crustaceans, and other small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the porcupinefishes, burrfishes have shorter, triangular spines that are always erect rather than long spines that can lie flat. They also tend to be smaller and have a more compact, rounded body shape.
children.funFact: When a burrfish inflates itself into a spiky ball, it can triple its normal size, making it nearly impossible for predators to swallow!

children.name: Diodon
children.description: Diodon is a genus of porcupinefish known for their remarkable ability to inflate their bodies into a spiky ball when threatened. These marine fish are covered in sharp spines that normally lie flat against their body but become erect when the fish puffs up with water or air.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other pufferfish, Diodon species have long, prominent spines that are always visible on their body surface, and they can inflate to a much more dramatic spherical shape.
children.funFact: When a porcupinefish inflates, it can triple its normal size, transforming from a streamlined swimmer into a floating spiky balloon that's nearly impossible for predators to swallow.

children.description: Porcupinefishes are fascinating marine fish that can dramatically transform their appearance when threatened by inflating their bodies like balloons and erecting sharp spines. These slow-moving fish have powerful beaks made of fused teeth that they use to crush hard-shelled prey like sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks. They're typically found in warmer coastal waters around the world, though some species occasionally visit New England waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close relatives the pufferfishes, porcupinefishes have prominent spines covering their bodies that become erect when they inflate. Their teeth are fused into a powerful beak-like structure with only two tooth plates (hence 'Diodon' meaning 'two teeth').
children.funFact: When a porcupinefish inflates, it can increase its size by up to three times, making it nearly impossible for predators to swallow, and the fish can remain inflated for several minutes even after the threat has passed.

children.name: Molidae
Mola
children.description: Mola is a genus of massive, unusual-looking ocean fish commonly known as ocean sunfish or molas. These are among the heaviest bony fish in the world, with flattened, disc-like bodies that appear almost tailless due to their extremely short, rounded rear fins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Molas are distinguished from other large ocean fish by their unique body shape that looks like a giant fish head with fins, lacking a traditional tail fin and instead having a wavy rear fin called a clavus.
children.funFact: A single female mola can release up to 300 million eggs at once, more than any other known vertebrate species.

children.description: Molas, also known as ocean sunfish, are among the world's largest and most unusual bony fish. These massive, flattened fish have a distinctive rounded body shape that looks like someone cut off the back half of a regular fish, giving them an almost disc-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Molas are easily recognized by their extremely flattened, oval body shape and lack of a true tail fin, instead having a wavy fin called a clavus that runs along their back edge.
children.funFact: Despite being the world's heaviest bony fish - weighing up to 5,000 pounds - molas feed primarily on jellyfish and can leap completely out of the water!

children.description: Puffers and filefishes are a diverse group of marine fish known for their unique body shapes and specialized feeding habits. Most members of this order have tough, leathery skin instead of typical fish scales, and many can dramatically change their body shape when threatened. They're often found in warmer waters, though several species visit New England waters seasonally.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, these species have fused or modified teeth that form beak-like structures perfect for crushing shells, coral, or scraping algae. Many can also inflate their bodies with water or air as a defense mechanism, or have rigid, box-like body armor.
children.funFact: Ocean sunfish (molas) in this group are the heaviest bony fish in the world, with some individuals weighing over 4,000 pounds - that's heavier than a small car!

children.name: Salmoniformes
Salmonidae
Salvelinus
children.description: Chars are a group of cold-water fish in the salmon family that thrive in the pristine lakes and streams of New England. These beautiful fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies, small scales, and preference for the cleanest, coldest waters in the region. Both Brook Trout and Lake Trout belong to this genus and are prized by anglers for their fighting spirit and delicate flavor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their salmon and trout cousins, chars have light-colored spots on a darker background (rather than dark spots on light backgrounds) and typically prefer colder water temperatures. They also have a distinctive white leading edge on their fins, particularly noticeable on the pectoral, pelvic, and anal fins.
children.funFact: Brook Trout, despite their name, are actually chars and not true trout - they're more closely related to Lake Trout than to Rainbow or Brown Trout!

children.name: Oncorhynchus
children.description: Pacific Salmons and Trouts are a group of fish known for their remarkable life cycles and adaptability to both freshwater and saltwater environments. These silvery, streamlined fish are famous for their incredible journeys, often traveling hundreds or thousands of miles between their birthplace and feeding grounds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Atlantic salmon, Pacific salmon typically die after spawning, completing a dramatic one-way journey from ocean back to their natal streams. They have distinctive hooked jaws during breeding season and their flesh ranges from white to deep red.
children.funFact: Some Pacific salmon can travel over 2,000 miles from the ocean back to the exact stream where they were born, using their incredible sense of smell to navigate home.

children.name: Salmo
children.description: Atlantic Salmons and Trouts are sleek, powerful fish that spend part of their lives in freshwater and part in saltwater. These fish are known for their incredible ability to navigate back to their birth streams to spawn, often swimming upstream against strong currents and even jumping over waterfalls.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike Pacific salmon species, Atlantic salmons and trouts can survive spawning and return to the ocean multiple times throughout their lives. They have distinctive spotted patterns and streamlined bodies perfectly adapted for both river and ocean environments.
children.funFact: Atlantic salmon can jump up to 12 feet high to clear obstacles like waterfalls during their upstream migration to spawning grounds.

children.name: Coregonus
children.description: Whitefishes are a group of cold-water fish in the salmon family that live in deep, clear lakes and northern rivers. These silvery fish have small mouths and feed primarily on tiny crustaceans, insects, and plankton rather than other fish. They are important both ecologically and commercially in northern freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their salmon and trout relatives, whitefishes have much smaller mouths, lack the hooked jaws of spawning males, and have a more herring-like appearance with deeply forked tails and compressed bodies.
children.funFact: Lake Whitefish can live over 20 years and are considered a delicacy, with their eggs sometimes used as a substitute for caviar in the Great Lakes region.

children.name: Prosopium
children.description: Prosopium is a genus of freshwater fish in the salmon family known as whitefishes. These cold-water fish are characterized by their silvery bodies, small mouths, and preference for deep, cold lakes and rivers. They are important members of northern aquatic ecosystems and have adapted to life in some of the coldest freshwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Prosopium whitefishes have relatively small mouths positioned at the front of their snouts (rather than underneath like some related fish) and lack the prominent teeth found in trout and salmon. Their bodies are more cylindrical and streamlined compared to other whitefishes in the region.
children.funFact: Round whitefish can live for over 20 years and are so well-adapted to cold water that they remain active even under ice, making them an important food source for northern predators during winter months.

children.description: The Salmonidae family includes some of New England's most iconic freshwater and anadromous fish, known for their streamlined bodies and exceptional swimming abilities. These cold-water fish are characterized by their adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) and their complex life cycles that often involve migrations between fresh and salt water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Salmonids are easily recognized by their distinctive adipose fin, which no other fish families in New England possess. They also have relatively large mouths with well-developed teeth and typically show beautiful coloration that can change dramatically during spawning season.
children.funFact: Many salmonids are anadromous, meaning they're born in freshwater, migrate to the ocean to grow and mature, then return to their exact birthplace to spawn using their incredible sense of smell to navigate back to the same stream where they hatched.

children.name: Esocidae
Esox
children.description: Pikes are freshwater predatory fish known for their elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies and large mouths filled with sharp teeth. These ambush hunters lurk in weedy areas of lakes, ponds, and slow-moving rivers, where they dart out to catch smaller fish, frogs, and other aquatic prey. All members of this genus share similar hunting behaviors and body structure, though they vary considerably in size.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pikes can be distinguished from other fish by their duck-like snouts, dorsal fins positioned far back near their tails, and distinctive light-colored spots or chain-like patterns on darker backgrounds. Their flattened heads and undershot jaws filled with needle-sharp teeth make them unmistakable predators.
children.funFact: Muskellunge, the largest member of the pike genus, can grow over 4 feet long and live for decades - some specimens have been aged at over 30 years old!

children.description: Pikes are freshwater predatory fish known for their elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies and fearsome hunting abilities. These aggressive fish have long snouts filled with sharp teeth and are perfectly built for ambush hunting in weedy lakes and slow-moving rivers. All members of this family are carnivorous and play important roles as top predators in freshwater ecosystems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pikes can be distinguished from other fish by their duck-like snouts, backward-angled teeth, and dorsal fins positioned far back near their tails. Their body pattern of light spots or bars on a darker background is also characteristic of the family.
children.funFact: Pike can accelerate from 0 to 20 mph in just milliseconds when striking prey, making them one of the fastest-attacking freshwater fish in North America.

children.name: Umbridae
Umbra
children.description: Mudminnows are small, hardy freshwater fish that are perfectly adapted for life in shallow, muddy waters with low oxygen levels. These tough little survivors can tolerate conditions that would kill most other fish, making them true champions of wetlands and sluggish streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true minnows, mudminnows have a rounded tail fin and can survive in oxygen-poor water by gulping air at the surface. They also have a distinctive dark bar at the base of their tail.
children.funFact: Mudminnows can survive being frozen in ice during winter by entering a state similar to suspended animation, earning them the nickname 'dogfish' for their incredible tenacity.

children.description: Mudminnows are small, hardy freshwater fish that are perfectly adapted to life in shallow, weedy waters with low oxygen levels. These tough little survivors can tolerate conditions that would kill most other fish, including near-freezing temperatures and muddy, stagnant ponds. They're called 'mudminnows' because of their ability to burrow into soft mud and their minnow-like appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true minnows, mudminnows have a rounded tail fin and can survive in extremely low-oxygen environments that most fish cannot tolerate. They also have the unique ability to gulp air from the surface when oxygen levels drop too low.
children.funFact: Mudminnows can survive being frozen in ice for short periods and can even live out of water for several hours by breathing air, making them one of the most resilient freshwater fish in New England.

children.description: Salmoniformes is an order of freshwater and anadromous fish that includes some of New England's most prized sport fish. These fish are characterized by having an adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) and typically lack spines in their fins, having only soft rays instead.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order can be distinguished from other fish by their adipose fin and the absence of fin spines. They also have a primitive swim bladder connected to their digestive tract, unlike many other fish groups.
children.funFact: Atlantic salmon can live up to 8 years and travel thousands of miles in the ocean before returning to the exact stream where they were born to spawn.

children.name: Centrarchiformes
Centrarchidae
Lepomis
children.description: Common sunfishes are small to medium-sized freshwater fish known for their round, flattened bodies and vibrant colors. These popular game fish are found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England, where they're easily recognized by their distinctive ear flaps and fan-shaped fins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sunfish family members, true sunfishes in the Lepomis genus have relatively small mouths and feed primarily on insects, small crustaceans, and plant matter rather than larger prey like bass do.
children.funFact: Male sunfishes are devoted fathers who build circular nests in shallow water by fanning away sediment with their tails, then aggressively guard their eggs and young fry from predators.

children.name: Micropterus
children.description: Black basses are popular freshwater game fish known for their fighting spirit and jumping ability when hooked. These robust, predatory fish have large mouths perfect for catching smaller fish, crayfish, and aquatic insects. They prefer warm, clear waters with plenty of cover like fallen logs, rocky areas, or vegetation.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Black basses can be distinguished from other bass species by their large mouths that extend past their eyes and their distinctive body shape with a notched dorsal fin. Unlike true bass (which are marine fish), black basses are actually members of the sunfish family.
children.funFact: Despite their name, black basses aren't actually black - they're typically greenish with dark markings, and they're not true bass at all but are more closely related to bluegills and other sunfish!

children.name: Pomoxis
children.description: Crappies are popular freshwater fish known for their silvery, laterally compressed bodies and excellent taste. These medium-sized members of the sunfish family are prized by anglers for both their fighting ability and their value as table fare.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Crappies can be distinguished from other sunfish by their more elongated bodies, larger mouths, and distinctive pattern of dark spots or vertical bars on their silvery sides.
children.funFact: Crappies are sometimes called 'papermouth' by anglers because their mouths are relatively soft and hooks can easily tear free if too much pressure is applied during the fight.

children.name: Ambloplites
children.description: Rock basses are freshwater fish known for their robust, laterally compressed bodies and distinctive spotted patterns. They are members of the sunfish family and are popular among anglers for their fighting spirit when hooked.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rock basses can be distinguished from other sunfish by their larger mouth, red eyes, and rows of dark spots along their sides rather than the solid coloration or different patterns seen in other sunfish species.
children.funFact: Rock bass have exceptionally keen eyesight and can spot prey in murky water, which is why they're often called 'redeye bass' due to their distinctive crimson-colored eyes.

children.name: Enneacanthus
children.description: Banded sunfishes are small, colorful freshwater fish that belong to the sunfish family. They are characterized by their distinctive dark vertical bands that run across their olive-green to brownish bodies, giving them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sunfish, banded sunfishes have a more compressed, deep body shape and prominent dark vertical bars rather than spots or solid coloration. They also tend to be smaller than most other sunfish species.
children.funFact: Male banded sunfish build circular nests in shallow water and can become quite aggressive in defending their territory, despite being only about 3-4 inches long.

children.description: Freshwater sunfishes are a diverse family of warm-water fish that includes popular game species like largemouth bass, bluegill, and crappie. These fish are characterized by their laterally compressed (flattened side-to-side) bodies and typically have two connected dorsal fins with both spiny and soft rays. Most species build circular nests in shallow water during breeding season and are known for their aggressive territorial behavior.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sunfishes can be distinguished from other freshwater fish by their unique combination of spiny and soft-rayed dorsal fins that are connected, plus their characteristic body shape that's deeper than it is wide. Unlike many other fish families, male sunfishes are devoted parents that guard their nests and fry.
children.funFact: Male sunfishes become incredibly colorful during breeding season and will fiercely attack anything that comes near their circular gravel nests, including fish many times their size!

children.description: Freshwater Sunfishes, Grunters, and Allies are a diverse group of fish that primarily live in freshwater environments like lakes, ponds, and rivers. Most members of this group are known for their colorful appearance, especially during breeding season, and their habit of building nests to protect their eggs and young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish are characterized by having spiny rays in their dorsal and anal fins, and most species show remarkable parental care behavior where males guard nests and protect their offspring.
children.funFact: Male sunfish are devoted dads who fan their eggs with their fins to keep them oxygenated and will aggressively chase away any intruders that come too close to their nest, even fish much larger than themselves!

children.name: Clupeiformes
Alosidae
Alosa
children.description: Anadromous shads are silvery fish that spend most of their adult lives in the ocean but return to freshwater rivers and streams to spawn. These herring-like fish are an important part of New England's coastal ecosystems and have been a valuable food source for both wildlife and humans for centuries. All four New England species share this remarkable life cycle of migrating between salt and fresh water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their ocean-dwelling herring relatives, anadromous shads must return to freshwater to reproduce, often traveling hundreds of miles upstream to reach their spawning grounds. They can be distinguished from other herring by their deeper bodies and the fact that adults are typically found in rivers during spring spawning season.
children.funFact: American Shad can live up to 13 years and may return to spawn in the exact same river where they were born, somehow remembering their birthplace after years at sea.

children.name: Brevoortia
children.description: Menhaden are medium-sized, silvery fish that belong to the herring family and live in coastal Atlantic waters. They are filter feeders that swim in massive schools, straining tiny plankton and algae from the water through their gill rakers. These fish play a crucial role in marine food webs, serving as a primary food source for many larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Menhaden can be distinguished from other herring-family fish by their deeply compressed, oval-shaped bodies and their specialized gill rakers that are particularly well-developed for filter feeding. They also have a distinctive dark spot behind their gill cover and often show a series of smaller spots along their sides.
children.funFact: Atlantic Menhaden are sometimes called 'the most important fish in the sea' because they filter up to 4 gallons of water per minute while feeding, helping to keep coastal waters clean, and their massive schools can contain millions of fish that feed everything from striped bass to whales.

children.description: Shads and sardines are silvery, herring-like fish that belong to the family Alosidae. Most members of this family are anadromous, meaning they spend their adult lives in the ocean but return to freshwater rivers and streams to spawn. These fish are important both ecologically as food sources for larger predators and economically as commercial fish species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their close herring relatives, most alosids have a distinctive saw-toothed belly formed by sharp, bony scales called scutes. They also typically have a deeper, more compressed body shape than true herrings.
children.funFact: American Shad can live up to 13 years and travel over 12,000 miles during their lifetime, with some individuals making multiple round trips between the ocean and their natal rivers to spawn.

children.name: Dorosomatidae
children.commonName: Thread Herrings, Gizzard Shads, and Sardinellas

children.name: Dorosoma
children.description: Gizzard shads are medium-sized freshwater fish with deep, compressed bodies and silvery scales. They get their name from their muscular, gizzard-like stomach that helps them digest plant matter and small organisms they filter from the water. These fish are important members of freshwater ecosystems, serving as food for larger predatory fish.
