children.distinguishingFeatures: Gizzard shads can be identified by their distinctive threadlike extension on the last ray of their dorsal fin and their small, toothless mouth designed for filter feeding.
children.funFact: Gizzard shads can live over 10 years and are sometimes called "mud shad" because they stir up sediment while feeding along lake and river bottoms.

children.name: Sardinella
children.description: Sardinellas are small, silvery marine fish that belong to the herring family. They are schooling fish that feed on plankton and small organisms in the water column, often forming large groups near the surface of coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sardinellas can be distinguished from other small herrings by their relatively deeper body shape and the presence of distinctive dark spots along their sides.
children.funFact: Round Sardinella can live up to 6 years and are known to migrate seasonally, following warm water currents along the Atlantic coast.

children.name: Opisthonema
children.description: Thread herrings are small, silvery schooling fish that belong to the herring family. They are characterized by their streamlined bodies and the distinctive thread-like extension of their dorsal fin that gives them their common name. These marine fish form large schools and feed primarily on plankton and small organisms in the water column.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Thread herrings can be distinguished from other herrings by the long, thread-like filament that extends from the last ray of their dorsal fin. They also have a more compressed body shape and a distinctive spot behind their gill cover.
children.funFact: The thread-like dorsal fin filament of these fish can be longer than their entire head, and scientists believe it may help them maintain position within their tightly packed schools.

children.description: Thread herrings, gizzard shads, and sardinellas are small to medium-sized silvery fish that form large schools in coastal waters and estuaries. These fish are filter feeders, using their gill rakers to strain tiny plankton, algae, and organic particles from the water. They play important roles as both predators of microscopic organisms and prey for larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other herring-like fish, members of this family have a distinctive thread-like extension on their dorsal fin and specialized gill rakers that form an efficient filtering system. They also have a sharp, saw-toothed belly edge called a scute that helps distinguish them from true herrings.
children.funFact: Gizzard shads get their name from their muscular, bird-like gizzard that helps them grind up the algae and detritus they filter from the water - making them one of the few fish that can efficiently digest plant material.

children.name: Clupeidae
Clupea
children.description: Clupea is a genus of herring fish that includes some of the most commercially important fish species in the world. These are medium-sized, silvery fish that travel in large schools and feed primarily on plankton and small marine organisms. They play a crucial role in marine food webs as both predators of small organisms and prey for larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Clupea are distinguished from other herring by their specific body proportions, scale patterns, and the arrangement of their gill rakers. They typically have a more streamlined body shape and different fin positioning compared to their close relatives in other herring genera.
children.funFact: Atlantic herring can live up to 25 years and form some of the largest fish aggregations on Earth, with schools sometimes containing billions of individuals that can be seen from space!

children.description: Herrings and sprats are silvery, streamlined fish that travel in large schools through ocean waters. These important commercial fish have compressed bodies, forked tails, and feed primarily on plankton and small organisms by filtering them from the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish families, herrings have a distinctive row of sharp, saw-like scales called scutes along their belly edge. They also lack a lateral line system that most other fish use to detect water movement.
children.funFact: A single school of Atlantic herring can contain over a billion fish, creating underwater formations so dense they appear like dark clouds on sonar equipment.

children.name: Engraulidae
Anchoa
children.description: Anchoa is a genus of small, slender fish commonly known as anchovies. These silvery marine fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies, large mouths, and schooling behavior in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Anchoa can be distinguished from other anchovy genera by their relatively deep body shape and specific fin ray counts. They typically have a more compressed body form compared to their closest relatives.
children.funFact: Bay anchovies can live in both saltwater and brackish water, making them one of the most adaptable small fish in New England's coastal ecosystems.

children.description: Anchovies are small, silvery fish that live in schools in coastal waters and estuaries. They have streamlined bodies built for fast swimming and feed primarily on plankton by filtering it from the water through their gill rakers. These important forage fish form massive schools that support many marine food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Anchovies can be distinguished from other small schooling fish by their distinctively large mouth that extends well behind their eye, and their deeply forked tail fin. They also have a single dorsal fin positioned toward the middle of their back.
children.funFact: Despite their reputation as a polarizing pizza topping, anchovies are one of the most important fish families in marine ecosystems, with their massive schools sometimes containing millions of individuals that can stretch for miles across the ocean.

children.name: Dussumieriidae
children.commonName: Rainbow Sardines and Red-eye Round Herrings

children.name: Etrumeus
children.description: Red-eye Round Herrings are small, silvery fish with distinctively large, prominent red eyes that give them their common name. These streamlined fish are members of the herring family and are built for life in open ocean waters, where they form schools and feed on small planktonic organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other herrings, red-eye round herrings have a more rounded, less compressed body shape and lack the sharp, saw-like belly scales that characterize many of their relatives. Their large red eyes are particularly distinctive and help separate them from similar-looking fish.
children.funFact: Red-eye Round Herrings are primarily tropical fish that only occasionally venture into New England waters during warm summer months, making them an exciting but rare find for local anglers and marine enthusiasts.

children.description: Rainbow sardines and red-eye round herrings are small, silvery fish that swim in large schools in coastal waters. They have streamlined bodies and are important members of the ocean food web, feeding on plankton while serving as prey for larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish can be distinguished from other herring-like fish by their distinctive red eyes and more rounded body shape. They lack the sharp, saw-like belly scales found in true herrings.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, red-eye round herrings can live up to 7 years and travel thousands of miles during their lifetime migrations.

children.description: Herrings are a diverse order of silvery, schooling fish that are incredibly important both ecologically and economically. These streamlined marine fish are known for forming massive schools that can contain millions of individuals, creating some of the ocean's most spectacular underwater displays. They feed primarily on plankton and small organisms, serving as a crucial link in marine food webs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Herrings are characterized by their compressed, silvery bodies, forked tails, and lack of a lateral line on their scales. Unlike many other fish orders, they have a unique arrangement of bones in their skull and most species have a serrated belly edge formed by specialized scales called scutes.
children.funFact: A single school of Atlantic herring can stretch for miles and contain over a billion fish, creating such dense formations that they can actually be detected by sonar and appear as solid walls underwater.

children.name: Gadiformes
Gadidae
Pollachius
children.description: Pollachius is a genus of marine fish in the cod family, known for their sleek, elongated bodies and strong swimming abilities. These fish are important commercial species found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic, where they feed on smaller fish, crustaceans, and marine worms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Pollachius can be distinguished from other cod family fish by their more streamlined body shape, longer lower jaw that extends beyond the upper jaw, and their relatively small or absent chin barbel (whisker-like projection).
children.funFact: Pollock are incredibly fast swimmers and can reach speeds of up to 25 miles per hour when chasing prey or escaping predators, making them one of the most athletic members of the cod family.

children.name: Gadus
children.description: Gadus is a genus of large, cold-water fish commonly known as true cod. These are bottom-dwelling fish with three dorsal fins, two anal fins, and a distinctive chin barbel that helps them locate food on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gadus are distinguished from other cod-like fish by their specific fin arrangement and the presence of a prominent barbel under the chin. They are typically larger and more robust than their close relatives in the cod family.
children.funFact: Atlantic cod have an incredible sense of taste and smell - they can detect food particles in the water from great distances using their barbel and can even taste potential prey before deciding whether to eat it.

children.name: Microgadus
children.description: Microgadus is a small genus of cod-like fish that includes the Atlantic Tomcod, a diminutive member of the cod family. These fish are much smaller than their famous Atlantic Cod relatives, typically reaching only 6-15 inches in length. They inhabit coastal waters and estuaries along the Atlantic coast.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger cod cousins, Microgadus species are characterized by their small size and preference for shallow, nearshore waters including brackish estuaries where few other cod family members venture.
children.funFact: Atlantic Tomcod can survive in nearly freezing water thanks to special antifreeze proteins in their blood that prevent ice crystals from forming in their bodies.

children.name: Melanogrammus
children.description: Melanogrammus is a genus of cod-like fish that contains only one species - the haddock. These marine fish are important members of the North Atlantic ecosystem and are closely related to Atlantic cod, sharing similar body shapes and habitats.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Haddock can be distinguished from their cod relatives by their distinctive black lateral line and a prominent dark spot behind their gill cover, often called a 'thumbprint.'
children.funFact: The dark spot behind a haddock's gill is said in folklore to be the thumbprint of Saint Peter, who according to legend caught the first haddock with his hands.

children.description: Cods and haddocks are a family of cold-water marine fish that are among the most commercially important species in the North Atlantic. These bottom-dwelling fish have elongated bodies, multiple fins, and small barbels (whisker-like projections) on their chins that help them locate food on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family can be identified by their three separate dorsal fins, two anal fins, and the distinctive barbel under their chin. They also have large mouths and relatively large scales compared to other similar fish.
children.funFact: Atlantic cod can live over 20 years and historically grew so large that early New England colonists reported catching specimens over 6 feet long, though overfishing has made such giants extremely rare today.

children.name: Phycidae
Urophycis
children.description: Urophycis is a genus of marine fish commonly known as hakes, which are bottom-dwelling cod relatives found in the Atlantic Ocean. These elongated fish have soft, scaleless skin and are important both commercially and ecologically in New England's coastal waters. All three New England species share similar body shapes with tapering tails and barbels (whisker-like projections) on their chins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Urophycis hakes can be distinguished from other cod family members by their distinctive barbels on the chin and their more elongated, eel-like body shape. They also lack the multiple dorsal fins typical of true cod, instead having long, continuous dorsal and anal fins.
children.funFact: White hake can live over 20 years and migrate from shallow coastal waters in summer to deeper waters in winter, sometimes traveling hundreds of miles along the continental shelf.

children.description: Phycid Hakes are a family of bottom-dwelling marine fish found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic. These elongated fish are relatives of cod and have two dorsal fins, with the second one being much longer, and a single long anal fin that gives them their distinctive streamlined appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their cod relatives, phycid hakes have a more slender body shape and their fins are positioned differently, with the long second dorsal and anal fins running most of the length of their body. They also have a small chin barbel that helps them locate food on the seafloor.
children.funFact: Some species of phycid hakes can live for over 20 years and are known to migrate vertically in the water column, moving from deep waters during the day to shallower areas at night to feed.

children.name: Lotidae
Lota
children.description: Lota is a genus of freshwater fish that includes only one living species - the burbot. These are elongated, eel-like fish that belong to the cod family but have adapted to live in cold freshwater lakes and rivers rather than the ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Burbots are the only members of the cod family that live exclusively in freshwater, and they're easily recognized by their single chin barbel and their long, continuous dorsal fin.
children.funFact: Burbots are unusual among freshwater fish because they spawn under the ice in winter, making them one of the few fish species that are most active during the coldest months of the year.

children.name: Brosme
children.description: Brosme is a genus containing just one species - the cusk, a deep-water cod relative found in the cold waters of the North Atlantic. This solitary fish is known for its elongated body and preference for rocky bottoms in deeper waters along the continental shelf.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other cod family members, cusk have a single long dorsal fin that runs almost the entire length of their back, and they lack the distinctive barbel (whisker-like appendage) under their chin that many cod relatives possess.
children.funFact: Cusk are sometimes called "torsk" by fishermen and can live for over 20 years, growing slowly in the cold depths where they make their home.

children.description: Hakes and burbots are bottom-dwelling fish in the cod family that live in cold northern waters. These elongated fish have soft, scaleless skin and typically feed on smaller fish, crustaceans, and worms along the ocean floor or lake bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their cod relatives, hakes and burbots have more elongated bodies and lack the prominent barbel (chin whisker) that many cod species display. They also tend to be more solitary hunters rather than schooling fish.
children.funFact: The burbot is the only member of the cod family that lives entirely in freshwater, earning it the nickname 'freshwater cod' or 'lawyer fish' due to its slimy, slippery skin.

children.name: Merlucciidae
Merluccius
children.description: Hakes are slender, elongated fish with large mouths and sharp teeth that live in marine waters. They are active predators that hunt smaller fish, squid, and crustaceans, typically staying near the ocean bottom during the day and moving toward the surface at night to feed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Hakes can be distinguished from other cod-family fish by their more streamlined body shape, prominent lower jaw that extends beyond the upper jaw, and their habit of forming large schools in open water.
children.funFact: Silver hake are sometimes called "whiting" and can live up to 14 years, growing to over 2 feet long while making daily vertical migrations from deep water to shallow areas following their prey.

children.description: Merlucciid hakes are elongated marine fish with large mouths and prominent teeth, perfectly designed for their life as active predators in deeper waters. They have streamlined bodies and two separate dorsal fins, with the second one being much longer than the first. These commercially important fish are found in temperate and cold waters around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other cod-like fish, merlucciid hakes have no chin barbel (whisker) and their lower jaw extends slightly beyond the upper jaw. Their large mouth and sharp teeth make them easily recognizable among bottom-dwelling fish.
children.funFact: Silver hake can actually make sounds by vibrating their swim bladders, and during spawning season, large groups create underwater choruses that can be heard by fishermen above!

children.name: Gaidropsaridae
Enchelyopus
children.description: Enchelyopus is a genus of marine fish known as rocklings that live in cold northern waters. These bottom-dwelling fish have elongated, eel-like bodies and are well-adapted to life on rocky seafloors and among kelp beds.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by having four distinctive barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) around their mouth, which they use to locate food in murky bottom waters.
children.funFact: The fourbeard rockling can survive in very shallow tide pools during low tide, using its barbels to hunt for small crustaceans and worms while waiting for the tide to return.

children.description: Rocklings are a small family of elongated marine fish that live near the bottom of rocky coastal waters. These slender fish have barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) around their mouths that help them find food in crevices and under rocks. They are closely related to cods but have adapted to live in shallow, rocky habitats rather than open water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rocklings can be distinguished from their cod relatives by their extremely elongated, eel-like bodies and the presence of prominent barbels on their chin and snout. They also have very long dorsal and anal fins that run almost the entire length of their body.
children.funFact: Despite their snake-like appearance, rocklings are actually members of the cod family and can sometimes be found hiding in tide pools during low tide.

children.description: Cods and hakes are bottom-dwelling marine fish that are incredibly important both ecologically and economically in New England waters. These fish typically have elongated bodies, multiple fins including distinctive dorsal and anal fins, and most have barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) on their chins that help them find food on the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other fish groups, cods and hakes have their pelvic fins positioned forward under their throats rather than further back on their bodies. Most also lack spines in their fins, having only soft rays instead.
children.funFact: Atlantic cod can live over 20 years and were once so abundant off New England that early explorers reported you could walk across their backs, though overfishing has dramatically reduced their numbers since then.

children.name: Cyprinodontiformes
Fundulidae
Fundulus
children.description: Typical topminnows are small, hardy fish that live in shallow coastal waters, salt marshes, and tidal areas throughout New England. These resilient little fish are perfectly adapted to life in brackish water where salt and fresh water mix, and they can tolerate dramatic changes in salinity and temperature that would kill most other fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, topminnows can survive in water ranging from completely fresh to fully saltwater, and they have upturned mouths designed for feeding at the water's surface.
children.funFact: Mummichogs can survive out of water for hours by breathing air, and they're so tough that they were among the first fish sent into space by NASA in 1973!

children.name: Lucania
children.description: Lucania is a genus of small freshwater fish known as rainwater killifish. These tiny fish are typically found in shallow, often temporary water bodies like ditches, ponds, and marsh edges where they've adapted to survive in varying water conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Rainwater killifish are distinguished from other killifish by their extremely small size (usually under 2 inches) and their remarkable tolerance for rapidly changing water conditions, including fluctuating salinity and temperature.
children.funFact: Despite their name, rainwater killifish don't actually kill other fish - the 'kill' comes from the Dutch word 'kil' meaning stream or creek!

children.description: Topminnows are small freshwater and brackish water fish that typically swim near the surface of ponds, streams, and coastal waters. They have upturned mouths perfectly designed for feeding on insects and other small prey at the water's surface, and most species are quite hardy and adaptable to different water conditions.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their upward-pointing mouths and flattened heads distinguish them from other small fish, along with their preference for staying in the top layer of water rather than swimming throughout the water column.
children.funFact: Some topminnows can survive in water that's nearly as salty as the ocean, making them one of the few freshwater fish families that can handle such extreme salinity changes.

children.name: Poeciliidae
Gambusia
children.description: Mosquitofishes are small, hardy freshwater fish known for their incredible appetite for mosquito larvae and other aquatic insects. These live-bearing fish (meaning they give birth to free-swimming young rather than laying eggs) are highly adaptable and can thrive in a wide range of water conditions from ponds to slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike egg-laying fish, mosquitofishes give birth to live young, and males have a modified anal fin called a gonopodium used for reproduction. They're also distinguished by their upturned mouths, perfectly designed for surface feeding on mosquito larvae.
children.funFact: A single mosquitofish can eat up to 500 mosquito larvae per day, making them so effective at mosquito control that they've been introduced worldwide - though this has sometimes caused problems for native fish species.

children.name: Poecilia
children.description: Mollies are a genus of small, colorful freshwater fish that are popular in the aquarium trade. These fish are livebearers, meaning females give birth to free-swimming young rather than laying eggs. They are naturally found in tropical and subtropical waters of the Americas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mollies are distinguished from other freshwater fish by their ability to give birth to live young and their tolerance for both fresh and brackish water conditions.
children.funFact: The common guppy, despite its name, is actually a member of the molly genus and can produce a new generation of offspring every 4-6 weeks under ideal conditions.

children.description: The Poeciliidae family includes small freshwater fish commonly known as guppies, mollies, platys, and swordtails. These fish are livebearers, meaning females give birth to free-swimming young rather than laying eggs. Most species are native to warm regions of the Americas, from the southern United States through Central and South America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish that lay eggs, poeciliids give birth to live young that are immediately capable of swimming and feeding. Males are typically smaller and more colorful than females, and often have modified anal fins called gonopodia used for reproduction.
children.funFact: Mosquitofish were intentionally introduced to many parts of the world, including New England, because they eat mosquito larvae and were thought to help control malaria and other mosquito-borne diseases.

children.name: Cyprinodontidae
Cyprinodon
children.description: Typical pupfishes are small, hardy freshwater and brackish water fish known for their remarkable ability to survive in extreme conditions. These compact fish have deep, laterally compressed bodies and are incredibly tolerant of varying salinity levels, temperatures, and oxygen conditions that would kill most other fish species.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pupfishes are distinguished from other small fish by their deep, chunky body shape, upturned mouth, and extraordinary tolerance for harsh water conditions including high salinity and extreme temperatures.
children.funFact: Some pupfish species can survive in water nearly three times saltier than the ocean and in temperatures ranging from near freezing to over 100°F!

children.description: Pupfishes are small, hardy freshwater and brackish water fish known for their incredible ability to survive in extreme environments. These compact fish typically have deep, laterally compressed bodies and are found in springs, desert pools, salt lakes, and coastal marshes where few other fish can survive.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pupfishes are distinguished from other small fish by their deep, chunky body shape, upturned mouth, and remarkable tolerance for high salinity, extreme temperatures, and low oxygen conditions that would kill most other fish species.
children.funFact: Some pupfish species can survive in water nearly three times saltier than the ocean and in temperatures exceeding 100°F, making them among the most environmentally tolerant vertebrates on Earth.

children.description: Cyprinodontiformes are small freshwater and brackish water fish known for their incredible adaptability to different environments. This diverse group includes popular aquarium fish like guppies and mollies, as well as hardy native species that can survive in everything from salt marshes to temporary pools. Many species in this order give birth to live young rather than laying eggs, which is unusual among fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish are distinguished by their small size, typically flattened heads, and upturned mouths that are perfect for feeding at the water's surface. Many species have the unique ability among fish to give birth to fully-formed live young instead of laying eggs.
children.funFact: Some pupfishes can survive in water three times saltier than the ocean and tolerate temperature swings from near-freezing to over 100°F, making them among the most environmentally tough fish on Earth.

children.name: Syngnathiformes
Syngnathidae
Syngnathus
children.description: Syngnathus is a genus of pipefish, which are slender, elongated marine fish with tube-like snouts and segmented, armored bodies. These unusual fish are closely related to seahorses and share many of their distinctive characteristics, including the male's role in carrying and caring for eggs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Syngnathus can be distinguished from other pipefish by their specific body proportions, fin arrangements, and the number of body rings that make up their segmented appearance.
children.funFact: Like their seahorse cousins, male Syngnathus pipefish are the ones that get pregnant - females deposit eggs into the male's brood pouch where he fertilizes and carries them until they hatch.

children.name: Hippocampus
children.description: Seahorses are unique marine fish with horse-like heads, curled prehensile tails, and upright swimming posture. They have bony plates instead of scales covering their bodies and swim by rapidly fluttering their dorsal fins. Male seahorses are famous for being the only creatures where males actually become pregnant and give birth to live young.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish, seahorses swim upright and use their curled tails to anchor themselves to seagrass and coral rather than for propulsion. Their tubular snouts and lack of teeth make them specialized suction feeders.
children.funFact: Seahorses have independently moving eyes that can look in two different directions at once, allowing them to watch for both prey and predators simultaneously.

children.description: The Syngnathidae family includes some of the ocean's most unusual fish - pipefishes, seahorses, and seadragons. These elongated fish all share a unique tube-like snout that they use to suck up tiny prey like small crustaceans and fish larvae. They're also famous for their incredible camouflage abilities and their distinctive body armor made of bony plates instead of scales.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish, male syngnathids are the ones that get pregnant and give birth to their young. They also have a distinctive long, tubular snout and segmented bony armor covering their bodies instead of typical fish scales.
children.funFact: Male seahorses and pipefishes have a special brood pouch where they carry and incubate eggs - making them the only creatures in the animal kingdom where males actually experience pregnancy!

children.name: Fistulariidae
Fistularia
children.description: Cornetfishes are extremely elongated, pipe-like marine fish with remarkably thin bodies that can stretch over 5 feet long. They have long, tube-shaped snouts that they use to suck up small fish and crustaceans from crevices in coral reefs and rocky areas. These unusual fish are masters of camouflage, often swimming vertically among sea grasses or floating debris to blend in perfectly.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cornetfishes are easily recognized by their incredibly long, thin bodies and extended tubular snouts that make up about one-third of their total length. They also have a distinctive long filament extending from their tail fin that can be longer than their head.
children.funFact: Cornetfishes are such effective mimics that they often swim alongside trumpet fish or even float motionless like pieces of drifting seaweed, allowing them to ambush unsuspecting prey.

children.description: Cornetfishes are elongated marine fish with extremely long, tube-like snouts that end in a small mouth. They have slender, compressed bodies and a distinctive whip-like filament extending from their tail fin that can be longer than their body.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their extraordinarily long snout (up to one-third of their total body length) and the thread-like tail filament make them unmistakable among fish families.
children.funFact: Cornetfishes can change color rapidly from bright red to pale yellow or brown to blend in with their surroundings, making them excellent ambush predators.

children.name: Mullidae
Mullus
children.description: Mullus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as goatfish, characterized by their distinctive pair of long, sensitive barbels (whisker-like projections) extending from their chin. These bottom-dwelling fish use their barbels to probe sandy and muddy seafloors in search of small invertebrates, worms, and crustaceans. They are typically found in warmer coastal waters and are known for their ability to rapidly change colors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of genus Mullus are distinguished from other goatfish by their specific body proportions and the positioning of their barbels directly under the chin. They also have a more elongated body shape compared to their Pacific relatives.
children.funFact: Red goatfish can change from pale pink to deep red in seconds, often displaying brilliant colors when excited or feeding, which is why they're sometimes called 'chameleons of the sea floor.'

children.name: Pseudupeneus
children.description: Pseudupeneus is a genus of goatfish, which are colorful marine fish known for their distinctive pair of long, whisker-like barbels under their chin. These barbels are used like sensitive fingers to probe the sandy bottom for small invertebrates, worms, and crustaceans to eat. Members of this genus are typically found in tropical and subtropical coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Pseudupeneus goatfish are distinguished from other goatfish genera by their specific scale patterns, fin ray counts, and coloration patterns. They tend to have more elongated bodies and distinctive spotting or striping compared to their relatives.
children.funFact: The barbels of Pseudupeneus goatfish are so sensitive they can detect buried prey in sand even in complete darkness, making them excellent nighttime hunters.

children.description: Goatfishes are medium-sized marine fish that are easily recognized by their distinctive pair of long, whisker-like barbels (called chin barbels) that hang down from their lower jaw. These barbels are highly sensitive and are used like fingers to probe the sandy or muddy ocean floor in search of small crustaceans, worms, and other buried prey. Most goatfishes are found in tropical and subtropical waters, though a few species venture into temperate regions like New England.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The paired chin barbels are the goatfish family's most distinctive feature, setting them apart from all other fish families. These barbels can be tucked into a groove under the chin when not in use, and when extended, they actively probe sediment with remarkable sensitivity.
children.funFact: Goatfishes can dramatically change their color patterns in seconds, often shifting from pale sandy colors while feeding on the bottom to bright reds, yellows, or striped patterns when swimming in open water or when excited.

children.name: Dactylopteridae
Dactylopterus
children.description: Dactylopterus is a genus of unique marine fish known as flying gurnards. These bottom-dwelling fish are characterized by their dramatically enlarged pectoral fins that can spread out like wings, giving them their distinctive appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other bottom fish, flying gurnards have massive, colorful pectoral fins that they can fan out to appear much larger when threatened or excited.
children.funFact: Despite their name and wing-like fins, flying gurnards don't actually fly - they use their enlarged fins primarily for gliding short distances underwater and for startling predators with impressive threat displays.

children.description: Flying gurnards are unusual bottom-dwelling marine fish with dramatically enlarged pectoral fins that resemble wings. Despite their name, they cannot actually fly but use their wing-like fins to glide short distances above the seafloor and to startle predators with impressive displays.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Flying gurnards are easily recognized by their massive, colorful pectoral fins that can spread like butterfly wings, along with their boxy head covered in bony plates and spines.
children.funFact: When threatened, flying gurnards can spread their enormous pectoral fins to appear much larger and more intimidating, creating a display that looks like an underwater butterfly with fins that can be twice the length of their body.

children.name: Centriscidae
Macroramphosus
children.description: Macroramphosus is a genus of unusual marine fish commonly known as bellowsfish or snipefish. These distinctive fish have extremely compressed, deep bodies and remarkably long, tube-like snouts that they use to capture small prey from crevices and tight spaces.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bellowsfish are easily recognized by their dramatically flattened, almost razor-thin bodies and disproportionately long snouts that can be nearly as long as their entire body. Their body shape is so compressed that they appear almost two-dimensional when viewed from the side.
children.funFact: Despite their odd appearance, bellowsfish are actually related to seahorses and pipefish, and like their relatives, they use suction feeding to vacuum up tiny crustaceans and other small prey through their elongated snouts.

children.description: Snipefishes and shrimpfishes are small, distinctive marine fish with extremely compressed, thin bodies and long, tube-like snouts. They have the unique ability to swim in a vertical position, often with their heads pointing downward, which helps them blend in with sea grass or other vertical structures in their environment.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish are easily recognized by their razor-thin, laterally compressed bodies and elongated snouts that can be nearly as long as their entire body. Unlike most fish, they often swim and rest in a head-down, vertical orientation.
children.funFact: Shrimpfishes often swim in synchronized schools while maintaining their vertical, head-down position, creating an unusual sight that resembles a group of floating sticks or blades of grass moving through the water.

children.description: Syngnathiformes is a diverse order of marine fishes that includes some of the ocean's most distinctive and unusual species. While they may look very different from each other, these fish share specialized mouth structures adapted for suction feeding and often have elongated, tube-like snouts perfect for capturing small prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group are characterized by their specialized feeding apparatus with protrusible jaws that create powerful suction to capture prey. Many species also have unique body shapes, from the horse-like seahorses to the wing-like pectoral fins of flying gurnards.
children.funFact: Seahorses are the only fish where males actually get pregnant - the female transfers eggs to the male's brood pouch, where he fertilizes and carries them until they hatch!

children.name: Siluriformes
Ictaluridae
Ameiurus
children.description: Bullheads are a group of freshwater catfish known for their scaleless, smooth skin and prominent whisker-like barbels around their mouths. These bottom-dwelling fish are excellent at finding food in murky water using their sensitive barbels to taste and feel their surroundings. They're hardy fish that can tolerate low oxygen conditions and muddy waters where other fish might struggle.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their larger catfish cousins, bullheads are relatively small (usually under 12 inches) and have a squared or slightly notched tail fin rather than a deeply forked one. Their barbels are also shorter and less numerous than those of larger catfish species.
children.funFact: Bullhead parents are devoted caregivers - they guard their dark, jelly-like egg masses and will even shepherd their young fry around in protective schools, looking like tiny black clouds moving through the water.

children.name: Noturus
children.description: Madtoms are small, secretive catfish that live in freshwater streams and rivers throughout eastern North America. These nocturnal fish are characterized by their whisker-like barbels around their mouth and their ability to deliver a painful sting with their pectoral and dorsal fin spines. They typically hide under rocks and logs during the day, emerging at night to hunt for small invertebrates.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other catfish, madtoms have venomous spines that can inject toxins when they feel threatened, causing a bee sting-like sensation. They're also much smaller than most catfish, rarely exceeding 5 inches in length.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, madtoms can deliver a surprisingly painful sting that has earned them the nickname 'willow cats' among some anglers who accidentally handle them.

children.name: Ictalurus
children.description: Ictalurus is a genus of freshwater catfish known for their smooth, scaleless skin and prominent whisker-like barbels around their mouths. These medium to large-sized fish are bottom-dwellers that use their sensitive barbels to locate food in murky water. They're popular both as sport fish and for commercial aquaculture.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Ictalurus catfish have deeply forked tails and relatively streamlined bodies compared to other catfish genera. They typically have 8 barbels and lack the armor plating found on some other catfish groups.
children.funFact: Channel catfish can live over 20 years and have an excellent sense of taste - they have taste buds not just in their mouths but all over their bodies, including their barbels and fins!

children.description: North American Freshwater Catfishes are a family of whiskered fish that live exclusively in freshwater rivers, lakes, and streams. All members have smooth, scaleless skin and prominent barbels (whiskers) around their mouths that help them locate food in murky water. They range in size from tiny madtoms just a few inches long to large channel catfish that can grow over three feet.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike marine catfishes or catfish from other continents, these species have evolved specifically for North American freshwater environments and lack the venomous spines found in some tropical catfish families. They also have a distinctive adipose fin and forked or rounded tail fins.
children.funFact: Many ictalurid catfish are excellent parents - the males guard their eggs and young fry, sometimes carrying the baby fish in their mouths to protect them from predators.

children.name: Pimelodidae
Pseudoplatystoma
children.description: Pseudoplatystoma is a genus of large freshwater catfish native to South America's river systems, particularly the Amazon and Orinoco basins. These impressive fish are known for their distinctive striped patterns and can grow to enormous sizes, making them popular among aquarium enthusiasts and anglers alike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are easily recognized by their bold tiger-like stripes or spots running vertically along their silvery bodies, combined with their flattened heads and prominent barbels (whiskers).
children.funFact: Tiger Sorubim can grow over 4 feet long and live for more than 20 years, making them one of the longest-lived catfish species in the aquarium trade.

children.description: Long-whiskered Catfishes are a diverse family of freshwater catfish known for their exceptionally long, sensitive whiskers called barbels that help them navigate and find food in murky waters. These catfish are native to South and Central America, where they inhabit rivers, lakes, and flooded forests. They range dramatically in size from small species just a few inches long to massive giants that can grow over 6 feet in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets these catfish apart from other catfish families is their extremely long barbels that can extend well beyond their body length, giving them their common name. They also typically have a more streamlined body shape compared to many other catfish groups.
children.funFact: Some species in this family, like the massive Piraíba catfish, can grow to over 400 pounds and are considered apex predators in their South American river systems!

children.description: Catfishes are a diverse group of freshwater fish known for their distinctive barbels - whisker-like sensory organs that help them navigate and find food in murky water. These bottom-dwelling fish lack scales and instead have smooth, slimy skin that helps protect them from parasites and infections. Most catfish are active at night and use their excellent senses of smell and taste to locate food along river and lake bottoms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Catfish are easily recognized by their prominent barbels (whiskers) around the mouth and their scaleless, smooth skin. Unlike most other fish, they have a strong, sharp spine at the front of their dorsal and pectoral fins that can inflict painful wounds.
children.funFact: Catfish have taste buds all over their body - not just in their mouth - with some species having over 100,000 taste buds covering their skin, making them swimming tongues that can taste their environment!

children.name: Blenniiformes
Pomacentridae
Abudefduf
children.description: Sergeant Majors are small, colorful marine fish that belong to the damselfish family. These tropical and subtropical fish are known for their bold vertical stripes and vibrant colors, typically featuring bright yellows and blues with distinctive black bars across their bodies.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other damselfish, Sergeant Majors have particularly prominent vertical black stripes that resemble military stripes, giving them their common name. They also tend to be more elongated and streamlined compared to their rounder damselfish relatives.
children.funFact: Male Sergeant Majors are devoted fathers who aggressively guard their nests of purple eggs, often charging at much larger fish and even divers who venture too close to their territory.

children.name: Stegastes
children.description: Gregories are small, colorful marine fish in the damselfish family that are known for their territorial behavior and vibrant patterns. These tropical fish typically inhabit coral reefs and rocky areas in warm coastal waters, where they aggressively defend their feeding territories from other fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gregories can be identified by their compressed, oval-shaped bodies and distinctive color patterns that often include bright blues, yellows, and contrasting spots or stripes. They have small mouths adapted for grazing algae from surfaces.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, gregories are surprisingly fierce defenders of their territory and will boldly chase away fish many times their size, including divers who venture too close to their claimed patch of reef.

children.name: Microspathodon
children.description: Microspathodon is a small genus of tropical marine fish known as jewelfish or damselfish. These colorful reef fish are characterized by their robust, oval-shaped bodies and their tendency to be highly territorial around coral reefs and rocky areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are distinguished from other damselfish by their relatively large size, deep compressed bodies, and distinctive coloration patterns that often include bright yellows and blues.
children.funFact: Despite being called damselfish, these fish are actually quite aggressive and will fiercely defend their algae gardens from much larger fish, including divers!

children.description: Damselfishes are small, colorful marine fish that are commonly found in coral reefs and rocky coastal areas. They are known for their bright patterns and territorial behavior, often aggressively defending their homes from much larger fish. Most species are quite small, typically measuring just a few inches in length.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Damselfishes can be identified by their compressed, oval-shaped bodies and single dorsal fin with both spiny and soft rays. They have small mouths and are typically more brightly colored and territorial than similar-sized reef fish.
children.funFact: Despite their small size, damselfishes are incredibly brave defenders of their territory and will boldly chase away fish many times their size, including divers who get too close to their nests!

children.name: Blenniidae
Hypsoblennius
children.description: Hypsoblennius is a genus of small, colorful marine fish commonly known as blennies that live in shallow coastal waters. These fish are characterized by their elongated bodies, large eyes, and the ability to breathe air for short periods when trapped in tide pools. They are bottom-dwellers that often hide among rocks, coral, or seaweed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Hypsoblennius are distinguished from other blenny genera by their distinctive feathery cirri (small tentacle-like projections) above their eyes and their particular fin ray patterns. They also have a more compressed body shape compared to many other blenny species.
children.funFact: Feather blennies can actually survive out of water for several hours by breathing air through their gills, making them perfectly adapted to life in the ever-changing environment of tide pools.

children.name: Hypleurochilus
children.description: Hypleurochilus is a genus of small marine fish known as combtooth blennies that live in shallow coastal waters. These fish are characterized by their elongated bodies, large heads, and prominent eyes that sit high on their heads, giving them an alert, curious appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have distinctive crest-like structures on their heads and specialized comb-like teeth that help them scrape algae and small organisms from rocks and surfaces.
children.funFact: These blennies are excellent jumpers and can leap from tide pool to tide pool when the tide goes out, using their strong pectoral fins to propel themselves across wet rocks.

children.description: Combtooth blennies are small, elongated fish that live in shallow coastal waters, often hiding among rocks, seaweed, and tide pools. They get their name from their comb-like teeth, which help them scrape algae and small organisms off surfaces. These bottom-dwelling fish are known for their curious personalities and tendency to peek out from crevices.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other blenny families, combtooth blennies have distinctive comb-shaped teeth and typically lack scales on their heads. They also have a continuous dorsal fin that runs along most of their back.
children.funFact: Many combtooth blennies can survive out of water for short periods by breathing through their skin and gills, allowing them to hop between tide pools during low tide.

children.name: Gobiesocidae
Gobiesox
children.description: Gobiesox is a genus of small marine fish known as clingfish, characterized by their ability to attach firmly to rocks and other surfaces using a powerful suction disc on their belly. These flattened, tadpole-shaped fish are specially adapted for life in rocky intertidal zones where strong waves and currents would otherwise sweep them away.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other small bottom-dwelling fish, Gobiesox species have a distinctive suction disc formed by modified pelvic fins that allows them to cling to surfaces with remarkable strength. Their flattened body shape and large head also distinguish them from similar-sized coastal fish.
children.funFact: A skilletfish can cling to rocks with such force that it can support over 230 times its own body weight, making it nearly impossible to pull off a surface without damaging the fish.

children.description: Clingfishes are small marine fish that have evolved a remarkable ability to stick firmly to rocks, corals, and other surfaces using a powerful suction disc on their belly. These typically colorful fish have flattened bodies and can be found in shallow coastal waters around the world. They use their incredible gripping ability to resist strong waves and currents in rocky intertidal zones.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Clingfishes are instantly recognizable by their prominent adhesive disc formed by modified pelvic fins, which creates such strong suction that they can support many times their own body weight while clinging to surfaces.
children.funFact: Some clingfishes can create suction so strong that researchers have difficulty removing them from rocks even when the fish are dead, and their adhesive disc continues to work effectively even when damaged.

children.description: Blenniiformes is an order of small, colorful marine fishes that includes blennies, damselfishes, and clingfishes. These fish are typically bottom-dwellers or live among rocks and coral reefs, with many species having specialized feeding habits and unique body adaptations for their specific lifestyles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group often have distinctive fin arrangements, with some having enlarged pectoral fins or modified gill covers, and many species lack swim bladders, making them well-suited for life on the seafloor.
children.funFact: Clingfishes in this order have a powerful suction disc on their bellies that allows them to stick to rocks so firmly they can withstand crashing waves without being swept away.

children.name: Beloniformes
Hemiramphidae
Hemiramphus
children.description: Hemiramphus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as halfbeaks or ballyhoo. These slender, fast-swimming fish are characterized by their distinctive jaw structure where the lower jaw extends much farther forward than the upper jaw, giving them their 'halfbeak' appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished from other needlefish and halfbeaks by their relatively shorter, more robust body shape and their specific jaw proportions where only the lower mandible is greatly elongated.
children.funFact: Ballyhoo are prized as bait fish by sport fishermen because their silvery, streamlined bodies and erratic swimming patterns make them irresistible to larger predatory fish like marlin and tuna.

children.name: Euleptorhamphus
children.description: Euleptorhamphus is a genus containing the Flying Halfbeak, a unique marine fish known for its ability to glide above the water's surface. These fish have elongated lower jaws and large pectoral fins that they use like wings to escape predators by launching themselves out of the water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other halfbeaks, Flying Halfbeaks have exceptionally large pectoral fins that enable true gliding flight above water. Their streamlined body and extended lower jaw give them a distinctive torpedo-like appearance.
children.funFact: Flying Halfbeaks can glide up to 150 feet above the ocean surface, making them one of the most accomplished 'flying' fish in the world.

children.description: Halfbeaks are sleek marine fish named for their distinctive asymmetrical jaws, where the lower jaw extends much farther forward than the upper jaw, creating a needle-like projection. These surface-dwelling fish are excellent swimmers that often leap out of the water when startled or chased by predators. They primarily feed on small fish, plankton, and marine vegetation near the water's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: The dramatically elongated lower jaw that extends far beyond the upper jaw is the defining characteristic that separates halfbeaks from all other fish families. Unlike their relatives the needlefish, which have both jaws extended, halfbeaks have only the lower jaw prominently lengthened.
children.funFact: Some halfbeak species can glide above the water's surface for short distances using their enlarged pectoral fins, similar to flying fish, helping them escape predators in the open ocean.

children.name: Belonidae
Strongylura
children.description: Strongylura is a genus of needlefish known for their extremely long, thin bodies and elongated jaws filled with sharp teeth. These sleek predatory fish are built for speed and precision hunting in coastal waters. They get their common name from their needle-like appearance and pointed snouts.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Strongylura have exceptionally long, slender jaws that are nearly equal in length, unlike some related needlefish where the lower jaw extends much further than the upper jaw.
children.funFact: Needlefish are famous for their ability to leap out of the water at high speeds, sometimes accidentally colliding with boats or people, which has earned them a reputation as one of the more dangerous fish encounters for night fishermen.

children.description: Needlefishes are slender, elongated marine fish with distinctive long, narrow jaws filled with sharp teeth. They are surface-dwelling predators that feed primarily on smaller fish and are known for their ability to leap out of the water when startled or hunting.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their most distinctive feature is their extremely long, beak-like jaws that can be several times longer than the rest of their head, making them unmistakable among New England's coastal fish.
children.funFact: Needlefishes can launch themselves out of the water at speeds up to 40 mph, and their silver coloration makes them nearly invisible when viewed from below against the bright surface of the water.

children.name: Scomberesocidae
Scomberesox
children.description: Scomberesox is a genus of slender, elongated fish known as sauries that live in open ocean waters. These fish are characterized by their needle-like appearance, with long, thin bodies and extended jaws that form a distinctive beak-like structure.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sauries can be distinguished from other needlefish by their smaller size and the presence of small finlets behind their dorsal and anal fins, similar to those found on tunas and mackerels.
children.funFact: Atlantic sauries are known to leap out of the water and glide short distances above the surface when escaping predators, using their large pectoral fins like wings.

children.description: Sauries are slender, elongated marine fish with distinctive needle-like beaks formed by extended jaws. These surface-dwelling fish are built for speed, with streamlined bodies and the ability to leap out of the water when pursued by predators.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other needlefish, sauries have relatively shorter beaks and more compressed, silvery bodies. They also have a distinctive row of small finlets behind their dorsal and anal fins, similar to tunas and mackerels.
children.funFact: Sauries can glide above the water's surface for short distances using their large pectoral fins, helping them escape from predators like larger fish and seabirds.

children.name: Exocoetidae
Cheilopogon
children.description: Cheilopogon is a genus of flying fish known for their remarkable ability to glide above the ocean surface using their enlarged pectoral fins as wings. These marine fish can launch themselves out of the water and soar for considerable distances to escape predators or travel efficiently through their ocean habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Cheilopogon have exceptionally large pectoral fins that extend well beyond their body length, along with enlarged pelvic fins that provide additional lift during flight. Their streamlined body shape and forked tail are specifically adapted for both underwater swimming and aerial gliding.
children.funFact: Flying fish in this genus can glide up to 650 feet in a single flight and reach speeds of up to 37 mph while airborne, sometimes staying aloft for over 40 seconds!

children.description: Flyingfishes are marine fish famous for their ability to leap out of the water and glide through the air using their enlarged, wing-like pectoral fins. These oceanic fish can glide for hundreds of yards above the water's surface, using this remarkable ability to escape from underwater predators. They are typically found in warm ocean waters around the world.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Flyingfishes are easily identified by their greatly enlarged pectoral fins that function like wings, allowing them to glide above the water surface. Their streamlined bodies and forked tails are specially adapted for high-speed swimming and launching into the air.
children.funFact: Flyingfishes can glide at speeds up to 35 mph and reach heights of up to 4 feet above the water, with the longest recorded glide covering nearly a quarter of a mile!

children.description: The Beloniformes are an order of marine fishes known for their elongated, needle-like jaws and streamlined bodies built for life near the ocean's surface. These fish are expert surface hunters, using their extended jaws to catch small fish, squid, and crustaceans in the upper layers of the water column. Most members of this group are fast swimmers that spend their time in the bright, open waters near the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets these fish apart is their distinctive jaw structure - many have greatly extended lower jaws, upper jaws, or both, creating a needle-like or beak-like appearance. Unlike most other fish orders, Beloniformes are specifically adapted for surface-dwelling life with their streamlined bodies and unique feeding apparatus.
children.funFact: Flying fish in this order can glide above the water surface for distances of over 1,300 feet using their enlarged pectoral fins as wings, reaching speeds of up to 37 mph while airborne.

children.name: Labriformes
Labridae
Tautogolabrus
children.description: Tautogolabrus is a genus of wrasse fish that includes only one species in New England waters - the cunner. These are small to medium-sized marine fish that belong to the wrasse family and are commonly found in rocky coastal areas and around structures like docks and piers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other wrasses in New England waters, cunners have a more elongated body shape and lack the prominent canine teeth found in their close relatives, the tautogs.
children.funFact: Cunners are known for their ability to change color rapidly, shifting from brown to blue-green depending on their surroundings and mood.

children.name: Tautoga
children.description: Tautoga is a genus containing just one species - the tautog, a distinctive marine fish found along the Atlantic coast. These robust fish are members of the wrasse family and are known for their thick lips, strong teeth, and ability to change color from blackish to mottled brown.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tautogs are distinguished from other wrasses by their heavy, deep bodies, blunt snouts, and powerful crushing teeth adapted for eating hard-shelled prey like mussels and crabs.
children.funFact: Tautogs are sometimes called 'blackfish' by anglers and can live over 30 years, with some individuals reaching ages of 40+ years, making them among the longest-lived fish in New England waters.

children.description: Wrasses and parrotfishes are a diverse family of marine fish known for their thick, fleshy lips and prominent teeth. These colorful fish are typically found in rocky or reef environments where they feed on small invertebrates, algae, and other marine organisms. Many species in this family are important cleaners in marine ecosystems, removing parasites from other fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive pharyngeal teeth (throat teeth) used for crushing food, and many species have protrusible mouths that can extend outward to capture prey. Their thick lips and often vibrant coloration help distinguish them from other marine fish families.
children.funFact: Many wrasses are sequential hermaphrodites, starting life as females and later changing to males as they grow larger and more dominant in their social groups.

children.name: Ammodytidae
Ammodytes
children.description: Ammodytes is a genus of small, slender fish known as sand lances that are perfectly adapted for life in sandy marine environments. These eel-like fish have the remarkable ability to quickly burrow into sand on the ocean floor when threatened or when resting. They are important forage fish that form large schools in coastal waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sand lances have extremely elongated, cylindrical bodies with pointed snouts and lack pelvic fins entirely. Their lower jaw extends beyond the upper jaw, giving them a distinctive underbite that helps them burrow efficiently into sand.
children.funFact: Sand lances can disappear into sand in less than a second by diving headfirst and using rapid undulating motions to literally swim through the sandy bottom.

children.description: Sand lances are small, elongated fish that spend much of their time buried in sandy ocean bottoms. These slender marine fish have the remarkable ability to quickly dive into sand when threatened, making them masters of underwater hide-and-seek.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Sand lances have extremely elongated, eel-like bodies with pointed snouts and lack pelvic fins, which helps them burrow efficiently into sand. Their lower jaw extends beyond the upper jaw, giving them a distinctive appearance.
children.funFact: Sand lances can burrow into sand so quickly that they seem to disappear in the blink of an eye, and they often emerge from the seafloor tail-first when it's time to feed.

children.name: Uranoscopidae
Astroscopus
children.description: Astroscopus is a genus of unusual bottom-dwelling fish known as stargazers. These fish are characterized by their flattened bodies and eyes positioned on top of their heads, allowing them to bury themselves in sand or mud while keeping watch for prey above.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish, stargazers in this genus have their eyes and mouth positioned on the top of their heads, and they possess the remarkable ability to generate electric shocks of up to 50 volts.
children.funFact: Northern Stargazers can deliver electric shocks strong enough to stun small fish and give humans a surprising jolt, making them one of the few electric fish found in New England waters.

children.description: Stargazers are unusual marine fish that spend most of their time buried in sand or mud with only their eyes and mouth exposed on top of their head. They are ambush predators that wait motionless for small fish and crustaceans to swim overhead, then quickly strike upward to capture their prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, stargazers have their eyes positioned on the very top of their flat head, allowing them to look upward while completely buried in sediment. Many species also have venomous spines and can deliver electric shocks.
children.funFact: The northern stargazer found in New England waters can generate electrical discharges of up to 50 volts to stun prey and defend against predators, making it one of the few electric fish in North American waters.

children.description: Wrasses and allies are a diverse group of marine fish that share certain jaw and tooth structures, though they look quite different from each other. This order includes colorful wrasses that clean other fish, slender sand lances that burrow in sandy bottoms, and bizarre stargazers that bury themselves and ambush prey from below.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this group have specialized pharyngeal jaws (a second set of jaws in their throat) that help them process food. Despite their varied appearances, they share similar bone structures in their skulls and jaws.
children.funFact: Some wrasses act as 'cleaning stations' on coral reefs, removing parasites from larger fish - and the bigger fish know not to eat their helpful cleaners!

children.name: Gobiiformes
Gobiidae
Gobiosoma
children.description: Gobiosoma is a genus of small marine fish known as gobies that live in coastal waters along the Atlantic seaboard. These tiny fish are typically less than 3 inches long and are known for their bottom-dwelling lifestyle, often hiding among rocks, shells, and marine vegetation in shallow waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Gobiosoma are distinguished from other gobies by their elongated, slender bodies and their tendency to live in very shallow coastal environments rather than deeper waters or coral reefs.
children.funFact: Despite their tiny size, Gobiosoma gobies are incredibly hardy fish that can survive in changing salinity levels where rivers meet the sea, making them well-adapted to New England's dynamic coastal environments.

children.description: Gobies are a large family of small fish that are among the most diverse groups of vertebrates on Earth. These compact fish typically have two separate dorsal fins and pelvic fins that are often fused together to form a sucker-like disc. Most gobies are bottom-dwellers that prefer shallow coastal waters, tide pools, and estuaries.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gobies can be distinguished from other small fish by their fused pelvic fins that form a ventral sucker disc, which helps them cling to rocks and other surfaces in strong currents. They also have two distinct dorsal fins rather than one continuous fin.
children.funFact: Many goby species have fascinating relationships with other animals - some live symbiotically with shrimp that act as their 'housekeepers,' while others clean parasites off larger fish at underwater 'cleaning stations.'

children.name: Oxudercidae
Ctenogobius
children.description: Ctenogobius is a genus of small bottom-dwelling fish known as darter gobies. These fish are characterized by their ability to quickly dart across sandy and muddy bottoms using their specialized fins, and they often rest directly on the seafloor rather than swimming in open water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have elongated bodies with large heads and can be distinguished from other gobies by their specific fin patterns and their preference for shallow coastal waters with soft substrates.
children.funFact: Darter gobies can change color rapidly to blend in with their surroundings, making them nearly invisible against sandy bottoms when they remain perfectly still.

children.description: Mudskippers and allies are a family of gobies that are specially adapted for life both in water and on land. These small fish have the remarkable ability to breathe air and move around on mudflats, mangrove roots, and other surfaces out of water using their strong pectoral fins.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, members of this family can survive out of water for extended periods and actually move around on land by using their muscular pectoral fins like legs.
children.funFact: Some mudskippers can climb trees and vertical surfaces, earning them the nickname 'walking fish' for their incredible terrestrial abilities.

children.name: Apogonidae
Apogon
children.description: Apogon is a genus of small marine fish commonly known as cardinalfish. These fish are typically found in tropical and subtropical waters, where they often inhabit coral reefs, rocky areas, and sometimes venture into estuarine environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of the Apogon genus are characterized by their relatively large eyes, two separate dorsal fins, and generally small size. They often display distinctive color patterns and markings that help distinguish different species.
children.funFact: Many Apogon cardinalfish are mouthbrooders, with males carrying and protecting the eggs in their mouths until they hatch.

children.description: Cardinalfishes are small, colorful marine fish that typically live in coral reefs and rocky areas. They have large eyes adapted for their nocturnal lifestyle, hiding in crevices during the day and emerging at night to feed on small crustaceans and plankton. Most species are tropical, making their presence in New England waters quite unusual.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cardinalfishes can be identified by their large eyes, two separate dorsal fins, and relatively large mouths for their body size. They also have a distinctive habit of hovering motionless near shelter rather than actively swimming like many other reef fish.
children.funFact: Male cardinalfishes are devoted fathers who carry their eggs in their mouths until they hatch, going without food for up to a week while protecting their developing young.

children.description: Gobies, cardinalfishes and allies are small marine and freshwater fish known for their compact bodies and fascinating behaviors. Many species in this group have specialized adaptations like fused pelvic fins that help them cling to rocks and coral, or the ability to breathe air and move on land like mudskippers.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most members of this group are characterized by their small size, typically measuring just a few inches long, and many have two separate dorsal fins. Unlike many other fish, gobies often have fused pelvic fins that form a sucker-like disc for gripping surfaces.
children.funFact: Some gobies are among the smallest vertebrates on Earth, with certain species measuring less than an inch long when fully grown, yet they can live in partnerships with shrimp that are larger than they are!

children.name: Atheriniformes
Atherinopsidae
Menidia
children.description: Menidia is a genus of small, slender fish known as silversides that are common in New England's coastal and inland waters. These silvery fish are characterized by their distinctive bright silver stripe running along each side of their body, which gives them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of Menidia can be distinguished from other silverside genera by their specific body proportions, fin positioning, and the precise location and width of their lateral silver stripe.
children.funFact: Atlantic Silversides can actually change the sex ratio of their offspring based on water temperature - warmer waters produce more females while cooler waters produce more males!

children.name: Labidesthes
children.description: Labidesthes is a genus of small, slender freshwater fish known as brook silversides. These delicate fish have translucent, silvery bodies and are typically found in quiet waters like ponds, lakes, and slow-moving streams.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Brook silversides can be identified by their extremely slender build, prominent silver stripe along their sides, and their habit of swimming in schools near the water's surface.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'brook' silversides, these fish actually prefer still or slow-moving waters and are often found in lakes and ponds rather than fast-flowing brooks.

children.description: Neotropical Silversides are small, slender fish with distinctive silvery stripes running along their sides. These schooling fish are found in both fresh and saltwater environments, where they feed on tiny plankton and small invertebrates near the water's surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They can be identified by their two separate dorsal fins, translucent bodies with prominent silver lateral stripes, and their tendency to form large, shimmering schools in shallow waters.
children.funFact: These fish are incredibly adaptable and can quickly adjust to different salinity levels, allowing some species to move freely between freshwater streams and coastal saltwater areas.

children.description: Silversides are small, slender fish that typically have a distinctive silvery stripe running along their sides. They are schooling fish that often swim near the surface of both marine and freshwater environments, feeding on small plankton, insects, and tiny crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Silversides can be distinguished from similar small fish by their characteristic bright silver lateral stripe and their tendency to form tight, fast-moving schools near the water's surface.
children.funFact: Many silverside species are incredibly hardy and can tolerate dramatic changes in water salinity, allowing some to move freely between freshwater streams and saltwater coastal areas.

children.name: Acipenseriformes
Acipenseridae
Huso
children.description: Atlantic sturgeons in the genus Huso are ancient, heavily-armored fish that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years. These prehistoric giants have bony plates called scutes instead of scales, and distinctive barbels (whisker-like sensors) that help them find food on river and lake bottoms. Both New England species are long-lived fish that can survive for decades in freshwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Huso sturgeons are distinguished from other sturgeon genera by their relatively shorter, blunter snouts and specific arrangement of bony plates along their bodies. They typically have four barbels positioned closer to the tip of their snout compared to other sturgeon groups.
children.funFact: Lake Sturgeon can live over 100 years and don't reach sexual maturity until they're 15-25 years old, making them one of the longest-lived freshwater fish in North America.

children.name: Acipenser
children.description: Sea sturgeons (Acipenser) are ancient fish that have remained virtually unchanged for over 200 million years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils.' These large, bottom-dwelling fish are characterized by their distinctive rows of bony plates called scutes along their bodies instead of regular scales. They are anadromous, meaning they live in saltwater but swim up rivers to spawn.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other sturgeon genera, Acipenser species have five rows of bony scutes and a heterocercal tail where the upper lobe is longer than the lower lobe. Their snouts are typically pointed and they have four barbels (whisker-like sensory organs) that help them locate food on the bottom.
children.funFact: Some Atlantic Sturgeon can live over 60 years and don't reach sexual maturity until they're 10-30 years old, making them one of the slowest-maturing fish in North American waters.

children.description: Sturgeons are ancient fish with distinctive bony plates called scutes running along their bodies instead of typical fish scales. These large, long-lived fish have shark-like tails and barbels (whisker-like sensors) near their mouths that help them find food on the bottom of rivers and coastal waters. They are famous for producing caviar, which is made from their eggs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bony fish, sturgeons have cartilaginous skeletons similar to sharks, but with rows of bony armor plates protecting their bodies. Their snouts are elongated and their mouths are positioned underneath, perfectly adapted for bottom-feeding.
children.funFact: Some sturgeon species can live over 100 years and don't reach sexual maturity until they're 10-20 years old, making them extremely vulnerable to overfishing.

children.description: Sturgeons and paddlefishes are ancient fish that have remained largely unchanged for over 200 million years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils.' These large freshwater and anadromous fish have cartilaginous skeletons like sharks, but unlike most fish, they lack scales and instead have rows of bony plates called scutes along their bodies. They are bottom-feeders that use their sensitive barbels (whisker-like organs) to locate food in murky water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most bony fish, sturgeons have cartilaginous skeletons and heterocercal tails (where the spine extends into the upper lobe). Their mouths are located on the underside of their heads and can extend outward like a tube to suction up food from the bottom.
children.funFact: Sturgeons are famous for producing caviar, and some species can live over 100 years and grow longer than 20 feet, making them among the largest freshwater fish in the world.

children.name: Anguilliformes
