Anguillidae
Anguilla
children.description: River eels are elongated, snake-like fish that spend most of their adult lives in freshwater rivers, lakes, and streams. These remarkable fish have smooth, scaleless skin covered in a protective mucus layer and can breathe through their skin as well as their gills. They are catadromous, meaning they migrate from freshwater to the ocean to spawn.
children.distinguishingFeatures: River eels have a continuous fin that runs along their back, around their tail, and under their belly, giving them their distinctive serpentine appearance. Unlike other eel-like fish, they have a single pair of gill openings and can move backwards as easily as forwards.
children.funFact: American eels can live for over 40 years and travel thousands of miles from New England rivers to the Sargasso Sea near Bermuda to spawn, with their larvae drifting back on ocean currents in a journey that can take up to two years.

children.description: Freshwater eels are long, snake-like fish that spend most of their adult lives in rivers, lakes, and streams but return to the ocean to spawn. They have smooth, scaleless skin covered in a protective mucus layer and can breathe through their skin as well as their gills. These remarkable fish are catadromous, meaning they migrate from fresh water to salt water to reproduce.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish that spawn in fresh water and may venture to sea, freshwater eels do the opposite - they live in fresh water but must return to the ocean to breed. Their elongated, serpentine body shape and ability to move overland through wet grass sets them apart from other freshwater fish.
children.funFact: American eels can live for over 40 years and travel thousands of miles to spawn in the Sargasso Sea, with some individuals making this epic journey only once in their lifetime before dying.

children.name: Congridae
Conger
children.description: Conger eels are large, powerful marine eels that live in rocky coastal waters and deep ocean environments. These muscular fish have long, snake-like bodies and strong jaws filled with sharp teeth, making them formidable predators that hunt fish, crabs, and other sea creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Conger eels are much larger and more robust than most other eel species, with thick, muscular bodies that can grow to impressive lengths. Unlike many eels, they have well-developed pectoral fins and lack the small scales found on some related species.
children.funFact: American conger eels can grow over 7 feet long and live for decades, with some individuals estimated to be over 60 years old!

children.description: The Congridae family includes conger eels and garden eels, which are large marine eels found in ocean waters around the world. These eels have long, snake-like bodies without pelvic fins and can grow to impressive sizes. They are primarily bottom-dwellers that hunt fish, crustaceans, and other marine prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Conger eels are distinguished from other eel families by their large size, powerful jaws filled with strong teeth, and their lack of scales. Unlike freshwater eels, they spend their entire lives in saltwater environments.
children.funFact: The American conger eel can grow over 7 feet long and live for more than 60 years, making it one of the largest and longest-lived fish species in New England waters.

children.description: True eels are long, snake-like fish with smooth, scaleless skin and continuous fins that run along their backs, tails, and bellies. They have elongated bodies perfectly adapted for swimming through tight spaces and burrowing into mud or sand. Most species can breathe through their skin as well as their gills, allowing them to survive in low-oxygen environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other elongated fish, true eels have their dorsal, tail, and anal fins fused into one continuous fin around the back half of their body. They also lack the paired pelvic fins that most other fish possess.
children.funFact: American eels born in New England rivers actually travel thousands of miles to the Sargasso Sea in the Atlantic Ocean to spawn, making one of the longest migrations of any fish.

children.name: Osmeriformes
Osmeridae
Osmerus
children.description: Osmerus is a genus of small, slender fish known as true smelts that live in cold northern waters. These silvery fish are important both ecologically as food for larger fish and birds, and economically as a commercial and recreational fishery.
children.distinguishingFeatures: True smelts in the genus Osmerus have a distinctive cucumber-like odor when fresh and possess an adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) that distinguishes them from similar-looking fish.
children.funFact: Rainbow smelt are anadromous, meaning they live in the ocean but swim up rivers and streams to spawn, and during winter spawning runs, they can sometimes be seen swimming under the ice in shallow coastal waters.

children.name: Mallotus
children.description: Capelin are small, silvery fish in the smelt family that live in cold northern waters. They are slender, schooling fish that typically measure 6-8 inches long and have a slightly forked tail and large eyes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Capelin can be distinguished from other smelts by their smaller size, more pointed snout, and the males' distinctive breeding ridges of enlarged scales along their sides during spawning season.
children.funFact: Capelin are so abundant during their spawning runs that they sometimes wash ashore in huge numbers, creating silvery carpets on beaches that locals have historically gathered by the bucketful.

children.description: Smelts are small, slender fish found in both marine and freshwater environments throughout New England's coastal waters and rivers. These silvery fish are known for their delicate, translucent appearance and their important role in the food web as prey for larger fish, seabirds, and marine mammals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Smelts have a distinctive adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin without rays) located between their dorsal and tail fins, and their mouths contain sharp, needle-like teeth despite their small size.
children.funFact: Rainbow smelt are anadromous, meaning they live in the ocean but swim up rivers and streams to spawn, and their spawning runs in early spring were historically so abundant that people could scoop them up by the bucketful.

children.description: Smelts and allies are small, slender fish that live in both marine and freshwater environments throughout the Northern Hemisphere. These silvery fish are known for their delicate build and soft-rayed fins, and many species migrate between salt and fresh water during their life cycles.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order have a distinctive adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) and lack spines in their fins, having only soft rays. They also possess a swim bladder connected to their digestive tract, which helps them regulate buoyancy.
children.funFact: Rainbow smelt are famous for their cucumber-like smell when fresh, which comes from compounds in their skin and gives them their distinctive aroma that many people find surprisingly pleasant.

children.name: Lophiiformes
Lophiidae
Lophius
children.description: Monkfishes are bottom-dwelling marine fish with enormous mouths and flattened bodies perfectly adapted for life on the seafloor. They are ambush predators that use a modified dorsal fin spine as a fishing rod, complete with a fleshy lure to attract prey within striking distance of their cavernous mouths.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other anglerfish, monkfishes have their fishing lure (illicium) positioned right at the front of their head and can open their massive mouths to incredible proportions - sometimes wider than their entire body length.
children.funFact: Monkfishes are such effective ambush predators that they've been known to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves, including seabirds, sharks, and even diving ducks that venture too close to the seafloor.

children.description: Goosefishes are bottom-dwelling marine fish known for their enormous mouths and flattened bodies that help them blend in with the seafloor. These ambush predators lie motionless on sandy or muddy bottoms, using a modified fin ray as a fishing rod with a fleshy lure to attract prey. When unsuspecting fish or other creatures come close to investigate the lure, the goosefish opens its massive mouth and sucks them in.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Goosefishes are easily recognized by their exceptionally large heads and mouths that can open wide enough to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves. They also have a distinctive fishing rod-like appendage called an illicium that extends from their head, topped with a fleshy lure.
children.funFact: A goosefish can unhinge its jaw and expand its mouth so dramatically that it can swallow fish up to half its own body length, and there are documented cases of them trying to eat prey so large that both predator and prey died in the attempt.

children.name: Antennariidae
Histrio
children.description: Histrio is a genus containing just one species - the remarkable Sargassumfish. This unique fish is perfectly adapted to life among floating Sargassum seaweed, where it uses incredible camouflage and specialized fins to navigate its drifting habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other frogfish that live on the seafloor, Histrio is the only member of its family that lives a pelagic lifestyle, floating freely in the open ocean among seaweed mats.
children.funFact: The Sargassumfish can change colors and patterns within seconds to perfectly match the Sargassum seaweed it calls home, making it nearly invisible to both predators and prey.

children.description: Frogfishes are unusual marine fish that are masters of disguise and ambush hunting. They have stocky, compressed bodies covered in warty skin and can change color to blend perfectly with their surroundings like coral reefs, sargassum seaweed, or rocky bottoms. These patient predators sit motionless waiting for prey to come within striking distance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Frogfishes are easily recognized by their fishing rod-like appendage called an illicium that extends from their head, topped with a lure to attract prey. They also have extremely large mouths and can expand their bodies dramatically when swallowing prey nearly as large as themselves.
children.funFact: Frogfishes have the fastest strike of any vertebrate - they can suck in and swallow prey in just 6 milliseconds, faster than the human eye can follow!

children.description: Anglerfishes are a fascinating order of marine fish known for their unique hunting strategy and unusual appearance. All members of this group have a modified dorsal fin spine that acts like a fishing rod, complete with a lure at the tip to attract prey. They are ambush predators that lie in wait and use their enormous mouths to quickly gulp down unsuspecting fish and other marine animals.
children.distinguishingFeatures: What sets anglerfishes apart from other fish is their distinctive 'fishing rod' called an illicium, which is actually a highly modified first dorsal fin spine with a fleshy lure at the end. They also have exceptionally large mouths relative to their body size and can expand their stomachs dramatically to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves.
children.funFact: Some deep-sea anglerfishes have bioluminescent lures that glow in the dark depths, but our New England species rely on wiggling their lures to mimic worms or other small prey items.

children.name: Lepisosteiformes
Lepisosteidae
Lepisosteus
children.description: Slender gars are ancient freshwater fish with long, narrow snouts filled with sharp teeth and diamond-shaped scales that form a tough, armor-like covering. These primitive predators have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years, representing a living link to prehistoric times. They are skilled hunters that lie motionless near the surface before striking at prey with lightning speed.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Slender gars are distinguished from other gar species by their exceptionally long, thin snouts that are much narrower than their heads. Their snout length is typically 15-20 times longer than its width, making them easily recognizable among North American freshwater fish.
children.funFact: Slender gars can breathe air using a swim bladder that functions like a primitive lung, allowing them to survive in low-oxygen waters where other fish would suffocate.

children.name: Atractosteus
children.description: Large Gars (Atractosteus) are massive, ancient freshwater fish that look like living fossils with their long, cylindrical bodies and elongated snouts filled with sharp teeth. These prehistoric predators are among the largest freshwater fish in North America, with some species growing over 8 feet long. They are easily recognized by their diamond-shaped, armor-like scales and their ability to breathe air at the surface using a primitive lung.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Large Gars are distinguished from other gar species by their enormous size and broader snouts compared to their smaller relatives. Their diamond-shaped ganoid scales are much thicker and more armor-like than those found on most other freshwater fish.
children.funFact: Alligator Gars are so ancient that they've remained virtually unchanged for over 100 million years, making them living fossils that swam alongside dinosaurs!

children.description: Gars are ancient freshwater fish with elongated, torpedo-shaped bodies and long, narrow snouts filled with sharp teeth. They are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years, perfectly adapted for life as ambush predators in slow-moving waters. These primitive fish are easily recognized by their diamond-shaped, armor-like scales and their ability to breathe air at the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Gars are distinguished from other fish by their ganoid scales (hard, diamond-shaped armor plates) and their ability to gulp air using a primitive lung-like swim bladder. Their elongated jaws packed with needle-sharp teeth and cylindrical body shape make them unmistakable among freshwater fish.
children.funFact: Gars are living time capsules - they've existed virtually unchanged for over 100 million years, meaning they swam alongside dinosaurs and survived the mass extinction that wiped out the giant reptiles.

children.description: Gars are ancient freshwater fish with long, cylindrical bodies covered in hard, diamond-shaped scales that act like armor. They have elongated snouts filled with sharp teeth and can breathe air using a specialized swim bladder, allowing them to survive in low-oxygen water.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most modern fish, gars have ganoid scales (thick, shiny, and non-overlapping) and can gulp air at the surface to supplement their gill breathing.
children.funFact: Gars are living fossils that have remained virtually unchanged for over 100 million years, making them older than many dinosaurs!

children.name: Aulopiformes
Synodontidae
Synodus
children.description: Synodus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as lizardfish, named for their reptile-like appearance with elongated bodies and large mouths filled with sharp teeth. These bottom-dwelling predators are masters of camouflage, burying themselves in sand or mud on the seafloor to ambush unsuspecting prey. They are voracious hunters that feed on smaller fish, crustaceans, and other marine creatures.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lizardfish can be distinguished from other fish by their cylindrical, torpedo-shaped bodies, large heads with wide mouths, and their habit of propping themselves up on their pelvic fins while resting on the bottom. Their eyes are positioned high on their heads, allowing them to watch for prey while partially buried in sediment.
children.funFact: Lizardfish are so well-camouflaged that they can remain motionless on the seafloor for hours, looking like a piece of debris or rock until an unsuspecting fish swims within striking distance.

children.name: Trachinocephalus
children.description: Trachinocephalus is a genus of marine fish commonly known as snakefish, named for their elongated, snake-like bodies and predatory hunting style. These bottom-dwelling fish are found in warm coastal waters where they bury themselves in sand or mud, waiting to ambush prey that passes overhead.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snakefish have distinctively large mouths filled with sharp teeth, along with eyes positioned on top of their heads to watch for prey while buried in sediment. Their elongated body shape and ability to completely bury themselves sets them apart from other bottom-dwelling fish.
children.funFact: When hunting, snakefish can launch themselves upward from their buried position with lightning speed to snatch fish, squid, and crustaceans swimming above them.

children.description: Lizardfishes are slender, elongated marine fish that get their name from their reptile-like appearance, with pointed snouts and large mouths filled with sharp teeth. These bottom-dwelling predators are excellent ambush hunters that bury themselves in sand or rest on the seafloor, waiting to strike at passing prey like small fish and crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Lizardfishes can be identified by their cylindrical bodies, large dorsal fins positioned in the middle of their backs, and distinctive lizard-like heads with prominent eyes positioned high on their skulls.
children.funFact: Lizardfishes are hermaphrodites that can change from female to male as they age, with smaller individuals typically being female and larger, older fish becoming male.

children.description: Aulopiformes is an order of marine fish that includes lizardfishes, grinners, and their relatives. These are typically deep-sea or bottom-dwelling predatory fish with large mouths and sharp teeth designed for catching prey. Most species in this group are found in deeper ocean waters, though some lizardfishes can be found in shallower coastal areas.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are characterized by their adipose fin (a small, fleshy fin behind the dorsal fin) and their predatory lifestyle with large mouths full of needle-like teeth. Unlike many other fish orders, they lack spines in their fins and have a more primitive skeletal structure.
children.funFact: Lizardfishes are ambush predators that can bury themselves in sand with only their eyes and mouth exposed, waiting to strike at unsuspecting prey with lightning-fast speed.

children.name: Mugiliformes
Mugilidae
Mugil
children.description: Common mullets are silvery marine fish with torpedo-shaped bodies that are perfectly designed for life in shallow coastal waters. These hardy fish are known for their ability to move between saltwater and brackish environments, often forming large schools in bays, estuaries, and near shorelines.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mullets have distinctive blunt, rounded heads with small mouths positioned low on their faces, and two separate dorsal fins. They can be identified by their habit of jumping out of the water and their unique feeding behavior of scooping up sediment to filter out organic matter.
children.funFact: Mullets are sometimes called 'water lawnmowers' because they feed by grazing on algae and organic debris from the bottom, helping to keep coastal ecosystems clean and healthy.

children.description: Mullets are medium-sized fish with torpedo-shaped bodies that are perfectly adapted for life in coastal waters, estuaries, and even freshwater rivers. They have small mouths and specialized teeth for scraping algae and organic matter from surfaces, making them important grazers in aquatic ecosystems. These hardy fish are known for their ability to move between saltwater and freshwater environments.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mullets can be identified by their two widely separated dorsal fins, large scales, and small triangular mouths positioned at the front of their heads. Unlike many other coastal fish, they lack a lateral line on their tail section.
children.funFact: Mullets are famous for their spectacular jumping ability and can leap several feet out of the water, though scientists aren't entirely sure why they do this - it might be to escape predators, dislodge parasites, or simply for the joy of it!

children.description: Mullets and glassfishes are a diverse order of ray-finned fish that includes the familiar mullets found in coastal waters. These fish are characterized by their streamlined bodies and ability to thrive in both marine and brackish water environments. Most species in this group are important both ecologically and commercially.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mullets are easily recognized by their blunt, rounded snouts and small mouths positioned on the underside of their heads, which they use to feed on algae and organic matter from sediment.
children.funFact: Many mullet species are famous for their spectacular jumping behavior, often leaping several feet out of the water in a behavior that scientists still don't fully understand!

children.name: Zeiformes
Zeidae
Zenopsis
children.description: Mirror Dories are deep-sea fish with distinctively tall, flattened bodies that look almost disc-like when viewed from the side. They have large eyes adapted for the dim light of deeper waters and possess a silvery, reflective appearance that gives them their "mirror" name. These fish are typically found at depths of several hundred to over a thousand feet below the surface.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Mirror Dories can be distinguished from other dory species by their extremely compressed, almost circular body shape and their particularly silvery, mirror-like scales. They also have a more pronounced forehead and larger eyes compared to their shallow-water relatives.
children.funFact: The Buckler Dory gets its name from the large, shield-like scales along its sides that resemble the round shields (bucklers) once carried by medieval warriors.

children.description: Mirror Dories and Girties are deep-sea fish with distinctively compressed, oval-shaped bodies that look almost paper-thin when viewed from the front. These unusual fish have large mouths and eyes, adaptations that help them survive in the darker depths of the ocean where they hunt for small fish and crustaceans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: They are easily recognized by their extremely flattened, disc-like bodies and the presence of bony plates or scutes along their sides, giving them an armored appearance that sets them apart from other deep-sea fish families.
children.funFact: Despite their delicate, paper-thin appearance, Mirror Dories are actually skilled predators that can unhinge their large jaws to swallow prey nearly as large as themselves.

children.name: Grammicolepididae
Xenolepidichthys
children.description: Xenolepidichthys is a genus of deep-sea fish known as tinselfish, named for their distinctive silvery, metallic appearance. These unusual fish have highly compressed, disk-like bodies and are found in the deep waters of the Atlantic Ocean. They are part of a small family of deep-sea fish that are rarely encountered due to their remote habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus are characterized by their extremely flattened, almost circular body shape and unique scale structure that gives them a shimmering, tinsel-like appearance. Their eyes are relatively large compared to their body size, an adaptation for life in the dim deep-sea environment.
children.funFact: The Spotted Tinselfish can be found at depths of over 3,000 feet below the surface, living in complete darkness where sunlight never reaches.

children.description: Tinselfishes are deep-sea fish that get their name from their silvery, metallic appearance that resembles tinsel or foil. These unusual fish have compressed, disc-like bodies and live in the deep ocean waters far from shore. They are rarely seen by humans due to their deep-water habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tinselfishes have extremely thin, almost transparent bodies with a distinctive silvery sheen created by reflective scales. Their bodies are so compressed laterally that they appear almost paper-thin when viewed from the front.
children.funFact: Tinselfishes are so rarely encountered that scientists know very little about their behavior, with most specimens collected accidentally in deep-sea fishing nets.

children.description: Dories are deep-bodied, compressed marine fish with distinctive oval or diamond-shaped profiles when viewed from the side. These fish are typically found in deeper waters and have large eyes adapted for their dim environment. They are known for their laterally flattened bodies that give them an almost paper-thin appearance when viewed head-on.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Dories can be distinguished from other fish by their extremely compressed, tall bodies and their protrusible mouths that can extend outward to capture prey. Many species also have reflective, silvery sides that help them blend into their deep-water surroundings.
children.funFact: The famous John Dory has a distinctive dark spot on each side of its body, which legend claims are the thumbprints of Saint Peter when he picked up the fish to pay temple tax, as described in the Bible.

children.name: Batrachoidiformes
Batrachoididae
Opsanus
children.description: Opsanus is a genus of bottom-dwelling marine fish commonly known as toadfish. These robust, heavy-bodied fish are characterized by their large, wide heads and mouth, giving them a distinctive toad-like appearance that earned them their common name.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike other fish in their family, Opsanus species have particularly broad, flattened heads and lack scales, instead having smooth, slimy skin. They also possess strong jaw muscles and can produce loud grunting or croaking sounds.
children.funFact: Male toadfish are devoted fathers that guard their eggs in nests under rocks or shells, fanning them with their fins and making loud humming calls to attract mates that can be heard by divers underwater.

children.description: Toadfishes are bottom-dwelling marine fish with wide, flattened heads and large mouths that give them a toad-like appearance. They are typically found in shallow coastal waters where they hide among rocks, coral, or in burrows in the sand. These fish are known for their ability to produce loud sounds using specialized muscles attached to their swim bladders.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Toadfishes can be distinguished from other fish by their extremely wide, flattened heads, frog-like mouths, and their habit of remaining motionless on the bottom. Many species also have fleshy projections or barbels around their heads and poisonous spines on their fins.
children.funFact: Male toadfishes are devoted fathers who guard their eggs in nests and produce loud humming or grunting sounds to attract mates - some species are so loud they can be heard above water and have even interfered with naval sonar equipment!

children.description: Toadfishes are bottom-dwelling marine fish with large, flattened heads and wide mouths that give them a toad-like appearance. They are ambush predators that lie camouflaged on sandy or muddy seafloors, waiting to snap up small fish, crabs, and worms that venture too close.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Toadfishes have uniquely large heads with eyes positioned on top, along with prominent barbels (whisker-like projections) around their mouths that help them detect prey in murky water.
children.funFact: Male toadfishes are devoted fathers that guard their eggs in nests and produce loud humming or grunting sounds to attract mates - these vocalizations can be so loud they've been known to keep people awake on houseboats!

children.name: Amiiformes
Amiidae
Amia
children.description: Bowfins are primitive freshwater fish that have remained virtually unchanged for millions of years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils.' They are hardy predators with long, ribbon-like dorsal fins and the ability to breathe air when water oxygen levels are low. These ancient fish can be found in slow-moving waters like swamps, backwaters, and vegetated lake shores.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bowfins are easily recognized by their long, undulating dorsal fin that extends along most of their back and their ability to gulp air at the surface. Males develop a distinctive dark eyespot bordered with orange or yellow at the base of their tail during breeding season.
children.funFact: Bowfins are one of the few fish species where the male provides extensive parental care, guarding and protecting their young for several months after they hatch.

children.description: Bowfins are ancient freshwater fish that have remained virtually unchanged for over 150 million years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils.' They are the sole surviving members of a once-diverse group of primitive bony fish that dominated ancient waters alongside the dinosaurs.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bowfins have a unique long, undulating dorsal fin that runs along most of their back, and they can breathe air using a primitive lung-like swim bladder when water oxygen levels are low.
children.funFact: Male bowfins are devoted fathers who build circular nests in shallow water and aggressively guard their young for several months, even allowing the baby fish to swim in and out of their mouth for protection.

children.description: Bowfins are an ancient order of freshwater fish that have remained virtually unchanged for over 150 million years, earning them the nickname 'living fossils.' They are primitive bony fish with a unique combination of features found in both ancient and modern fish groups. These hardy predators are characterized by their long, undulating dorsal fin and ability to breathe air when water oxygen levels are low.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Bowfins are distinguished from other fish by their extraordinarily long dorsal fin that ripples along most of their back, their ability to gulp air at the surface, and their primitive swim bladder that functions like a lung.
children.funFact: Male bowfins are devoted fathers who build circular nests in shallow water, aggressively guard their eggs, and then shepherd their bright green offspring in protective schools for several weeks after hatching.

children.name: Stomiiformes
Sternoptychidae
Maurolicus
children.description: Maurolicus is a genus of small, deep-sea fish known as pearlsides or lanternfish. These silvery fish live in the ocean's twilight zone and are characterized by rows of light-producing organs called photophores along their sides that create a pearlescent appearance.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus can be distinguished by their specific arrangement of photophores and their relatively small size compared to other deep-sea fish. They have a distinctive silvery coloration with a compressed body shape typical of mesopelagic fish.
children.funFact: Atlantic Pearlsides participate in one of the largest migrations on Earth, swimming hundreds of feet upward each night to feed near the surface before returning to deeper waters at dawn.

children.description: Marine hatchetfishes are deep-sea fish with distinctively flattened, silvery bodies that resemble the blade of a hatchet when viewed from the side. These small to medium-sized fish live in the ocean's twilight zone, typically found at depths between 200 and 1,000 meters. They are part of the larger group of deep-sea lanternfishes and their relatives.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Their compressed, blade-like body shape and rows of light-producing organs (photophores) along their belly make them easily recognizable. Unlike many other deep-sea fish, they have large, upward-facing eyes adapted for spotting prey and predators above them.
children.funFact: Marine hatchetfishes use their belly lights for 'counterillumination' - they adjust the brightness to match the faint sunlight filtering down from above, making them nearly invisible to predators looking up from below.

children.description: Dragonfishes and their allies are a diverse order of deep-sea fish that live in the ocean's twilight and midnight zones. These remarkable fish have evolved incredible adaptations to survive in the perpetual darkness of the deep ocean, including bioluminescent light organs and expandable jaws for capturing prey.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Most members of this group possess photophores (light-producing organs) arranged in distinctive patterns along their bodies, and many have large mouths with sharp teeth designed for catching other fish in the nutrient-poor deep sea.
children.funFact: Many dragonfishes can produce their own red light, which is invisible to most other deep-sea creatures, giving them a secret advantage when hunting in the darkness.

children.name: Ophidiiformes
Ophidiidae
Ophidion
children.description: Snake-like Cusk-Eels are elongated marine fish with eel-like bodies that live on or near the ocean bottom. They get their name from their serpentine appearance and their relationship to the cod family, though they look quite different from their chunky cod cousins. These fish are typically found in deeper waters along the continental shelf.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, cusk-eels have small pelvic fins positioned under their throat area and lack the continuous fin that wraps around a true eel's tail. Their bodies are more compressed from side to side compared to the cylindrical shape of most eels.
children.funFact: Despite their eel-like appearance, cusk-eels are more closely related to cod than to true eels, showing how similar body shapes can evolve independently in unrelated fish groups.

children.description: Cusk-eels are elongated, eel-like fish that live in marine environments, despite their name suggesting they are true eels. These fish have long, tapering bodies with continuous fins that run along their backs and bellies, giving them their distinctive snake-like appearance. They are bottom-dwelling fish that prefer deeper waters and often burrow in sand or mud.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, cusk-eels have pelvic fins positioned under their throat area and their dorsal and anal fins are separate from their tail fin. Their gill openings are also positioned differently than true eels, being located on the sides of their head rather than underneath.
children.funFact: Despite being called 'cusk-eels,' these fish are not related to true eels at all - they're actually more closely related to cod and other members of the cod family!

children.description: Cusk-eels are elongated marine fish with eel-like bodies, though they're not true eels. They have long dorsal and anal fins that often connect with their tail fin, giving them a continuous fin edge around much of their body. Most species live in deep ocean waters and have adapted to life on or near the seafloor.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike true eels, cusk-eels have pelvic fins positioned under their throat or chin area, and their gill openings are located on the sides of their head rather than underneath. Their long, tapering bodies end in a pointed tail rather than the rounded tail typical of true eels.
children.funFact: Some cusk-eels are among the deepest-living fish ever discovered, with species found at depths exceeding 26,000 feet in ocean trenches where the pressure is over 800 times greater than at sea level.

children.name: Percopsiformes
Percopsidae
Percopsis
children.description: Percopsis is a small genus of freshwater fish that includes the trout-perch, unique fish that combine characteristics of both trout and perch families. These small, silvery fish have both an adipose fin like trout and spiny rays in their fins like perch. They are found in cool, clear lakes and streams across northern North America.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trout-perch are the only fish that possess both an adipose fin (found in trout and salmon) and ctenoid scales with spiny fin rays (found in perch). This unusual combination makes them easily distinguishable from all other freshwater fish.
children.funFact: Trout-perch are considered a 'living fossil' - they represent an ancient lineage that bridges the evolutionary gap between soft-rayed fish like trout and spiny-rayed fish like perch.

children.description: Trout-perches are small freshwater fish that combine characteristics of both trout and perch, representing an ancient lineage that bridges these two groups. They have elongated bodies with two dorsal fins and are typically found in cool, clear lakes and streams. These primitive fish are considered living fossils, having changed very little over millions of years.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Trout-perches are unique in having both an adipose fin like trout and spiny rays in their fins like perch, a combination not found in other fish families. They also have cycloid scales and a distinctive pattern of head pores that sets them apart from related species.
children.funFact: Trout-perches are sometimes called 'sand rollers' because they have the unusual habit of burrowing into sandy lake bottoms during the day and emerging at night to feed.

children.description: Trout-perches, pirate perches, and cavefishes are a small but fascinating group of freshwater fish that combine features of both trout-like and perch-like fish. These ancient fish have soft-rayed fins like trout but also possess some spiny fin rays like perches, making them evolutionary bridges between these major fish groups. Most species in this order are found in North American freshwaters, from clear lakes and streams to underground cave systems.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this order are unique in having both soft rays and some spiny rays in their fins, plus they possess a distinctive mix of primitive and advanced skeletal features. Unlike true perches, they have softer, more flexible fin membranes and different jaw structures.
children.funFact: The pirate perch gets its swashbuckling name from its habit of 'stealing' eggs and fry from other fish species' nests, and remarkably, its anus actually migrates forward from its tail toward its throat as it matures!

children.name: Cichliformes
Cichlidae
Oreochromis
children.description: Tilapias are freshwater fish native to Africa and the Middle East that are now found worldwide due to aquaculture and introductions. They are cichlid fish known for their adaptability to different water conditions and their importance as a food source for millions of people globally.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Tilapias can be distinguished from other cichlids by their relatively deep, compressed bodies and their ability to tolerate a wide range of water temperatures and salinity levels, making them extremely hardy fish.
children.funFact: Tilapia parents are mouth-brooders, meaning they carry their eggs and young fry safely in their mouths until the babies are large enough to survive on their own.

children.description: Cichlids are a diverse family of freshwater fish known for their complex behaviors and devoted parenting skills. These fish are characterized by having a single nostril on each side of their head and specialized teeth in their throats for processing food. Most cichlids are found in tropical regions like Africa and South America, making their presence in New England quite unusual.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Cichlids can be distinguished from other fish by their single nostril per side and their pharyngeal teeth - specialized grinding teeth located in their throat rather than their mouth. They also typically have spiny rays in their dorsal and anal fins.
children.funFact: Many cichlid species are incredibly devoted parents that carry their eggs and young in their mouths for protection, with some species continuing this 'mouthbrooding' behavior for weeks after the babies hatch.

children.description: Cichlids and their allies are a diverse group of freshwater fish known for their incredible variety of colors, shapes, and behaviors. Most members of this group are found in tropical regions like Africa and Central America, where they've evolved into thousands of different species with specialized feeding habits and complex social behaviors.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish typically have a single nostril on each side of their head (unlike most fish which have two) and possess specialized throat teeth called pharyngeal jaws for processing food. Many species also show remarkable parental care, with parents guarding and tending to their young.
children.funFact: Cichlids are famous for being one of the fastest-evolving groups of animals on Earth - in Africa's Great Lakes, hundreds of species evolved from just a few ancestors in less than a million years!

children.name: Anabantiformes
Channidae
Channa
children.description: Asian snakeheads are freshwater fish native to Asia that get their name from their elongated, snake-like heads and cylindrical bodies. They are predatory fish known for their ability to breathe air and survive out of water for extended periods. These hardy fish have become established in some North American waters after being introduced by humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, snakeheads have a specialized air-breathing organ that allows them to gulp air at the surface and survive in low-oxygen water or even on land for hours. They also have a distinctive long dorsal fin that runs most of the length of their back.
children.funFact: Snakeheads can actually "walk" on land using their fins and tail, allowing them to move between water bodies during wet weather - earning them the nickname "fishzilla" in popular media.

children.description: Snakeheads are a family of freshwater fish known for their elongated bodies and snake-like heads, which give them their distinctive name. These predatory fish are native to Africa and Asia but have been introduced to other regions, including parts of North America. They are air-breathing fish that can survive out of water for extended periods and are capable of moving short distances on land.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Snakeheads can be distinguished from other fish by their ability to breathe air using a specialized organ called a labyrinth, allowing them to survive in low-oxygen water or even briefly on land. They also have large mouths with sharp teeth and a distinctive elongated dorsal fin that runs most of the length of their body.
children.funFact: Northern snakeheads can survive up to four days out of water and can actually 'walk' on land using their fins to move between bodies of water, earning them the nickname 'walking fish.'

children.description: Anabantiformes is an order of freshwater fish that includes some remarkable air-breathing species like snakeheads, gouramis, and climbing perch. These fish are known for their ability to survive in low-oxygen water or even out of water for short periods, thanks to a special breathing organ called a labyrinth organ. Most members of this group are found in tropical Asia and Africa, with only one species now present in New England waters.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish that rely solely on gills, many members of this order have a labyrinth organ that allows them to breathe air directly from the surface. This adaptation helps them survive in stagnant, oxygen-poor waters where other fish would suffocate.
children.funFact: Some snakeheads can actually crawl across land using their fins and survive out of water for several days, allowing them to move between different bodies of water during droughts or in search of new territory.

children.name: Characiformes
Serrasalmidae
Piaractus
children.description: Piaractus is a genus of large, deep-bodied freshwater fish native to South America's river systems, particularly the Amazon and Orinoco basins. These fish are closely related to piranhas but are primarily plant-eaters, using their strong, human-like teeth to crush fruits, nuts, and vegetation that fall into the water. They are popular in the aquarium trade and have established populations in some New England waters through releases or escapes.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their piranha relatives, Piaractus species have flatter, more molar-like teeth adapted for grinding plant material rather than tearing flesh. They also grow much larger than most piranhas, with some species reaching over 2 feet in length.
children.funFact: Red-bellied pacus are sometimes called 'vegetarian piranhas' and have been known to crack open Brazil nuts with their powerful jaws!

children.description: The Serrasalmidae family includes freshwater fish known for their deep, compressed bodies and powerful jaws with sharp or flat teeth. These South American natives are famous for including both fearsome piranhas with razor-sharp teeth and their peaceful cousins like pacus and silver dollars that primarily eat plants and fruits.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this family have distinctive deep, laterally flattened bodies and strong jaw muscles, with tooth shape varying dramatically from the blade-like teeth of piranhas to the flat, molar-like teeth of plant-eating species.
children.funFact: Despite their fearsome reputation, most serrasalmids are actually peaceful fruit and seed eaters that play important roles as seed dispersers in South American rivers and forests.

children.description: Characins are a diverse order of freshwater fish that includes some of South America's most famous species like piranhas, tetras, and pacus. These fish are characterized by having teeth, a swim bladder connected to their inner ear, and typically streamlined bodies adapted for life in rivers and streams. Most characins are found in tropical waters of South America and Africa.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike many other freshwater fish, characins have a small, fleshy fin called an adipose fin located between their dorsal fin and tail. They also have specialized jaw structures with well-developed teeth that vary greatly depending on their diet.
children.funFact: While piranhas get all the attention for their fearsome reputation, most characins are actually peaceful fish, and even piranhas primarily eat fruits, seeds, and smaller fish rather than attacking large animals.

children.name: Argentiniformes
Argentinidae
Argentina
children.description: Argentina is a genus of deep-sea fish commonly known as argentines or herring smelts. These silvery fish live in cold, deep waters and are characterized by their streamlined bodies and large eyes adapted for life in the dark depths of the ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Argentina fish are distinguished from other deep-sea fish by their distinctive silvery coloration, large eyes, and elongated dorsal fin that extends far back along their body.
children.funFact: Despite their common name 'herring smelts,' argentines are not closely related to true herrings or smelts, but belong to their own unique family of deep-sea fish.

children.description: Argentines are deep-sea fish with elongated, silvery bodies that live in the cold waters of the Atlantic and Pacific oceans. They are small to medium-sized fish that typically inhabit depths between 200-2,000 meters, where they feed on small crustaceans and other marine organisms.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Argentines are distinguished by their distinctively large eyes adapted for deep-water vision and their bright silvery coloration that helps them blend with filtered sunlight from above.
children.funFact: Despite living in the deep ocean, argentines undertake daily vertical migrations, swimming hundreds of meters toward the surface at night to feed and returning to deeper waters during the day.

children.description: Marine smelts are deep-sea fish that live in the open ocean, typically found at depths of several hundred to thousands of feet below the surface. These silvery fish are part of an ancient lineage that includes some of the most primitive bony fish species alive today. They are generally small to medium-sized fish with streamlined bodies adapted for life in the deep ocean.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike their shallow-water smelt relatives, marine smelts have specialized adaptations for deep-sea life including large eyes for gathering light in dark waters and swim bladders that help them maintain buoyancy at great depths.
children.funFact: Some marine smelts have light-producing organs called photophores that create their own bioluminescent glow in the darkness of the deep ocean.

children.name: Polymixiiformes
Polymixiidae
Polymixia
children.description: Polymixia is a genus of deep-sea fish commonly known as beardfishes, named for the distinctive barbels (whisker-like projections) that hang from their chins like a beard. These ancient fish live in deep waters along continental slopes and have remained relatively unchanged for millions of years. They are small to medium-sized fish with large eyes adapted for the dim light of their deep-water habitat.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beardfishes are distinguished by their prominent chin barbels, large eyes, and primitive jaw structure that sets them apart from other deep-sea fish families. They also have a unique fin arrangement with their pelvic fins positioned unusually far forward on their body.
children.funFact: Polymixia species are considered "living fossils" - they belong to one of the most ancient lineages of modern bony fish, with fossils dating back over 100 million years to the Cretaceous period.

children.description: Beardfishes are deep-sea fish with distinctive barbels (whisker-like projections) hanging from their chins that give them their common name. These ancient fish are considered living fossils, representing one of the most primitive groups of modern bony fish still alive today.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beardfishes are distinguished by their prominent chin barbels and their primitive skeletal structure that shows characteristics of both ancient and modern fish groups.
children.funFact: Beardfishes are so ancient that they're sometimes called 'missing links' in fish evolution, with fossils dating back over 100 million years to the Cretaceous period.

children.description: Beardfishes are deep-sea fish belonging to an ancient order that was once much more diverse during prehistoric times. These moderately-sized fish live in deep ocean waters and have a distinctive appearance with large eyes adapted for low-light conditions. They represent one of the more primitive groups of modern bony fish.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Beardfishes are characterized by their pair of long, barbel-like chin whiskers (giving them their 'beard' name) and their relatively large pectoral fins. They have a unique jaw structure and fin arrangement that sets them apart from other deep-sea fish groups.
children.funFact: Beardfishes are considered 'living fossils' - their order was at its peak diversity over 100 million years ago, and today only about 10 species remain worldwide from what was once a much larger group.

children.name: Lampriformes
Trachipteridae
Trachipterus
children.description: Trachipterus is a genus of deep-sea ribbonfishes known for their extremely long, ribbon-like bodies and silvery appearance. These unusual fish live in the open ocean at moderate depths and are rarely seen near shore, making encounters with them quite special for marine biologists and fishermen alike.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Members of this genus have dramatically elongated, compressed bodies that can reach several feet in length while remaining very thin, giving them their distinctive ribbon-like appearance that sets them apart from typical fish.
children.funFact: Dealfish occasionally wash up on New England beaches after storms, creating quite a spectacle since their ribbon-like bodies can measure up to 8 feet long but only a few inches tall!

children.description: Ribbonfishes are extraordinary deep-sea fish with extremely long, ribbon-like bodies that can stretch several feet in length but remain very thin and compressed from side to side. These silvery fish live in the open ocean at moderate depths and are rarely seen at the surface, making encounters with them quite special for marine biologists and fishermen.
children.distinguishingFeatures: Unlike most fish, ribbonfishes have dramatically elongated, tape-like bodies with a bright red dorsal fin that runs along most of their length, and they often lose their tail fin as adults, giving them a distinctive tapered appearance.
children.funFact: Ribbonfishes are such fragile creatures that they often break apart when brought to the surface, which is why complete specimens are rarely seen and these mysterious fish were once thought to be sea serpents by sailors.

children.description: Lampriformes are a diverse group of deep-sea and open-ocean fishes that includes some of the most unusual-looking fish in the world. Despite their varied appearances, they all share certain skeletal features and typically have soft, scaleless or small-scaled skin. Most members of this order live in deep waters and are rarely seen by humans.
children.distinguishingFeatures: These fish are characterized by their protrusible jaws (jaws that can extend outward) and a unique arrangement of bones in their skulls. Many species have extremely elongated, ribbon-like bodies or unusual fin structures that set them apart from other fish orders.
children.funFact: The ribbonfishes in this group can grow incredibly long - some species reach lengths of over 25 feet, making them among the longest bony fish in the ocean!
